192:
## 7. Chronicle of the Buddha Revata

After the Blessed One Sumana, when his Dispensation had disappeared, humans who had a lifespan of ninety thousand years gradually decreased until reaching a lifespan of ten years. Then, they gradually increased again until reaching an incalculable (asaṅkheyya) lifespan, and once again decreased. When the lifespan reached sixty thousand years, the Teacher named Revata, the Buddha, appeared in the world. This Bodhisatta Revata, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), was reborn in the Tusita heaven, which shines with many jewels. Passing away from there, he took conception in the womb of the Chief Queen named Vipulā, who was endowed with a multitude of delightful and pleasing virtues, and whose face was as radiant as a beautiful lotus pond with eyes like blooming blue lotuses, attracting the eyes of all people. She was the consort of King Vipula, in the city of Sudhaññavatī, which was abundant with all kinds of wealth and grain, adorned with incomparable and beautiful retinues, and filled with the glory of prosperity. After ten months had passed, he was born from his mother's womb like a golden swan king descending from Mount Cittakūṭa.

At the time of the Bodhisatta's conception and birth, the miracles that occurred were just as they had been for previous Buddhas. The Bodhisatta had three palaces named Sudassana, Ratana, and Āveḷa. Thirty-three thousand maidens, headed by Sudassanā-devī, attended upon him. Surrounded by those maidens, he lived in the palace for six thousand years, enjoying sensual pleasures like a celestial youth surrounded by goddesses. When his son named Varuṇa was born to Queen Sudassanā, the Bodhisatta saw the four great omens. Wearing fine, noble garments dyed in various colors, adorned with strings of pearls, jeweled earrings, armlets, a diadem, and bracelets, decorated with highly fragrant flowers, he departed on the Great Renunciation. Like the moon surrounded by a host of stars in the night of the month of Kattikā, like Sakka surrounded by a host of devas, or like the Great Brahma Hārita surrounded by a host of Brahmas, he went forth in a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses, surrounded by a great fourfold army. He removed all his ornaments and handed them to the royal treasurer. Then, with a very sharp sword as keen as the petal of a pure, dark blue lotus grown in water, he cut off his hair together with the diadem and threw it into the sky. Sakka, the king of devas, received it with a golden casket and took it to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, where he enshrined it in a stupa made of the seven jewels on the summit of Mount Sineru.

That Great Man, having put on the saffron-dyed robes offered by a deity, became a monk. One crore of men followed him and also became monks. Surrounded by those monks...
193:
Sakka received the hair and the diadem with a golden casket, took them to the Tāvatiṃsa realm, and built a stupa made of the seven jewels on the summit of Mount Sineru.

The Great Man (the Bodhisatta) also put on the saffron-dyed robes offered by a deity and entered the monkhood. One crore of men followed his example and also became monks. Surrounded by those monks, he practiced the conduct of austerities (padhāna-cariya) for seven months. On the full moon day of Vesākha, he partook of the milk-rice with honey (madhupāyāsa) offered by the daughter of a merchant named Sādhudevī. After spending the day in a Sal grove, in the evening, he took eight handfuls of grass offered by an Ājīvaka. Walking with the gait of a noble elephant in rut, he circumambulated the Nāga-bodhi tree (Ironwood tree). He spread the grass mat fifty-three cubits wide and sat down, resolving with fourfold effort. Having defeated the host of Māra, he realized Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) and uttered the solemn utterance (udāna): "Through many a birth in saṃsāra... I have attained the destruction of craving."

Therefore, the Buddha said:
"After Sumana, the leader named Revata appeared, incomparable, peerless, matchless, the supreme Conqueror."

It is said that the Teacher Revata spent seven weeks near the Bodhi tree. Accepting the request of Brahma to preach the Dhamma, he considered, "To whom should I first preach the Dhamma?" Seeing the one crore of monks who had gone forth with him, as well as many other devas and humans who possessed the supporting conditions (upanissaya), he traveled through the air and descended at the Varuṇārāma monastery. Surrounded by them, he turned the incomparable Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka), which is profound, subtle, having three rounds, and which cannot be turned back by anyone else. He established one crore of monks in the Fruit of Arahantship. There was no limit to the number of those established in the three lower paths and fruits. Therefore, the Buddha said:

"That Revata, the Buddha, requested by Brahma, preached the Dhamma that defines the aggregates and elements, which prevents rebirth in various existences."

In that verse, "khandhadhātuvavatthānaṃ" means the analysis of the five aggregates and eighteen elements by way of discerning mind and matter (nāma-rūpa). The comprehension of material and immaterial phenomena by way of their individual characteristics (sabhāva-lakkhaṇa) and common characteristics (sāmañña-lakkhaṇa) is called the definition of aggregates and elements. Alternatively, it should be understood as defining the aggregates and elements by way of metaphors: material form (rūpa) is like a lump of foam because it cannot withstand pressure and is full of holes; feeling (vedanā) is like a bubble because it is pleasant only for a moment; perception (saññā) is like a mirage because it deceives; mental formations (saṅkhāra) are like a plantain trunk because they have no core; and consciousness (viññāṇa) is like a magic trick because it deludes; and also by way of contemplation on impermanence (aniccānupassanā), etc. In the phrase "appavattaṃ bhavābhave," "bhava" means increase or prosperity, and "abhava" means decrease or ruin. Alternatively, "bhava" is the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi) and "abhava" is the nihilist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi). Alternatively, "bhava" is a small existence and "abhava" is a great existence. Alternatively, "bhava" is the sense-sphere existence (kāma-bhava) and "abhava" refers to the fine-material and immaterial existences (rūpa-bhava and arūpa-bhava).
194:
Feeling (vedanā) should be understood as a bubble because it is pleasant for only a moment; perception (saññā) as a mirage because it deceives; formations (saṅkhāra) as a plantain trunk because they lack essence; and consciousness (viññāṇa) as a magic trick because it is deceptive. In this way, and through the power of the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) and so forth, the determination of the aggregates and elements should be understood.

In the phrase 'appavattaṃ bhavābhave', 'bhava' means increase and 'abhava' means decrease. 'Bhava' means the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi) and 'abhava' means the annihilationist view (ucchedadiṭṭhi). 'Bhava' means a small existence and 'abhava' means a great existence. 'Bhava' means the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava) and 'abhava' means the fine-material and immaterial existences (rūpa-arūpabhava). In this way, the meaning of 'bhava' and 'abhava' should be understood. It means that He [the Buddha] proclaimed the Dhamma which is the cause for the non-occurrence of those existences and non-existences.

Alternatively, it is called 'bhava' because one becomes through this; it refers to the wholesome and unwholesome kamma, etc., which are the causes for arising in the three realms of existence. Resultant existence (upapattibhava) is called 'abhava'. It means He taught the Dhamma that brings about the abandonment of desire for both types of existence and prevents their recurrence. For that Blessed One Revata, there were three realizations (abhisamaya) of the Four Noble Truths. The first realization of that Buddha surpassed the path of calculation (it was innumerable). Therefore, it was said:

'There were three realizations during His teaching of the Dhamma;
The first realization was such that it cannot be expressed by number.'

In that verse, 'tīṇi' means 'tayo' (three); it is used with a change of grammatical gender. This was the first realization.

At another time, in the city of Uttara, the most excellent of cities, there was a king named Arindama. Hearing that the Blessed One had arrived at his city, he went out to welcome the Blessed One accompanied by thirty million people. He invited the Buddha for the next day and for seven days provided a great alms-giving to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. Having made an offering of lamps extending over three gāvutas, he approached the Blessed One and sat down. Then the Blessed One taught him the Dhamma in various ways according to his disposition. On that occasion, the second realization occurred for ten billion (koṭi-sahassa) deities and humans. Therefore, it was said:

'When the Sage Revata disciplined King Arindama,
Then the second realization occurred for ten billion beings.'

## Ayaṃ dutiyo abhisamayo.
195:
Then at another time, while the Teacher Revata was dwelling in dependence on the market town of Uttara, He entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) and remained so for seven days. At that time, the people living in the market town of Uttara brought gruel, rice, food, medicine, drinks, and so forth, and after giving a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of monks, they asked: "Venerable sirs, where is the Blessed One?" Then the monks said to those people: "Friends, the Blessed One has entered the attainment of cessation."

When those seven days had passed, they saw the Blessed One, who had emerged from the attainment of cessation, shining with His incomparable Buddha-glory like the sun in the autumn season, and they asked about the benefits of the attainment of cessation. The Blessed One then explained the benefits of the attainment of cessation to them. At that time, one billion (koṭi-sata) deities and humans were established in the fruit of Arahantship. This was the third realization (abhisamaya). Therefore, it was said:

'Having emerged from seven days of seclusion, the Bull among Men,
Disciplined one billion humans and deities in the supreme fruit.'

In the city of Sudhaññavatī, at the first great recitation of the Pātimokkha, there was the first assembly of Arahants who had been ordained by the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination and who were beyond the path of calculation. In the city of Mekhala, there was the second assembly of one trillion (koṭi-sata-sahassa) Arahants who had been ordained by the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination. Now, the Blessed One Revata's chief disciple who followed the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma was named Varuṇa; he was the foremost among the wise and he became ill. At that time, to the great multitude who had come to inquire after the ill Elder Varuṇa, the Buddha taught the Dhamma illustrating the three marks of existence (tilakkhaṇa). Having ordained one trillion men as 'Ehi Bhikkhu' monks and establishing them in Arahantship, He recited the Pātimokkha in an assembly of four factors. This was the third assembly. Therefore, it was said:

'There were three assemblies of the Great Sage Revata's disciples,
Who were canker-free, stainless, well-liberated, and steadfast (tādi).

Those who gathered at the first assembly were beyond the path of calculation;
The second gathering was of one trillion Arahants.

He who was peerless in wisdom, the follower of His Wheel,
Was then ill and had reached a state of uncertainty regarding his life.'
196:
At that time, one hundred thousand Arahants approached that Chief Disciple to inquire after his illness. That was the third assembly of those monks.

In those verses, 'Cakkānuvattako' means one who turns the Wheel of Dhamma. In the phrase 'Patto jīvitasaṃsayaṃ', 'jīvitasaṃsayaṃ' means doubt regarding life. It means reaching a state of uncertainty about whether life will end or not; because the illness is so severe, one reaches doubt about life, wondering whether one will die or not. In the phrase 'Ye tadā upagatā munī', if 'munī' is long (dīgha), it refers to the monks (bhikkhūnaṃ); if 'muni' is short (rassa), it occurs above the Elder Varuṇa along with the anusvāra (niggahīta).

At that time, our Bodhisatta was a Brahmin named Atideva in the city of Rammavatī. Having reached the further shore of Brahminical lore, he saw the Revata Buddha and, after hearing His Dhamma discourse, established himself in the Three Refuges. He praised the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala) with a thousand verses and made an offering to the Blessed One with an upper robe worth a thousand pieces of currency. That Buddha also prophesied to him: "Two asankheyyas and a hundred thousand aeons from now, he will become a Buddha named Gotama." Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"At that time, I was a Brahmin named Atideva,
Having approached the Revata Buddha, I went to Him for refuge.

Having praised His virtue, concentration,
And the supreme quality of His wisdom as much as I could, I offered my upper robe.

That Buddha, Revata, the Leader of the World, also prophesied to me:
'In an immeasurable aeon, this person will become a Buddha.'

'Having exerted effort in meditation... [etc.] ...may we be in the presence of this Buddha,'" they prayed.

Thus, the eight verses should be expanded.

"Having heard His words, I gladdened my mind even more,
I undertook a superior practice to fulfill the ten perfections.

At that time, I also remembered and cultivated those Buddha-making qualities,
I shall carry out those qualities (pāramīs) that lead to the Buddhahood I have aspired for."

In those verses, 'Saraṇaṃ tassa gañchahaṃ' means I went to that Buddha for refuge.
197:
In those verses, "Saraṇaṃ tassa gañchahaṃ" means "I went to that Buddha for refuge." Here, the genitive case (chaṭṭhī) is to be understood in the sense of the accusative case (dutiyā). "Paññāguṇaṃ" refers to the perfection of wisdom. "Anuttamaṃ" means noble (praiseworthy). There is also a reading "Paññāvimuttiguṇamuttamaṃ," and its meaning is quite clear. "Thomayitvā" means having praised (having extolled). "Yathāthāmaṃ" means according to one's own strength. "Uttarīyaṃ" refers to the upper robe. "Adāsahaṃ" means "I gave." "Buddhadhammaṃ" refers to the qualities that make one a Buddha, meaning the pāramī qualities. "Saritvā" means having repeatedly reflected. "Anubrūhayiṃ" means I greatly increased. "Āharissāmi" means I shall bring/carry out. "Taṃ dhammaṃ" refers to those qualities of Buddhahood. "Yaṃ mayhaṃ abhipatthitaṃ" means "I shall carry out those Buddha-making qualities for the Buddhahood I have aspired for."

The city of that Revata Blessed One was named Sudhaññavatī. His father was a King named Vipula, and His mother was a Queen named Vipulā. Varuṇa and Brahmadēva were the two Chief Disciples (aggasāvaka). He had an attendant named Sambhava. Bhaddā and Subhaddā were the two Chief Female Disciples (aggasāvikā). The Nāga (Ironwood) tree was His Bodhi tree. His body was eighty cubits in height, and His lifespan was sixty thousand years. He had a Chief Queen named Sudassanā and a son named Varuṇa. He renounced the world in a chariot drawn by noble horses.

"At that time, the supreme net of radiance emitted from the body of that Revata Buddha,
Always spread for one yojana, both by day and by night."

"That Victorious One, Revata, of great exertion,
Who had compassion for all beings, made a resolution:
'May all my relics be dispersed.'"

"That Revata Buddha, in the Mahānāga garden of the great city of Sudhaññavatī,
Passed away into Parinibbāna, receiving the offerings of humans and devas."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:

## "The city was named Sudhaññavatī; King Vipula was the father.
## The mother of the Great Sage Revata was the Queen named Vipulā.

## Varuṇa and Brahmadēva were the Chief Disciples.
## The attendant of the Great Sage Revata was named Sambhava."
198:
The Elders Bhaddā and Subhaddā were the Chief Female Disciples. That peerless Buddha attained Enlightenment at the foot of a Nāga (Ironwood) tree.

The lay disciples Paduma and Kuñjara were the chief male attendants. The lay disciples Sirimā and Yasavatī were the chief female attendants.

In height, that Buddha rose eighty cubits. Like the raised banner of Indra, He illuminated all directions.

The supreme garland of radiance arose from the body of that Buddha. Whether by day or by night, that radiance spread for one yojana all around.

At that time, the lifespan was sixty thousand years. Remaining for that long, He saved many beings.

Having demonstrated the power of the Buddhas and proclaiming the Deathless Nibbāna to the world, He attained Parinibbāna without clinging, like a fire that goes out when its fuel is exhausted.

That body which was like a gem existed, and that peerless Dhamma existed. All of them have disappeared. Are not all conditioned things (saṅkhāra) indeed empty?

In those verses, "Obhāseti" means to make manifest or to illuminate. "Uggato" means high or raised. "Pabhāmālā" means the circle of radiance. "Yathaggi" means like a fire. "Upādānasaṅkhayā" means due to the exhaustion of fuel. "So ca kāyo ratananibho" means that the body of the Blessed One had a color like gold. There is also a reading "Tañca kāyaṃ ratananibhaṃ"; although it is stated with a change of gender (liṅgavipallāsa), the meaning is the same. The meaning of the remaining verses is clear in every respect.

## The Commentary on the Chronicle of Revata Buddha is finished.
## The Fifth Chronicle of the Buddhas is finished.
199:
## 8. Sobhitabuddhavamsa-vaṇṇanā (The Chronicle of the Buddha Sobhita)

After the dispensation of the Buddha Revata had disappeared, in the period following that dispensation, the Bodhisatta named Sobhita fulfilled all the perfections for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons. He was reborn in the Tusita heaven and remained there for the full lifespan. Being requested by the deities and Brahmas, he passed away from the Tusita heaven and took conception in the womb of the Chief Queen named Sudhammā, in the palace of King Sudhamma in the city of Sudhamma. When ten months had passed, the Bodhisatta was born in the Sudhamma Garden from his mother's womb, like the full moon emerging from a dense, pure, and radiant cloud. The miracles that occurred at the time of his conception and birth were exactly as previously described.

The Bodhisatta Sobhita lived as a householder for ten thousand years, ruling the palace. When his son named Sīhakumāra was born to the Chief Queen Makhila, who was the foremost among thirty-seven thousand dancing women, he saw the four signs. Being struck by religious urgency (saṃvega), he renounced the world while still in the palace. In that very palace, he developed Anāpānasati-samādhi, attained the four jhānas, and practiced austerities (dukkharacariya) for seven days. Then, after partaking of the most delicious honey-rice-milk (madhupāyāsa) offered by Queen Makhila, he made a mental resolution for his Great Departure: "May this decorated and prepared palace travel through the sky while the great multitude watches, and descend to the earth, placing the Bodhi tree in its center. And may these women, without being told, come out of the palace of their own accord while I am sitting at the foot of the Bodhi tree."

Simultaneously with his thought, the palace rose from the residence of King Sudhamma and ascended into the sky, which was dark blue like collyrium. The surface of the palace, adorned with uniformly hanging and highly fragrant garlands of flowers, shone as if decorating the entire vault of heaven. It was radiant like the sun with its beautiful mass of rays resembling a stream of liquid gold, and like the moon of the autumn season. The various and wonderful networks of hanging bells, when stirred by the wind, produced a sound that was sweet, pleasing, and delightful, like a five-fold musical ensemble played by a highly skilled person.

With a sweet sound that could be heard from afar, capturing the ears of all beings, the palace traveled through the sky near the tops of the great forest trees, neither too low nor too high above the people standing and conversing at houses, junctions, and crossroads. It moved through the sky as if enticing the eyes of the people with the brilliance of various jewel-like colors on the noble branches and twigs, and as if proclaiming the power of past merits. While thus traveling through the sky, the dancing women sang and lamented with the sweet sound of the noble five-fold musical ensemble. The four-fold army of the Bodhisatta also followed, surrounding the palace through the sky as if on solid ground, shining with the radiance of the garments and ornaments worn on their bodies, appearing extremely beautiful and delightful like the army of Sakka, the king of devas, adorned with various fragrant floral ornaments.
200:
The Bodhisatta Sobhita ascended into the sky, as if enticing [the world], drawing the eyes of the people with the radiant and brilliant colors of various jewels atop the branches of the great forest trees, and as if proclaiming the power of his past merits. As he traveled through the sky, the dancing women sang and lamented with the sweet sounds of the noble five-fold musical instruments. His four-fold army, adorned with the brilliance of their ornaments and garments, and beautified by various delightful and fragrant flowers and robes, appeared as magnificent as the army of the King of Gods (Sakka). They followed, surrounding the palace through the sky as if it were on the ground.

Then, the palace descended and settled on the ground, centering itself upon a Nāga tree (Ironwood) that was eighty-eight cubits in height, with a straight, broad, and round trunk, equally adorned with flowers, young leaves, and buds. Without being told by anyone, the dancing women descended from that palace and departed. That Great Being (Mahāpurisa) named Sobhita, though adorned with many virtues and surrounded by a great multitude, attained the three-fold knowledge (tevijjā) during the three watches of the night. The host of Māra's army retreated by the power of nature (dhammatā) just as they had come. The palace remained right there near the Bodhi tree. Having attained Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi), the Buddha Sobhita uttered the solemn utterance (udāna): 'Through many births in saṃsāra... I have reached the destruction of craving.' He spent the seven weeks (satta-sattāha) near the Bodhi tree. Having accepted the request of the Brahmā to preach the Dhamma, he looked with his Buddha-eye, wondering, 'To whom should I first preach the Dhamma?' He saw his younger half-brothers, Prince Asama and Prince Sunetta. Thinking, 'These two princes are endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya) and are capable of penetrating the profound and subtle Dhamma; I shall preach the Dhamma to them,' he traveled through the air and descended in Sudhamma Park. He had the park keeper summon the two princes and, surrounded by them and their retinue, he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka) in the midst of the great multitude. Therefore, it was said:

## After Revata, there was a leader named Sobhita, who was concentrated and of peaceful mind, peerless and without a rival.

After Revata, the leader named Sobhita appeared in the world. That Buddha was steadfast, possessed a peaceful mind, was without equal, and had no rival.

## That Conqueror (Jina) turned back his mind in his own home; having attained complete Enlightenment, he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma.

That victorious Buddha turned back his mind while still in his own palace. Having reached the full Supreme Enlightenment, he preached the Dhammacakka discourse.

## From Avīci below to the peak of existence (Bhavagga) above, within this interval, there was a single assembly during the preaching of the Dhamma.

When he preached the Dhamma, from Avīci below to the peak of existence above, and from the peak of existence above to Avīci below, within this range, there arose a single vast assembly.

In those verses, 'saka-gehamhi' means in his own home, specifically on the inner floor of the palace. 'Mānasam vinivattayi' means he turned back his mind. It signifies that while staying in his own home, within seven days, he turned his mind away from the state of a worldling (puthujjana) and attained Buddhahood. 'Heṭṭhā' means from Avīci below. 'Bhavaggā' means from the Akaniṭṭha realm. 'Tāya parisāya' means in the midst of that assembly. 'Gaṇanāya na vattabbo' means it has surpassed the path of counting. 'Paṭhamābhisamayo' means the first penetration of the Four Noble Truths. It means a vast assembly that could not be counted had arisen. There is also a reading 'paṭhame abhisamiṃsuyevā'. The meaning of that reading is that those beings who first...
201:
“The Buddha set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma in that assembly. At that time, there was the first realization of the Four Noble Truths, which cannot be expressed in numbers.”

In those verses, ‘saka-gehamhi’ means in his own home, specifically on the inner floor of the palace. ‘Mānasam vinivattayi’ means he turned back his mind; it means that while staying in his own home, within seven days, he turned his mind away from the state of a worldling and reached the state of a Buddha. ‘Heṭṭhā’ means from Avīci below. ‘Bhavaggā’ means from the Akaniṭṭha realm. ‘Tāya parisāya’ means in the midst of that assembly. ‘Gaṇanāya na vattabbo’ means they have surpassed the path of counting. ‘Paṭhamābhisamayo’ means the first penetration and realization of the Four Noble Truths. ‘Ahū’ means there was an assembly that cannot be described by counting. There is also a reading ‘paṭhame abhisamiṃsuyeva’; the meaning of that reading is that at the time of the first preaching of the Dhamma, those multitudes of beings who penetrated and realized the Four Noble Truths cannot be expressed by counting or calculation.

Thereafter, at another time, at the gate of Sudassana city, at the foot of a marvelous Trumpet-flower tree (Cittapāṭali), having performed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya) of water and fire, etc., he sat on the Paṇḍukambala emerald stone seat at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, in a mansion made of new gold and rubies, and preached the Abhidhamma. At the conclusion of the teaching, there was the realization of the Dhamma by nine hundred billion (90,000 crores) of devas and brahmās. This was the second realization. Therefore, it was said:

“Thereafter, while he was preaching further in the assembly of the gods, there was the second realization by nine hundred billion (90,000 crores) [of beings].”

Thereafter, at another time, in the city of Sudassana, a prince named Jayasena had a great monastery built measuring one league (yojana). He planted a garden-monastery densely filled with trees such as Asoka, Punnāga, Sāla, Champaka, Nāga, Punnāga, Vakula, fragrant Mango, Jackfruit, Pitala, Great Sāla, Thinkhwe, fragrant Sahakāra mango, and Karavīra (Rhododendron), and offered it to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. Having given the discourse of appreciation for the gift and praising the offering, the Blessed One Sobhita preached the Dhamma. At that time, there was the realization of the Dhamma by a hundred thousand crores (one trillion) of beings. This was the third realization. Therefore, it was said:

“Again, a kshatriya prince named Jayasena, having planted a garden-monastery, then offered it to the Buddha.

At that time, the Buddha possessed of the five eyes, praising the gift of that prince, preached the Dhamma. At that time, there was the third realization by ten billion (1,000 crores) of gods and men.”
202:
“The Blessed One, possessed of the five eyes, praising the prince's gift, preached the Dhamma; at that time, the third realization of the Four Noble Truths (abhisamaya) occurred for ten thousand million (one thousand crores) devas and humans,” so it was said.

Again, a king named Uggata had a monastery named Sunanda built in the city of Sunanda and offered it to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. At that offering, there was an assembly of one hundred crore Arahants who had been ordained by the ‘Ehi Bhikkhu’ formula; in the midst of those Arahants, the Blessed One Sobhita recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha. This was the first assembly.

Again, in the city of Mekhalā, the group named Dhammagaṇa had a great monastery, a noble park named Dhammagaṇārāma, built and offered it to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, along with all the requisites. At that gathering, in an assembly of ninety crore Arahants who had been ordained as ‘Ehi Bhikkhus’, he recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha. This was the second assembly.

When the Blessed One, after spending the rains retreat in the city of Dasasatanayana (Tāvatiṃsa Heaven), descended on the day of the Great Pavāraṇā at the end of the retreat, surrounded by a host of noble devas, he performed the Pavāraṇā in a fourfold assembly together with eighty crore Arahants. This was the third assembly. Therefore, it was said:

“For the Blessed One Sobhita, the Great Seeker,
There were three assemblies of Arahants,
Who were free from the taints, pure,
Of peaceful minds, and possessed of the quality of equanimity (tādi).

That king named Uggata gave a gift to the Supreme Man,
At that offering, one hundred crore Arahants assembled together.

Again, a group of citizens gave a gift to the Supreme Man,
At that time, the second assembly of ninety crore Arahants took place.

When the Victor, after residing in the celestial realm, descended,
At that time, the third assembly of eighty crore Arahants took place.”

At that time, our Bodhisatta was a Brahmin named Sujāta, well-born on both sides, in the city of Rammavatī. Having heard the Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One Sobhita, he established himself in the Three Refuges and gave a great gift for the three months of the rains retreat to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. That Blessed One Sobhita also prophesied of him: “In the future, he will become a Buddha named Gotama.” Therefore, it was said:
203:
## At that time, I was a Brahmin named Sujāta; then, I satisfied the Buddha together with his disciples with food and drink.

## That Blessed One Sobhita, the Leader of the World, also prophesied of me: “In an incalculable eon from this one, this person will become a Buddha named Gotama.”

## Having exerted effort in meditation... may we be in the presence of this [Blessed One Gotama] (thus they prayed).

## Having heard the words of that Blessed One, with a mind full of joy and spiritual urgency (saṃvega), I made a supreme effort to attain that very goal of Buddhahood.

In those verses, “tamevattham-anuppattiyā” means for the sake of attaining that state of Buddhahood. Furthermore, having heard the words of the Blessed One Sobhita, “In the future, this person will become a Buddha named Gotama,” and reflecting that “The words of the Buddhas are never false,” it means for the sake of attaining Buddhahood. “Uggaṃ” means supreme or intense. “Dhitiṃ” means energy or effort (viriya). “Akāsahaṃ” means “I made” (akāsiṃ ahaṃ).

The royal city of that Blessed One Sobhita was named Sudhamma. His father was a king named Sudhamma, and his mother was a queen named Sudhammā. The Elders Asama and Sunetta were the two chief disciples. The attendant was named Anoma. The female Elders Nakulā and Sujātā were the two chief female disciples. The Nāga tree (Ironwood) was his Bodhi tree. The height of his body was fifty-eight cubits. His lifespan was ninety thousand years. His chief queen was named Makhilā, and his son was named Sīhakumāra. There were thirty-seven thousand dancers. He lived in the household for nine thousand years. He renounced the world by means of a palace. King Jayasena was his attendant. It is said that he resided in the Setārāma monastery. Therefore, it was said:

## The city of the Blessed One Sobhita was named Sudhamma; his father was the king named Sudhamma; his mother was the mother named Sudhammā.

## The Elders Asama and Sunetta were the chief disciples. The attendant of the Blessed One Sobhita was named Anoma.

## The female Elders Nakulā and Sujātā were the chief female disciples. When that Buddha attained enlightenment, he did so at the foot of a Nāga tree.
204:
The Great Sage, fifty-eight cubits in height, illuminated all directions like the rising sun. 

Just as a great forest in full bloom is perfumed with various scents, so too was the word of that Blessed One perfumed with the fragrance of virtue. 

Just as the ocean is never satiated by sight, so too was the word of that Blessed One never satiated by hearing. 

At that time, the lifespan was ninety thousand years; remaining for that long, he saved many beings. 

Having given advice (ovāda) and instruction (anusiṭṭhi) to the remaining people, he, together with his disciples, attained parinibbāna like a fire that goes out after burning brightly. 

That incomparable Buddha and those disciples who had attained power have all disappeared; are not all conditioned things indeed empty? 

In those verses, 'Sataramsīva' means illuminating all directions like the sun. 'Pavanaṃ' refers to a great forest. 'Dhūpitaṃ' means perfumed or scented with fragrance. 'Atappiyo' means one who causes insatiability or produces a lack of satiety. 'Tāvade' means at that time, for that much duration. 'Tāresi' means he saved. 'Ovādaṃ' refers to advice given once. 'Anusiṭṭhiṃ' refers to repeated instruction. 'Sesake jane' refers to the remaining people who have not yet realized the Four Noble Truths; here, the locative case (sattami) is used in the sense of possession (chatti). 'Hutāsanova tāpetvā' means having shone like a fire. Alternatively, this is the correct reading: the Blessed One attained parinibbāna due to the exhaustion of clinging. In the remaining verses, all meanings are clear. 

## The Explanation of the Chronicle of Sobhita Buddha is finished. 

## The Sixth Chronicle of Buddha is finished.
205:
## 9. The Explanation of the Chronicle of Anomadassī Buddha 

After the parinibbāna of Sobhita Buddha, there was a period of one asankheyya devoid of the appearance of a Buddha. In one kappa within that past asankheyya, three Buddhas appeared: Anomadassī, Paduma, and Nārada. Among those three, the Blessed One Anomadassī, having fulfilled the perfections for sixteen asankheyyas and one hundred thousand kappas, was reborn in the Tusita heaven. Being requested by the devas and brahmas, he passed away from there and took conception in the womb of Chief Queen Yasodharā, who possessed beautiful breasts, in the palace of King Yasavā in the royal city named Candavatī. 

While Prince Anomadassī was in the womb of Queen Yasodharā, due to the power of his merit, his radiance spread and remained over an area of eighty cubits. That radiance could not be overcome even by the light of the moon and sun. After ten months, the Queen gave birth to the Bodhisatta in the Sucandana garden. The miracles were just as described previously. 

On the day of the naming ceremony, when they were choosing a name for the prince, because seven kinds of gems fell from the sky at the time of his birth, and because he was the cause for the appearance of superior (anoma) gems, they named him 'Anomadassī'. Prince Anomadassī reached maturity in due course and, enjoying divine sensual pleasures, lived in the palace for ten thousand years. He had three palaces: Siri, Upasiri, and Sirivaḍḍha. Twenty-three thousand attendants, headed by Queen Sirimā, served him. When a son named Upavāṇa was born to Queen Sirimā, Prince Anomadassī saw the four signs and, departing for the Great Renunciation by palanquin, became an ascetic. Thirty million people followed him into the homeless life. 

Surrounded by those thirty million monks, the Great Man practiced asceticism for ten months. Then, on the full moon day of Visākha, having wandered for alms in the brahmin village of Anupama and consumed the honey-milk rice offered by the daughter of the merchant Anupama, he spent the day-rest in a Sal grove. Taking eight handfuls of grass offered by an Ajivaka named Anoma, he circumambulated the Ajjuna Bodhi tree to the right. Spreading the grass mat thirty-eight cubits wide and resolving with fourfold energy, he sat in the cross-legged posture. Having defeated Mara and his army, he attained the three knowledges during the three watches of the night and uttered the solemn utterance: 'Through many a birth in saṃsāra... I have attained the destruction of craving.' Therefore, the Blessed One said: 

1. After Sobhita Buddha, there appeared the Buddha named Anomadassī, supreme among two-legged beings, gods, and men, possessing incomparable followers and fame, of great power, and invincible. 

2. That Blessed One, having cut all fetters and destroyed the three worlds of existence, [showed] the path of the Magga which leads to Nibbāna, where there is no returning...
206:
After the Buddha Sobhita, there appeared the Fully Enlightened One, the supreme among bipeds, named Anomadassī, of immeasurable fame, powerful, and invincible.

Having cut all bonds and fetters, and having destroyed the three realms of existence, He taught the Path leading to Nibbāna—the state of no-return—to gods and humans.

He was unshakeable like the ocean, unapproachable like a mountain, infinite like space, and beautiful like a Sāla tree in full bloom.

Beings were satisfied just by the sight of that Buddha. Upon hearing His spoken words of Dhamma, they reached the deathless Nibbāna.

In those verses, ‘Anomadassī’ means one with incomparable vision or immeasurable vision. ‘Amitayaso’ means one with an immeasurable retinue or immeasurable fame. ‘Tejassī’ means being endowed with the power of virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā). ‘Duratikkamo’ means difficult to overcome; it signifies that no other deity, Māra, or anyone else is able to surpass Him. ‘So chetvā bandhanaṃ sabbaṃ’ means having cut all ten kinds of fetters (saṃyojana). ‘Viddhaṃsetvā tayo bhave’ means having destroyed the kamma that leads to the three realms of existence through the knowledge that brings the end of kamma, thereby rendering it non-existent. ‘Anivattigamanaṃ maggaṃ’: Nibbāna is called ‘anivatti’ because it is the opposite of returning to the process of existence; the path by which one goes to that Nibbāna is called ‘anivattigamana’. It means He taught the Noble Eightfold Path that leads to Nibbāna. There is also a reading ‘deseti’, which has the same meaning. ‘Devamānuse’ means to gods and humans; it should be understood that the accusative case is used here in the sense of the genitive.

‘Asaṅkhobho’ means unshakeable, because He cannot be disturbed or moved. Just as the ocean, which is eighty-four thousand leagues deep and the abode of many thousands of beings, is unshakeable, so too is He unshakeable. ‘Ākāsova ananto’ means just as space has no end or limit, and is immeasurable and boundless, so too the Blessed One is infinite, immeasurable, and boundless in terms of Buddha-qualities. ‘So’ refers to that Blessed One. ‘Sālarājāva phullito’ means He shines like a Sāla tree in full bloom because His body is adorned with all the major and minor marks of a great man. ‘Dassanenapi taṃ buddhaṃ’ means even by the sight of that Buddha. In such instances, those learned in grammar also employ the genitive case. ‘Tositā’ means fully satisfied and delighted. ‘Byāharantaṃ’ refers to the voice that is spoken; it should be noted that the accusative case is used in the sense of the genitive. ‘Amataṃ’ refers to Nibbāna. ‘Pāpuṇanti’ means they reach or they realize. Those beings who hear the sound of the Buddha’s Dhamma teaching reach Nibbāna.

Furthermore, after the Buddha Anomadassī had spent the seven weeks (49 days) at the foot of the Bodhi tree and was requested by the Great Brahmā to teach the Dhamma, He surveyed the world with His Buddha-eye. He saw three crores of people who had gone forth with Him and were endowed with the supporting conditions (upanissaya) to attain the Path and Fruit. He then reflected, “Where are they living now?”
207:
The accusative case is used in the sense of the genitive. ‘Amata’ means Nibbāna. ‘Pāpuṇanti’ means they obtain, realize, or reach. It means that those who hear the sound of the Buddha's Dhamma teaching reach Nibbāna.

After the Blessed One had spent the seven weeks (49 days) at the foot of the Bodhi tree, being requested by the Great Brahmā to teach the Dhamma, He surveyed the world with His Buddha-eye and saw three crores of people who had gone forth with Him and were endowed with the strong supporting conditions (upanissaya) for attaining the Path and Fruit. Reflecting on where they were currently residing, He saw them living in the Sudassana Grove in the city of Subhavatī. He then traveled through the air and descended in the Sudassana Grove. Surrounded by them, He turned the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka) in the midst of the assembly of gods and humans. At that time, the first realization of the Four Noble Truths (paṭhamābhisamaya) occurred for one hundred crores of beings. Therefore, the Buddha said:

“At that time, His realization of the Dhamma was prosperous and widespread; one hundred crores of beings realized the Dhamma during the first teaching.”

In that verse, ‘phīto’ means having reached prosperity because of the great number of people involved. ‘Koṭisatāni’ means a hundred crores. There is also a reading ‘koṭisatayo’, which also means one hundred crores.

Thereafter, on another occasion, at the gate of the city of Osadhī, at the foot of an Asana tree, He performed the Twin Miracle (yamaka-pāṭihāriya). Then, in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, which is difficult for the Asuras to overcome, He sat upon the Paṇḍukambala emerald stone and caused the rain of the Abhidhamma to fall for the three months of the rainy season. At that time, eighty crores of deities realized the Truths. Therefore, the Buddha said:

“Thereafter, at the second realization, while raining down the rain of Dhamma, eighty crores realized the Truths during the second teaching.”

In that verse, ‘vassante’ means while the great cloud of the Buddha was raining. ‘Dhamma-vuṭṭhiyo’ means the raindrops of the Dhamma discourse.

Thereafter, on another occasion, during the teaching of the Maṅgala Pañhā Niddesa, seventy-eight crores of beings realized the Truths. That was the third realization (tatiyābhisamaya). Therefore, the Buddha said:
208:
“Afterwards, while raining (the Dhamma) and satisfying (beings), there was the third realization (abhisamaya) of seventy-eight crores of beings,” thus He said.

In that verse, ‘vassante’ means raining the stream of water which is the Dhamma discourse. ‘Tappayante’ means satisfying beings with the rain of the nectar of Dhamma; it means the Blessed One brings about satisfaction.

For the Blessed One Anomadassī, there were also three assemblies of disciples. Among them, while preaching the Dhamma to King Isidatta in the city of Soreyya, He recited the Pātimokkha in the midst of eight hundred thousand Arahants who had gone forth through the ‘Ehi Bhikkhu’ ordination upon gaining faith. This was the first assembly. While preaching the Dhamma to the king named Sundarindhara in the city of Rādhavatī, He recited the Pātimokkha in the midst of seven hundred thousand Arahants who had gone forth through the ‘Ehi Bhikkhu’ ordination. This was the second assembly. Again, in the city of Soreyya itself, He recited the Pātimokkha in the midst of six hundred thousand Arahants who had gone forth through the ‘Ehi Bhikkhu’ ordination along with King Soreyya. This was the third assembly. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“For that Blessed One, the Great Seer (Mahesī), 
There were three assemblies 
Of Arahants who had attained the power of direct knowledge (abhiññā), 
And who had blossomed through liberation (vimutti).

At that time, there was an assembly 
Of eight hundred thousand Arahants, 
Who had abandoned intoxication and delusion, 
Who were of peaceful mind and were steadfast (tādi).

There was a second gathering 
Of seven hundred thousand Arahants, 
Who were stainless, without blemishes, 
Who were tranquil and steadfast.

There was a third gathering 
Of six hundred thousand Arahants, 
Who had attained the power of direct knowledge, 
Who were cooled and were practitioners of austerity.”

In those verses, ‘tassāpi ca mahesino’ means for that Great Seer, the Blessed One Anomadassī. There is also a variant reading ‘tassāpi dvipaduttamo,’ which means for that Blessed One who is supreme among two-footed beings (humans and gods). The grammatical characteristic should be taken from the grammar texts. ‘Abhiññābalappattānaṃ’ means those who have reached the power of the direct knowledges; it means those who have attained stability in the direct knowledges by way of rapid reflection due to practiced mastery (vasībhāva). ‘Pupphitānaṃ’ means those who have reached great beauty through full blossoming. ‘Vimuttiyā’ means (blossomed) through the liberation of the fruition of Arahantship.
209:
In the word “anangaṇānaṃ,” this word “angaṇa” is found in some Pali texts to mean defilements. As He said: “Among those three, what are the three blemishes (angaṇa)? Greed is a blemish, hatred is a blemish, delusion is a blemish” (Vibh. 924). It is also said: “Friends, ‘angaṇa’ is a designation for the evil, unwholesome states of desire” (M. Ni. 1.60). In some Pali texts, it is found to mean some kind of impurity. As He said: “He strives for the abandoning of that dust or blemish” (M. Ni. 1.184). In some Pali texts, it is found to mean a certain area of ground, such as “the courtyard of a shrine (cetiyaṅgaṇa), the courtyard of a Bodhi tree (bodhiyaṅgaṇa), or a royal courtyard (rājaṅgaṇa).” In this context, however, it should be understood as defilements. Therefore, it means those without defilements (M. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.57).

“Virajānaṃ” is also a synonym for that same “anangaṇānaṃ.” “Tapassīnaṃ” refers to the Arahants called ‘tapassī’ because they possess the practice (tapo) known as the Noble Path which exhausts the defilements; it means Arahants (khīṇāsava).

At that time, our Bodhisatta was a Yakkha general of great psychic power and majesty, the lord of many hundreds of thousands of crores of Yakkhas. Having heard that “a Buddha has arisen in the world,” he came and created a pavilion made of the seven jewels, most beautiful to behold and resembling the disc of the moon, and there for seven days he gave a great gift to the Sangha headed by the Buddha. Then, at the time of the appreciation of the meal, the Blessed One prophesied: “In the future, after the passing of one incalculable period (asaṅkheyya) and a hundred thousand aeons (kappa), he will become a Buddha named Gotama.” Regarding that matter, He said:

12. “At that time, I was a Yakkha of great psychic power, a ruler who held sway over many crores of Yakkhas.

13. Then also, having approached that Excellent Buddha, the Great Seer, I satisfied the World Leader and His Sangha with food and drink.

14. That Sage of pure vision also prophesied to me: ‘In an immeasurable aeon from now, this person will become a Buddha.’

15. Having exerted effort in meditation... may we be in the presence of this Buddha.

16. Hearing the prophecy of that Blessed One, with a joyful and stirred mind, I undertook further practices to fulfill the ten perfections (pāramī).”
211:
In those verses, "pabhā niddhāvatī" means that radiance emitted from the body of that Blessed Anomadassī. The radiance of his body constantly spread and remained over an area of twelve yojanas. "Yugāni tāni" refers to the pairs such as the chief disciples. "Sabbaṃ tamantarahitaṃ" means that all the various things mentioned have entered the path of impermanence and perished. There is also a variant reading "nanu rittakameva saṅkhārā." Its meaning is: "Are not all formations indeed empty and void?" The letter "ma" is a sandhi consonant. In the remaining verses, the meaning is clear everywhere.

In the presence of this Blessed Anomadassī, these two chief disciples, Sāriputta and Mahāmoggallāna, made their aspiration for the status of chief disciples. Although the story of these elders should be told here, I have not extracted and presented it for fear of the book becoming too extensive.

## The Commentary on the Chronicle of Anomadassī Buddha is finished.
## The Seventh Chronicle of the Buddhas is finished.
## 10. Commentary on the Chronicle of Paduma Buddha

After the time of the Blessed Anomadassī, the lifespan of humans gradually decreased from one hundred thousand years to ten years, then gradually increased again to an incalculable (asaṅkhyeyya) age, and then decreased again. When the lifespan reached one hundred thousand years, the Teacher named Paduma appeared in the world. He also fulfilled the perfections, was reborn in the Tusita heaven, and after passing away from there, took conception in the womb of Queen Asamā, who was peerless in beauty and other qualities, in the palace of King Asama in the city of Campā.

After ten months had passed, he emerged from his mother's womb in the Campaka garden. When the prince was born, a rain of lotuses (paduma) fell from the sky throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, as far as the ocean. Therefore, on the naming day, the fortune-tellers and relatives gave him the name "Prince Mahāpaduma." Prince Mahāpaduma lived in the household life for ten thousand years. There were three palaces named Nanduttara, Vasuttara, and Yasuttara. Thirty-three thousand women, headed by Queen Uttarā, attended upon him.
212:
Then, when the Bodhisatta’s son, Prince Ramma, was born to the Chief Queen named Uttarā, he saw the four signs and departed on the Great Renunciation in a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses. Following the Bodhisatta as he left to ordain, one crore of men also went forth. Surrounded by those monks, the Bodhisatta practiced asceticism (dukkara-cariyā) for eight months. On the full moon day of Visākha, in the city of Dhanyavatī, he partook of the honey-milk rice (madhupāyāsa) offered by the daughter of the merchant Sudhanya, named Dhanyavatī. After spending the day in the Mahāsāla grove, in the evening, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by the Ājīvaka named Titthaka and approached the Mahāsoṇa (Trumpet flower) Bodhi tree. Having spread a grass mat thirty-eight cubits wide and sitting in a cross-legged posture, he resolved with fourfold energy (caturanga-vīriya). He defeated the forces of Māra and, in the three watches of the night, realized the three knowledges (vijjā).

He then uttered the solemn utterance (udāna): “Through many a birth in saṃsāra... I have reached the end of craving” (Dhammapada 153-154). He spent seven weeks (satta-sattāha) near the Bodhi tree itself. Accepting the request of the Great Brahmā, he surveyed the individuals who were suitable vessels for the Dhamma and saw the crore of monks who had ordained along with him. At that very moment, he traveled through the air and descended at the Dhanañjaya Garden near the city of Dhanyavatī. Surrounded by those monks, he turned the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakkappavattana) in their midst. At that time, there was the realization of the Four Noble Truths (abhisamaya) by one hundred crores of beings. Therefore, it was said:

“After Anomadassī, the Fully Enlightened One, the Supreme among bipeds, named Paduma by name, unrivaled and without peer, appeared.

His virtue (sīla) was unrivaled, his concentration (samādhi) was infinite, his noble knowledge (ñāṇa) was immeasurable, and his liberation (vimutti) was beyond compare.

At the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma by that Buddha of incomparable power, who dispels the great darkness, there were three realizations (abhisamaya).”

In those verses, ‘asamaṃ sīlaṃ’ means virtue that is unlike the virtue of others, meaning it is supreme and excellent. ‘Samādhipi anantako’ means his concentration is also immeasurable and beyond measure; its infinite nature is to be understood in such instances as the miracle of revealing the worlds (loka-vivaraṇa) and the twin miracle (yamaka-pāṭihāriya). ‘Ñāṇavaraṃ’ refers to the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) or the uncommon knowledges (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa). ‘Vimuttipi’ refers to the Blessed One’s liberation of the fruit of Arahatship (arahatta-phala-vimutti). ‘Anūpamā’ means it is devoid of any comparison or simile. ‘Atulatejassa’ means the power of incomparable knowledge. There is also a reading ‘atulañāṇatejā’. Of that, ‘tayo...’
213:
—is to be understood as connected with the subsequent word 'abhisamayā'. 'Mahātamapavāhanā' means the destroyer of great darkness, the destroyer of the darkness of delusion (moha) which is ignorance (avijjā). Then, at another time, the Blessed One Paduma caused his younger brothers, Prince Sāla and Prince Upasāla, together with their retinues, to go forth at a gathering of relatives. While teaching them the Dhamma, he caused ninety crores of beings to drink the nectar of the Dhamma. When he taught the Dhamma to the Elder Ramma, there was the third realization (abhisamaya) of the Four Noble Truths by eighty crores of beings. Therefore, it is said in the Pali:

"At the first realization, the Buddha awakened one hundred crores; at the second realization, the Wise One awakened ninety crores.

"And when the Buddha Paduma exhorted his own son, then occurred the third realization of eighty crores."

When the King named Subhāvitatta went forth through the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination together with a retinue of one hundred thousand crores in the presence of the Buddha Paduma, whose face was like a lotus, the Blessed One recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha in that assembly. That assembly was the first assembly. Then, at another time, the Great Paduma, the Bull among Sages, who was like a noble bull, entered the rainy season retreat (vassa) depending on the city of Usabhavatī. The people living in the city, desiring to see the Blessed One, approached him. The Blessed One taught them the Dhamma. There, many people, having hearts full of faith, went forth. Then the Ten-Powered One performed the 'Visuddhi Pavāraṇā' (the pure invitation) together with those monks and another three hundred thousand monks who were pure Arahants. That was the second assembly. Those who did not go forth there, having heard the discourse on the benefits of the Kathina, offered the Kathina robes which bestow the five benefits for five months starting from the first day after the full moon of Tazaungmon (Kattika). Then the monks, having requested the Elder Sāla, who was the General of the Dhamma, the Chief Disciple, and one of broad wisdom, to spread the Kathina, offered the Kathina robe to that Elder. While the Kathina robe was being prepared for the Elder, the monks assisted in the sewing. The Fully Enlightened One Paduma himself threaded the needles and gave them. When the robe was finished, the Blessed One set out on a journey together with the three hundred thousand monks.
214:
Then, on another occasion, the Blessed One—who possessed the valiant gait of a lion king and was like a lion among men—entered the rains retreat in a forest that was similar to the Gosiṅga Sāla forest. This forest had branches and twigs bending under the weight of extremely fragrant flowers and fruits, was adorned with stainless red and white lotuses, and was surrounded by clouds carrying cool and sweet water. It was a place where various wild animals such as deer, yaks (camarī), lions, tigers, elephants, horses, gayals, and buffaloes roamed. It was frequented by swarms of young female bees whose hearts were captivated by the fragrant scents of flowers, and it resounded with the sweet, melodious songs of female cuckoos delighted by the taste of fruits. It was an exceedingly delightful, secluded, and uninhabited place, suitable for spiritual practice (yoga).

Seeing the Blessed One, the King of Dhamma, who possessed the ten powers and shone with the glory of a Buddha while staying in that forest with his retinue, people were inspired by hearing the Dhamma and were ordained through the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination. At that time, surrounded by two hundred thousand monks, he performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony. That was the third assembly. Referring to this, it was said:

'For the Great Sage (Mahā-isi) Paduma Buddha, there were three assemblies of disciples. The first assembly was a gathering of one hundred thousand crores of monks.'
'When the time for spreading the Kathina robe arrived and the Kathina cloth appeared, the monks sewed the robe for the General of the Dhamma (Elder Sāla).'
'At that time, three hundred thousand stainless monks, who were endowed with the six higher powers, possessed great psychic power, and were unconquerable by enemies, assembled.'
'Furthermore, that best of men (the Buddha) entered the rains retreat in a forest. At that time, there was an assembly of two hundred thousand monks.'

In those verses, 'kathiṇatthārasamaye' means at the time of spreading the Kathina robe. 'Dhammasenāpatitthāya' means for the sake of the General of the Dhamma, Elder Sāla. 'Aparājitā' means those who are not conquered by enemies; here, it should be noted that the case-ending is elided. 'So' refers to that Buddha Mahāpaduma. 'Pavane' means in the great forest. 'Vāsaṃ' means the rains retreat (vassāvāsa). 'Upāgamī' means he approached (arrived). 'Dvinnāṃ satasahassināṃ' means of two hundred thousand monks. If there were a reading 'Tadā āsi samāgamo', it would also be good.

At that time, while the Blessed One was staying in that forest grove, our Bodhisatta, having become a lion, saw the Buddha sitting after entering the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) for seven days...
215:
(Our Bodhisatta, the lion king,) with a heart full of faith, performed the circumambulation (padakkhiṇā). With joy and happiness arisen, he roared the lion's roar three times. For seven days, without letting go of the joy that had the Buddha as its object, he did not depart to search for food, but stood attending [the Buddha], having sacrificed his life, sustained only by the bliss of joy.

Then the Teacher, the lion among men, emerged from the attainment of cessation after those seven days. Looking at the lion, he thought, 'May this lion king also have faith in the Saṅgha of monks; let the Saṅgha come.' Instantly, many tens of millions of monks arrived. The lion also clarified his mind with faith in the Saṅgha.

Then the Teacher, looking into the lion's mind, pronounced the prophecy: 'In the future, he will become a Buddha named Gotama.' Therefore, it was said:

'At that time, I was a lion, the king of beasts. I saw the Victor (Jina) in the forest, cultivating seclusion (attainment).'
'Having bowed my head at his feet and performed the circumambulation, I roared three times and attended to the Victor for seven days.'
'The Tathāgata, having emerged from the noble attainment after seven days, thought with his mind and brought together tens of millions of monks.'
'At that time also, that Great Hero (Mahāvīra) prophesied in the midst of them: "In an immeasurable aeon from now, this person will become a Buddha."
'Having exerted effort in the practice... may we be in the presence of this Buddha.'
'Hearing his words, I further clarified my mind with faith. I undertook a superior practice for the fulfillment of the ten perfections (pāramī).'

In those verses, 'pavivekamanubrūhantaṃ' means entering the attainment of cessation. 'Padakkhiṇaṃ' means having performed the circumambulation three times. 'Abhināditvā' means having roared the lion's roar three times. 'Upaṭṭhahaṃ' means I attended to him; or this very reading 'upaṭṭhahaṃ' is the original. 'Varasamāpattiyā' means having emerged from the attainment of cessation. 'Manasā cintayitvānā' means having thought only with the mind, "Let all monks come here." 'Samānayi' means he brought together well.

The capital city of that Blessed One, Paduma, was named Campaka. His father was the king named Asama, and his mother was also named Asamā...
216:
The Elders Sāla and Upasāla were the pair of chief disciples (aggasāvaka). There was an attendant (upaṭṭhāka) named Varuṇa. The Therīs Rādhā and Surādhā were the pair of chief female disciples (aggasāvikā). The great Mahāsoṇa tree was the Bodhi tree. His body was fifty-eight cubits in height. The lifespan was one hundred thousand years. There was a chief queen named Uttarā, peerless in qualities such as beauty. There was a son named Rammakumāra, who was exceedingly delightful. Therefore, it was said:

“The city was named Campaka, the king was named Asama. The mother of the Great Sage Paduma was named Asamā.

“Sāla and Upasāla were the chief disciples. The attendant of the Great Sage Paduma was named Varuṇa.

“Rādhā and Surādhā were the chief female disciples. The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called the Mahāsoṇa.

“The Great Sage was exceedingly tall, fifty-eight cubits in height. His radiance spread peerlessly in all directions.

“The light of the moon, the light of the sun, the light of jewels, the light of fire and gems—all these were eclipsed upon reaching the supreme radiance of the Conqueror.

“At that time, the lifespan was one hundred thousand years. Remaining for that long, the Buddha saved many beings.

“Having awakened those beings whose minds were fully mature without exception, and having exhorted the remaining ones, he attained Nibbāna together with his disciples.

“Like a snake shedding its old skin, or like a tree shedding its old leaves, he relinquished all conditioned things and was extinguished like a great fire.”

In those verses, 'ratanaggimaṇippabhā' means the light of jewels, the light of fire, and the light of gems (or emeralds). 'Hatā' means overcome or eclipsed. 'Jinapabhuttamam' means reaching the supreme radiance of the Conqueror's body and being eclipsed. 'Paripakkāmānase' refers to the beings to be taught (veneyya) whose faculties are mature. 'Vaddhapattam' means an old leaf. 'Pādapo vā' means like a tree. 'Sabbasaṅkhāre' means...
217:
(Having abandoned) all formations, both internal and external. There is also a reading "hitvā sabbasaṅkhāraṃ," and that is indeed the meaning. Just as a fire is extinguished when its fuel is exhausted, the Sugata has attained peace without any clinging. The remaining words in these verses are clear, following the method previously mentioned below.

## The Commentary on the Chronicle of Paduma Buddha is finished.

## The Eighth Chronicle of the Buddhas is finished.

## 11. Commentary on the Chronicle of Nārada Buddha

After Paduma Buddha attained Parinibbāna and his dispensation had disappeared, the lifespan of humans, which was then one hundred thousand years, gradually decreased until it reached ten years. Increasing again to an incalculable (asaṅkheyya) lifespan and then decreasing once more, when it reached ninety thousand years, the Teacher named Nārada, the best of beings, who possessed the ten powers, was endowed with the three knowledges (tevijja), was confident in the four intrepidities (vesārajja), and was proficient in the essence of liberation (vimutti), appeared in the world. 

Having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons (kappas), he was reborn in the Tusita heaven. Passing away from there, he took conception in the womb of the peerless Chief Queen named Anomā, in the palace of King Sudeva, also known as Vāsudeva, who had conquered through his own effort, in the city of Dhanyavatī. After ten months had passed, he was born in the Dhanañjaya Garden. On the day of his naming ceremony, ornaments suitable for the use of people throughout the entire Jambudīpa fell from the sky and from wish-fulfilling trees (kappa-rukkhas). Therefore, because he gave ornaments worthy of men (narānaṃ arahāni), they named him "Nārada."

Prince Nārada lived in the palace for nine thousand years. He had three palaces suitable for the three seasons: Vijita, Vijitāvī, and Vijitābhirāma. For Prince Nārada, the princess named Vijitasenā, who was endowed with noble birth, virtue, conduct, and beauty, and who was pleasing to his mind and very auspicious, was made the Chief Queen. With her at the head, there were one hundred and twenty thousand court ladies. When the son named Nanduttara, who brought joy to the people of the world, was born to Queen Vijitasenā, he (the Bodhisatta) saw the four omens. Surrounded by a great fourfold army, wearing thin, noble garments dyed with various dyes, with ruby earrings adorned with strings of pearls, and noble ornaments...
218:
Wearing noble garments of various dyes and thin texture, adorned with ruby earrings set with pearls, wearing noble armlets, a crown, and bracelets, and decorated with highly fragrant perfumes and flowers, he went to the park on foot. Having removed all his jeweled ornaments and handed them to the treasurer, he himself cut his crown along with his hair, which was beautiful and ornate with jewels, using a very sharp sword like the petal of a dark blue lotus, and threw it into the sky. Sakka, the king of gods, received that hair in a golden casket, took it to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, and built a seven-jeweled stupa three yojanas high on the summit of Mount Sineru.

The Great Being donned the saffron-dyed robes offered by the devas and brahmas and ordained in that very park. One hundred thousand men followed him in ordination. The Great Being practiced austerities for seven days in that park. On the full moon day of Vesākha, he partook of the thick milk-rice offered by Chief Queen Vijitasenā and spent the day in that park. Taking the eight handfuls of grass offered by the park keeper named Sudassana, he circumambulated the Mahāsoṇa Bodhi tree. He spread the grass over an area of fifty-eight cubits and sat down. Having conquered the army of Māra, he attained the three knowledges during the three watches of the night and realized Omniscience. He then uttered the solemn utterance: 'Through many a birth in saṃsāra... I have reached the destruction of craving.' After spending the seven weeks (satta-sattāha) and accepting the request of the Brahma, he turned the Wheel of Dhamma in the Dhanañjaya Park, surrounded by the one hundred thousand monks who had ordained with him. At that time, one hundred billion beings attained the Dhamma. Thus, the Blessed One said:

After the Buddha Paduma, the Buddha named Nārada appeared, the best of bipeds, peerless and without equal.

That Bodhisatta, the eldest and beloved son of a Universal Monarch, approached the park adorned with flowers and ornaments.

In that park, there was a famous, beautiful, great, and pure Mahāsoṇa tree. Having reached it, he sat beneath that Mahāsoṇa tree.

There, the noble, infinite, and diamond-like insight arose. With that insight, he investigated formations, both in their arising and passing away.
219:
Beneath that tree, he completely destroyed all defilements. He reached the complete Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi) and the fourteen knowledges of a Buddha. Having reached Enlightenment, he turned the Wheel of Dhamma, and the first realization of the Four Noble Truths occurred for one hundred billion beings.

In those verses, 'Cakkavattissa' means 'of the Universal Monarch'. 'Jeṭṭho' refers to the eldest son. 'Dayita-oraso' means the beloved son of the breast, the son who was cherished and fondled in the bosom. 'Āmukkamālābharaṇo' means adorned with pearls, armlets, bracelets, crown, earrings, and garlands. 'Uyyānaṃ' refers to going to the park named Dhanañjaya outside the city.

In that park, there was a tree named 'Rattasoṇa'. That tree was ninety cubits high, with a symmetrical and round trunk, full of various branches, and provided good shade with its thick, dark green leaves. Because it was inhabited by deities, flocks of birds did not frequent it. It was like a beauty mark of the earth, acting as the king of trees, and was extremely pleasant to behold. Every branch was decorated with red flowers, serving as a medicine that cooled the eyes of gods and humans. 'Yasavipulo' means of great fame, well-known in the world, famous in every direction due to its own excellence. Some read it as 'Tatthāsi rukkho vipulo'. 'Braha' means great, similar to the Pāricchattaka tree of the gods. 'Tam-ajjhappatvā' means having reached and approached that Rattasoṇa tree. 'Heṭṭhato' means beneath that tree.

'Ñāṇavaruppajji' means the noble insight (vipassanā) arose. 'Anantaṃ' means incomparable and immeasurable. 'Vajirūpamaṃ' is a name for insight such as the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), which is sharp like a diamond. 'Tena vicini saṅkhာရေ' means he investigated formations such as form (rūpa) with that insight. 'Ukkujjam-avakkujjakaṃ' means repeatedly investigating the arising and passing away of formations. Therefore, having contemplated Dependent Origination, emerged from the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna), and focused on the five aggregates, he saw the fifty characteristics through the lens of arising and passing away. Developing insight up to the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa), he attained all the qualities of a Buddha through the sequence of the Noble Path.
220:
## 
'Tattha' means in the Indian Trumpet tree (soṇa). 'Sabbakilesāni' refers to all defilements, expressed with a change of gender (into the neuter). Some teachers recite it as 'tattha sabbakilesehi'. 'Asesaṃ' means without remainder. 'Abhivāhayi' means he destroyed all defilements through the limit of the Path and the limit of defilements; the meaning is that he brought them to ruin. 'Bodhi' refers to the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship. 'Buddhañāṇe ca cuddasa' refers to the fourteen Buddha-knowledges. What are these Buddha-knowledges? They are the eight knowledges of the Paths and Fruits and the six uncommon knowledges (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa); thus, these fourteen are called the Buddha-knowledges. The word 'ca' (and) has the sense of conjunction; by that word 'ca', it is meant that he attained other qualities such as the four knowledges of analytical insight (paṭisambhidā), the four knowledges of intrepidity (vesārajja), the knowledges of the four types of birth, the knowledges of the five destinations, the ten powers (dasabala), and all the Buddha's attributes.

Having thus attained Buddhahood and accepting the request of the Brahmā, he turned the Wheel of Dhamma in the Dhanañjaya Park in the presence of one hundred thousand monks who had gone forth together with him. At that time, there was the first realization of the Four Noble Truths (pathama-abhisamaya) by one hundred thousand crores of beings. At that time, it is said, a Naga king named Doṇa lived on the banks of the Ganges in the city of Mahādoṇa. He was of great psychic power and majesty, respected, revered, honored, and worshipped by the people. If the people living in the districts within his domain did not perform sacrificial offerings to him, he would destroy their lands by causing drought, excessive rain, or rain of gravel.

Then, the Blessed One Nārada, the Seer of the Shore, seeing the strong supporting condition (upanissaya) for many beings to attain the Paths and Fruits through the taming of the Naga king Doṇa, went to the dwelling place of that Naga king surrounded by a large community of monks. When the people saw the Blessed One, they said, 'O Blessed One, a Naga king of fierce poison, great heat, great psychic power, and great majesty lives here. That Naga king will harm you; do not go there.' The Blessed One went as if not hearing their words. Having arrived, he sat upon the very fragrant carpet of flowers prepared for the honoring of that Naga king. The great multitude of people gathered, thinking, 'We shall witness the battle between the Sage-King Nārada and the Naga king Doṇa.'

Then the Naga king, seeing the Sage-Naga (the Buddha) sitting thus, unable to endure the slight, manifested his body and emitted smoke. The Possessor of the Ten Powers (Dasabala) also emitted smoke. Again, the Naga king emitted flames, and the Sage-King also emitted flames. Then, that Naga king, becoming greatly exhausted by the smoke and flames emerging from the Blessed One's body and unable to endure the suffering, thought, 'I will kill him with the force of my poison,' and released his poison. By the force of that poison, the entire great island of Jambudīpa...
221:
The Naga king Doṇa emitted flames. The Sage-King Nārada also emitted flames in return. Then, that Naga king, having a body greatly exhausted by the smoke and flames emerging from the Blessed One's body and unable to endure the suffering, thought, 'I will kill this monk with the force of my poison,' and released his poison. Although the entire island of Jambudīpa could have been destroyed by the force of that poison, it was not able to move even a single hair on the Blessed One's body.

Then, that Naga king, looking to see 'What is the state of this monk?', saw the Blessed One shining with the six-colored Buddha-rays like the sun or the moon in the autumn season, with the beauty of a serene countenance. Thinking, 'Oh! This monk is indeed of great psychic power; I have offended him, not knowing my own strength,' he sought a refuge and approached the Blessed One for refuge.

Then, the Sage-King Nārada, having tamed the Naga king, performed the Twin Miracle (yamaka-pāṭihāriya) for the purpose of inspiring faith in the hearts of the great multitude gathered there. At that time, ninety thousand crores of beings were established in Arahatship. That was the second realization of the Truths (abhisamaya). Regarding this, it was said:

'While the Great Sage was taming the Naga king Mahādoṇa,
He then performed a miracle, showing it to the world of devas.
At that time, during that proclamation of the Dhamma to devas and humans,
Ninety thousand crores crossed over all doubts.'

In that verse, 'pāṭiheraṃ tadākāsi' means he performed the Twin Miracle. This is the reading. There is also a reading 'tadā devamanussā vā'. There, 'devamanussānaṃ' is the nominative case (paccatta) in the sense of possession (sāmi-attha). Therefore, it means ninety thousand crores of devas and humans. 'Tariṃsu' means they crossed over.

When he exhorted his own son, Prince Nanduttara, there was the third realization of the Truths by eighty thousand crores. Regarding this, it was said:

'At the time when the Great Hero exhorted his own son,
There was the third realization of the Truths by eighty thousand crores.'

In the city of Thullakoṭṭhita, two Brahmin friends named Bhaddasāla and Vijitamitta, while searching for the Lake of the Deathless, saw the most confident Nārada, the Perfectly Enlightened One, sitting in the midst of the assembly. They, upon the Blessed One's body...
222:
Seeing the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and reaching the conclusion that "This Lord is the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) who has removed the veil [of ignorance] in the world," they developed faith in the Blessed One and, along with their retinues, went forth as monks in the presence of the Blessed One. When they had gone forth and attained Arahatship, the Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha in the midst of one hundred thousand kotis of Arahats; that was the first assembly. Regarding this, it was said in the Buddhavamsa:

"There were three assemblies of the Great Sage Nārada; the first gathering was of one hundred thousand kotis of Arahats."

At the time when Nārada the Fully Enlightened One, in the assembly of His relatives, preached the Buddhavamsa (Chronicle of Buddhas) starting from His initial aspiration, there was the second assembly of ninety thousand kotis of monks. Regarding this, it was said:

"When the Buddha proclaimed the Buddha-qualities along with the origin story, ninety thousand kotis of stainless ones (Arahats) then assembled."

In that verse, 'vimalā' means those who are free from the stains of defilements, meaning Arahats.

Furthermore, at the time when the Naga King named Verocana, who was inspired by the taming of the Naga King Mahādoṇa, created a pavilion made of the seven kinds of jewels measuring three gāvutas in the Ganges River, he invited the Blessed One with His retinue to reside there. He then invited the people of the countryside to witness his supreme alms-giving and gathered Naga dancers and musicians wearing various costumes and ornaments. With great honor and offerings, he gave a great donation (Mahādāna) to the Blessed One and His retinue.

At the conclusion of the meal, the Blessed One gave a discourse of appreciation (Anumodanā) as if making the great Ganges flow downwards. At that time, having heard the Dhamma of appreciation for the meal, eight million monks who had gone forth through the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination assembled, and the Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha in their midst; that was the third assembly. Regarding this, it was said:

"When the Naga Verocana gave a gift to the Teacher, then assembled eighty hundred thousand (eight million) sons of the Conqueror."

In that verse, 'asītisatasahassiyo' means eighty times one hundred thousand (eight million).
223:
At that time, our Bodhisatta, having gone forth as an ascetic, created a hermitage at the foot of the Himalayas and lived there, having mastered the five supernormal powers (abhiññā) and the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti). Then, out of compassion for him, the Blessed One Nārada, surrounded by eighty crore Arahants, ten individuals who stood in the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi), and a thousand lay followers, went to that hermitage. Upon seeing the Blessed One, the ascetic, with a joyful heart, created a hermitage for the Blessed One and his followers to stay in. Having praised the qualities of the Teacher throughout the night and listened to the Dhamma talk of the Blessed One, he went to Uttarakuru the next day, brought food from there, and gave a great gift to the Buddha and his followers. Having given this great gift for seven days, he brought priceless red sandalwood (lohitacandana) from the Himalayas and worshipped the Blessed One with that red sandalwood. Then the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala), surrounded by gods and men, preached the Dhamma and prophesied: "In the future, he will be a Buddha named Gotama." Therefore, it was said:

13. "At that time, I was a matted-hair ascetic (jaṭila) of fierce austerity; I was one who could travel through the air and was a master of the five supernormal powers."

14. "Then I also satisfied the Peerless One (Asamasama), who is equal to the Buddhas of the past, along with the Sangha and the followers, with food and drink, and worshipped him with sandalwood."

15. "Then Nārada, the Leader of the World, also prophesied to me: 'In an incalculable aeon from now, he will be a Buddha in the world.'"

16. "Having exerted effort in meditation... (the people prayed:) 'May we be in the presence of this Buddha.'"

17. "Hearing his words, I made my heart even more joyful and undertook the fierce practice to fulfill the ten perfections (pāramīs)."

In those verses, "Tadāpāhaṃ" means "Tadā api ahaṃ" (At that time also I). "Asamasama" means the Buddhas of the past are called "Asama" because they are peerless; being equal to those peerless ones, he is called "Asamasama." Alternatively, the wicked are called "Visama," and the virtuous are called "Sama"; among them, because he is equal to the peerless Buddhas, it should be said "Asamasamasama," but it should be understood that one "Sama" was elided to say "Asamasama." The meaning is one who is equal to the peerless ones. "Saparizzanaṃ" means together with the group of lay followers. There is also a variant reading: "Sopī maṃ tadā naramarūnaṃ, majjhe byākāsi cakkhumā."
224:
