The text has a clear meaning. Having gladdened the mind even more, and having satisfied the heart by making it even more joyful, he undertook a severe vow. There is also a reading: "He undertook a more severe vow to fulfill the ten perfections."

The city of that Blessed One, Nārada, was named Dhanyavatī. His father was the khattiya named Sudeva, and his mother was named Anomā. The Elders Bhaddasāla and Jitamitta were the two chief disciples. He had an attendant named Vāseṭṭha. The female Elders Uttarā and Phagguṇī were the two chief female disciples. His Bodhi tree was the Great Soṇa (Trumpet flower tree). His body was eighty-eight cubits in height. The radiance of his body constantly spread for one league (yojana). His lifespan was ninety thousand years. His chief queen was named Vijitasenā, and his son was named Prince Nanduttara. There were three palaces: Vijita, Vijitāvī, and Vijitābhirāma. He lived in the household for nine thousand years. He departed for the Great Renunciation on foot. Therefore, it was said:

"The city was named Dhanyavatī; the khattiya was named Sudeva.
The mother of the Great Sage Nārada was named Anomā.

Bhaddasāla and Jitamitta were the chief disciples.
The attendant of the Great Sage Nārada was named Vāseṭṭha.

Uttarā and Phagguṇī were the chief female disciples.
The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called the Mahāsoṇa.

The Great Sage was eighty-eight cubits high.
Resembling a golden archway, he shone in the ten thousand world systems.

The fathom-wide radiance from his body streamed in every direction.
Continuously, day and night, it always spread for one league.

At that time, the people within one league around him
Did not light torches or lamps, being suffused by the Buddha's rays.

At that time, the lifespan was ninety thousand years.
Remaining for that long, he saved many beings."
225:
“Just as the sky is beautifully adorned with stars, so too his Dispensation shone with Arahants.

To cross the stream of Saṃsāra, that Bull among Men, having built the firm bridge of Dhamma for the remaining practitioners, attained Nibbāna.

That Buddha, the peerless one, and those Arahants of immeasurable power, have all vanished. Are not all conditioned things indeed empty?”

In those verses, ‘kañcanagghiya-saṅkāso’ means having a beautiful form resembling a golden archway adorned with various jewels. ‘Dasasahassī virocati’ means that the ten thousand world systems shine and glow with the radiance of that Blessed One. To clarify this meaning, the Blessed One said: “The fathom-wide radiance from his body streamed in every direction.” Here, ‘byāmappabhā kāyā’ means it is just like the fathom-wide radiance of our Blessed One.

In the phrase ‘na keci’, the word ‘na’ has the sense of negation and should be understood in connection with the word ‘ujjālenti’ (they light). ‘Ukkā’ means torches. Some people did not light torches or lamps. Why? Because they were illuminated by the radiance of the Buddha’s body. ‘Buddharaṃsīhi’ means by the rays of the Buddha. ‘Otthaṭā’ means overspread or suffused.

‘Uḷūhi’ means by the stars. Just as the sky is beautifully adorned with stars, so too his Dispensation was beautifully adorned with Arahants. ‘Saṃsārasotaṃ taraṇāya’ means for the purpose of crossing the ocean of Saṃsāra. ‘Sesake paṭipannake’ refers to the remaining seven types of noble practitioners (sekha) along with the virtuous worldlings (kalyāṇa-puthujjana), excluding the Arahants. ‘Dhamma-setu’ means the bridge of the Path (magga). It means that having laid down the bridge of the Path to enable the remaining persons to cross over from Saṃsāra, and having completed all that was to be done, he attained Parinibbāna. The remaining terms have been explained previously and are entirely clear.

## The Commentary on the Chronicle of the Buddha Nārada is finished.

## The Ninth Chronicle of the Buddhas is finished.
226:
## 12. Padumuttarabuddhavaṃsavaṇṇanā

The dispensation of the Buddha Nārada lasted for ninety thousand years and then disappeared. That aeon (kappa) also perished. After that, for an incalculable period (asaṅkhyeyya) of aeons, no Buddhas appeared in the world. It was a time empty of Buddhas, devoid of the light of a Buddha. Then, after those incalculable aeons had passed, in an aeon one hundred thousand aeons prior to this present Bhadda-kappa, the Buddha named Padumuttara appeared in the world—he who had conquered the five Māras, who had laid down the burden of the aggregates, who was as firm as the core of Mount Meru, who possessed the essence of strength, who was the essence of all beings, and who had transcended the entire world.

That Bodhisatta Padumuttara, having fulfilled the perfections, was reborn in the Tusita heaven. Passing away from there, he took conception in the womb of Queen Sujātā, who was born of a distinguished lineage and was the chief consort of King Ānanda, the bringer of joy to all people in the city of Haṃsavatī. Queen Sujātā, being protected by deities, gave birth to Prince Padumuttara in the Haṃsavatī garden after ten months had passed. At the time of his conception and birth, extraordinary miracles occurred as described previously.

It is said that at the time of his birth, a rain of lotuses (paduma) fell. Therefore, on the day of his naming ceremony, his relatives named him "Prince Padumuttara." The prince lived in the palace for ten thousand years. He had three palaces suitable for the three seasons, named Naravāhana, Yasavāhana, and Vasavatti. One hundred and twenty thousand ladies, headed by Queen Vasudattā, attended to him. When Prince Padumuttara’s son, Prince Uttara, who was endowed with all excellent qualities, was born to Queen Vasudattā, the prince saw the four signs and thought, "I shall depart on the Great Renunciation."

As soon as he thought this, the palace named Vasavatti rose into the air like a potter's wheel and, traveling through the sky like a celestial mansion or the full moon, descended to the earth, centering itself around the Bodhi tree, just like the palace mentioned in the commentary on the Chronicle of the Buddha Sobhita.

The Great Man descended from that palace, donned the saffron-dyed robes which are the banner of Arahantship and were offered by deities, and ordained as a monk right there. The palace then rose back and stood in its original place. Except for the women, all the followers who had accompanied the Bodhisatta ordained as monks. The Great Man, together with those monks, practiced the noble exertion (dukkara-cariyā) for seven days, and on the full moon day of Vesākha...
227:
The Great Man, having partaken of the honey-rice milk offered by the daughter of the merchant Rucānanda in the market town of Ujjenī, spent the day in a Sal grove. In the evening, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by the Ājīvaka Sumitta and approached the Salala Bodhi tree. After circumambulating it, he spread a carpet of grass thirty-eight cubits wide, sat down in a cross-legged posture, and resolved upon the fourfold effort. Having defeated the King Māra and his host, in the first watch of the night, he recollected his past lives (pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa). In the second watch, he purified the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). In the third watch, he contemplated the factors of Dependent Origination (paṭicca-samuppāda). Emerging from the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing, he applied his mind to the five aggregates and, by way of rise and fall, perceived the fifty characteristics equally. Developing insight up to the change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa), he realized all the qualities of a Buddha through the Noble Path. He then uttered the solemn utterance common to all Buddhas: "Through many a birth in saṃsāra... I have reached the destruction of craving." At that time, a great rain of lotuses fell, as if decorating the entire ten-thousandfold world system. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"After Nārada, there appeared the Buddha, the Supreme among two-legged beings,
the Conqueror named Padumuttara, unshakeable and like the ocean."

"That was a Maṇḍa-kappa in which the Buddha was born;
a multitude of people with abundant merit were born in that aeon."

In those verses, "sāgarūpamo" means having a depth like the ocean. In the phrase "maṇḍakappo vါ သော အာသိ", an aeon in which two Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas appear is called a Maṇḍa-kappa. Indeed, there are two kinds of aeons: the empty aeon (suñña-kappa) and the non-empty aeon (asuñña-kappa). Among them, in an empty aeon, Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Cakkavatti kings do not appear. Therefore, because it is empty of virtuous persons, it is called an "empty aeon."

The non-empty aeon is of five types: Sāra-kappa, Maṇḍa-kappa, Vara-kappa, Sāramaṇḍa-kappa, and Bhadda-kappa. Among them, in an aeon otherwise devoid of the essence of virtue, the appearance of a single Perfectly Enlightened Buddha who produces and generates the essence of virtue causes it to be called a "Sāra-kappa." An aeon in which two Leaders of the World appear is called a "Maṇḍa-kappa." An aeon in which three Buddhas appear—where the first Buddha gives a prophecy to the second, and the second to the third—is one where people, with joyful hearts, take the noble boon by the power of their own aspirations. Therefore, it is called a "Vara-kappa." But in which aeon...
228:
In a world cycle (kappa) where four Buddhas arise, that cycle is called 'Sāramanda-kappa' because it is more distinguished and more substantial than previous cycles. In a cycle where five Buddhas arise, that cycle is called 'Bhadda-kappa'. That Bhadda-kappa is extremely rare. In that cycle, beings generally have abundant good happiness. Mostly, those with three roots (tihetuka) can achieve the destruction of defilements, those with two roots (duhetuka) go to good destinations (sugati), and those with no roots (ahetuka) acquire roots. Therefore, that cycle is called 'Bhadda-kappa'. With reference to this, it was said: 'The non-empty cycle (asuñña-kappa) is of five kinds,' and so on. The ancient teachers also said this:

'One Buddha in a Sāra-kappa, two Jinas in a Manda-kappa,
Three Buddhas in a Vara-kappa, four Buddhas in a Sāramanda-kappa,
Five Buddhas in a Bhadda-kappa; there are no more Jinas than that.'

In the cycle where Padumuttara, the One of Ten Powers, arose, although it was a Sāra-kappa, it was called 'Manda-kappa' because it was similar to a Manda-kappa in its abundance of qualities. Alternatively, the word 'vā' should be understood in the sense of a metaphor. 'Ussannakusalā' means those who have accumulated merit. 'Janatā' means a multitude of people.

Padumuttara, the Exalted One, the best among men, after spending seven days on the Bodhi-throne (Bodhi-pallaṅka), thought, 'I shall place my foot on the ground,' and extended his right foot. Then, breaking through the earth, land-grown and water-grown lotuses arose, pure and delicate with pollen-filled centers, and broad petals free from water-born impurities. It is said that their leading petals were ninety cubits, the pollen was thirty cubits, and the pericarp was twelve cubits; in each lotus, there was pollen equivalent to the measure of nine pots. The Teacher was fifty-eight cubits in height. The span between his two arms was eighteen cubits, his forehead was five cubits, and his hands and feet were eleven cubits. When the Teacher stepped with his eleven-cubit foot upon the twelve-cubit pericarp, pollen equivalent to nine pots rose up, ascended to the height of his fifty-eight-cubit body, and covered him as if he were painted with powders of red arsenic (manosilā). Because of this, the Teacher became known in the world as 'Padumuttara' (Superior to the Lotus), so say the Saṃyutta-bhāṇaka elders.

Then, the Exalted One Padumuttara, the most excellent in all the world, having accepted the request of the Brahmā, was surveying beings who were fit vessels for the Dhamma teaching. He saw in the city of Mithilā two princes, Devala and Sujāta, who possessed the supporting conditions (upanissaya) for attaining the Paths and Fruits. At that very moment, he traveled through the air, descended into the Mithilā garden, and sent the gardener to call the two princes. Those princes thought, 'Prince Padumuttara, the son of our paternal aunt, has gone forth, attained Perfect Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi), and has arrived at our city of Mithilā. Let us now go to see that Exalted One Padumuttara.' Accompanied by their retinue, they approached the Exalted One and sat down surrounding him. Then, the Exalted One Padumuttara, surrounded by those monks...
229:
The Exalted One saw in the city of Mithilā two princes, Devala and Sujāta, who possessed the supporting conditions (upanissaya) for attaining the Paths and Fruits. At that very moment, he traveled through the air, descended into the Mithilā garden, and had the gardener call both princes. Those princes thought, "Prince Padumuttara, the son of our paternal aunt, has gone forth, attained Perfect Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi), and has arrived at our city. Let us now approach to pay homage to that Exalted One." Accompanied by their retinue, they approached the Exalted One Padumuttara and sat down surrounding him. Then the One of Ten Powers, surrounded by them, shining brilliantly like the full moon surrounded by a host of stars, turned the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka) there in the Mithilā garden. At that time, the first realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) of one hundred thousand crores of beings took place. Therefore, it was said:

"In the first Dhamma teaching of the Exalted One Padumuttara,
There was the realization of the Dhamma by one hundred thousand crores."

Later, at another time, at the gathering of the hermit Sarada, while preaching the Dhamma by making the multitude feel the heat of hell's torment, he made the assembly of seven million beings drink the nectar of Dhamma. That was the second realization of the Dhamma. Therefore, it was said:

"After that, while it was raining and satisfying the living beings,
There was the second realization by three million seven hundred thousand."

Again, when King Ānanda, together with twenty thousand men and twenty ministers, arrived in the presence of Padumuttara the Perfectly Enlightened One in the city of Mithilā, the Exalted One Padumuttara ordained them all with the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination. Surrounded by those monks, he went to the capital city of Haṃsāvatī, performing a service for his father, and resided there. In that city of Haṃsāvatī, just as our Exalted One walked on the jeweled walkway in the sky in the city of Kapilavatthu and taught the Buddhavaṃsa, he also walked on a walkway in the sky and taught the Buddhavaṃsa. At that time, the third realization of the Dhamma by five million beings took place. Therefore, it was said:

"At the time when the Great Hero approached Ānanda,
Having gone to his father's presence, he beat the drum of the Deathless.
While the drum of the Deathless was being beaten and the rain of Dhamma was falling,
There was the third realization by five million."
230:
In that (verse), 'Ānandaṃ upasaṅkami' is said with reference to King Ānanda, the father. 'Āhani' means he struck. 'Āhate' means while striking. 'Amatabherimhi' means on the drum of the Deathless; here, the change of gender (using masculine/neuter instead of feminine) should be noted. There is also a reading 'Āsevite', which means practiced or cultivated. 'Vassante dhammavuṭṭhiyā' means while raining down the great rain of Dhamma. Now, wishing to show the means of achieving the realization of the Truths (abhisamaya):

7. The Buddha, who admonishes all beings,
Who makes known the Four Noble Truths,
Who delivers (beings from saṃsāra),
And is skilled in teaching,
Has delivered a great multitude of beings.

In that verse, 'Ovādako' means one who admonishes by praising the benefits of undertaking the refuges, virtue (sīla), and dhutaṅga practices. 'Viññāpako' means one who makes known the Four Noble Truths, hence Viññāpako or Bodhaka (one who awakens others). 'Tārako' means one who delivers beings from the four floods (ogha).

On another occasion, the Teacher, in the city of Mithilā, in the Mithilā Park, in the midst of a group of one hundred thousand crores of monks, on the full moon day of Māgha, with a face like the full moon, recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha; that was the first assembly. Therefore, it is said:

"There were three assemblies of the disciples of the Teacher Padumuttara;
The first gathering was of one hundred thousand crores (of Arahants)."

Again, when the Blessed One, after spending the rains retreat on the peak of Mount Vebhāra, preached the Dhamma to the great multitude who had come to see the mountain, he ordained ninety thousand crores of people as Ehi Bhikkhus and, surrounded by those monks, recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha; that was the second assembly. Therefore, it is said:

"When the Buddha, the peerless one, dwelt on Mount Vebhāra,
The second gathering was of ninety thousand crores (of Arahants)."

Again, while the Blessed One, the virtuous one, the Lord of the Three Worlds, was releasing the great multitude from the bonds of defilements and wandering through the countryside, there was an assembly of eighty thousand crores of monks. Therefore, it is said:

"Again, when he set out on a journey through villages, market towns, and kingdoms,
The third gathering was of eighty thousand crores (of Arahants)."
231:
In that Pali, 'Gāmanigamaraṭṭhato' means (those who went forth as monks) from villages, market towns, and kingdoms. Or, this reading itself is the correct one, meaning (the assembly) of those who went forth after leaving those villages, market towns, and kingdoms.

At that time, our Bodhisatta was a wealthy merchant of Haṃsāvatī named Jaṭila, possessing many crores of wealth, and he gave a noble gift of robes together with food to the Saṅgha with the Buddha at the head. That Buddha also, at the conclusion of the appreciation (anumodanā) for the meal, prophesied: "In the future, one hundred thousand aeons from now, he will become a Buddha named Gotama." Referring to that, it was said:

11. "At that time, I was a merchant of Haṃsāvatī named Jaṭila, and I gave robes and cloth for robes together with food to the Saṅgha with the Buddha at the head.

12. That Buddha also, seated in the midst of the Saṅgha, prophesied of me: 'One hundred thousand aeons from this one, this man will become a Buddha.'

13. Having exerted effort in the practice of meditation... (they prayed:) 'May we be in the presence of this Blessed One Gotama.'

14. Having heard the words of that Buddha, I undertook further practices and made an extremely firm effort to fulfill the ten perfections (pāramīs)."

In those verses, 'Sambuddhappamukhaṃ saṅghaṃ' means to the Saṅgha with the Buddha at the head; the accusative case is used in the sense of the genitive. 'Sabhattaṃ dussaṃ adāsahaṃ' means I gave robes together with food. 'Uggadaḷhaṃ' means very firm. 'Dhitiṃ' means effort/energy, and 'akāsiṃ' means I made.

In the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, there were no other sects (titthiyas). All devas and humans approached only the Buddha as their refuge. Referring to that, it was said:

"At that time, all the other sects were frustrated, dejected, and unhappy; their pride vanished. No one attended to them, and they were driven out of the kingdom.

Then all those of other sects came together in harmony and approached the presence of the Buddha. (They said:) 'O Great Hero, the One with Vision, O Lord, please be our refuge.'

The Blessed One, who is compassionate, merciful, and seeks the welfare of all living beings, established all the other sects who had arrived in the Five Precepts (pañca-sīla)."
232:
Thus, the Dispensation of that Blessed One was undisturbed and empty of heretics. It was adorned with Arahant elders who had attained mastery and were endowed with the quality of 'tādi' (equanimity).

In that verse, 'byāhatā' refers to those whose pride and arrogance have been destroyed (those who were once proud). In the term 'titthiyā', one should understand 'tittha' (the ford), 'titthakara' (the founder of a sect), and 'titthiyā' (the followers of a sect). Among these three, it is called 'tittha' because they cross over by means of views such as eternalism; it refers to a doctrine (laddhi). The teacher who gives rise to that doctrine is called 'titthakara'. Those who are born in the doctrine that is like a ford are called 'titthiyā'.

It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, there were no heretics. One should understand that the phrase 'byāhatā titthiyā' etc., was spoken to show that even if they existed, they would have become like this (those established in the refuges and precepts). 'Vimanā' refers to those with a disturbed mind. 'Dummanā' is a synonym for that same 'vimanā'. 'Na tesaṃ keci paricaranti' means that even some men no longer perform services for those heretics of other sects, nor do they offer alms, nor pay respect, nor show deference, nor cherish, nor worship, nor rise from their seats for them, nor perform the act of salutation with joined palms. 'Raṭṭhato' means from the entire country. 'Nicchubhanti' means they expel them, remove them, and do not give them permission to reside. 'Te' refers to the heretics.

'Upagañchuṃ buddhasantike' means that all those heretics of other sects, being thus expelled by the people of the country, gathered together and sought refuge only with the Ten-Powered Padumuttara. It means they sought refuge by saying, 'Venerable Sir, You are our Teacher, our Protector, our Resort, our Ultimate Goal, and our Refuge.' He is called 'anukampaka' because he constantly sympathizes and protects. He is called 'kāruṇika' because he acts with compassion. 'Sampatte' refers to the heretics who arrived together and sought him as their refuge. 'Pañcasīle patiṭṭhahi' means he established them in the five precepts.

'Nirākulaṃ' means undisturbed, not mixed with those of other doctrines. 'Suññakaṃ' means empty and void of those heretics. In the word 'taṃ', the remaining words 'that Dispensation of the Blessed One' should be added and noted. 'Vicittaṃ' means varied and adorned in various ways. 'Vasībhūtehi' means by those who have attained mastery.

The royal city of that Blessed One Padumuttara was named Haṃsavatī. His father was the Khattiya named Ānanda, and his mother was the Queen named Sujātā. Devala and Sujāta were the two chief disciples. There was an attendant named Sumana. Amitā and Asamā were the two chief female disciples. The Bodhi tree was the Salala tree. His body was fifty-eight cubits in height, and the radiance of his body spread for twelve yojanas all around.
233:
His radiance extended for twelve yojanas. His lifespan was one hundred thousand years. His chief queen was named Vasudattā, and his son was named Uttara. The Blessed One Padumuttara attained Parinibbāna in the extremely delightful Nandārāma monastery. His relics were not dispersed. The people living in the entire Jambudīpa gathered and built a cetiya twelve yojanas high, made of the seven kinds of jewels. Thus it was said:

## 19. The city was named Haṃsavatī. The father was the Khattiya named Ānanda. The mother was named Sujātā. This is the account of the Teacher Padumuttara.

## 20. Devala and Sujāta were the chief disciples. The attendant was named Sumana. This is the account of the Great Sage Padumuttara.

## 21. Amitā and Asamā were the chief female disciples. The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called the Salala.

## 22. The Great Sage, the Buddha, was fifty-eight cubits in height. He was like a golden sacrificial post and was endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.

## 23. Enclosures, door-leaves, walls, trees, and rocky mountains did not obstruct the radiance of that Blessed One. It remained spread for twelve yojanas all around.

## 24. At that time, the lifespan was one hundred thousand years. Remaining for that long a period, he saved a great multitude of beings.

## 25. Having saved many people and cut off all doubts, he, like a great mass of fire, attained Parinibbāna together with his disciples.

In those verses, 'nagasiluccayā' refers to the rocky mountains known as 'naga'. 'Āvaraṇa' means covering or obstructing with a curtain. 'Twelve yojanas' means that the radiance of the Blessed One's body spread to a distance of twelve yojanas all around and remained there day and night. The meaning of the remaining verses is clear in every respect.

From this point onward, I shall proceed by summarizing the repeatedly occurring matters such as the fulfillment of the perfections from the Chronicle of Padumuttara Buddha, and stating only the special meanings. If I were to repeat what has already been said over and over, when would this commentary ever reach its end?

## The Explanation of the Chronicle of Padumuttara Buddha is finished.
## The Tenth Chronicle of the Buddhas is finished.

After the Blessed One Padumuttara attained Parinibbāna and his Dispensation disappeared, for seventy thousand aeons, there were no Buddhas, and the world was empty. Counting back from this aeon, thirty thousand aeons ago, in a single aeon, two Buddhas named Sumedha and Sujāta appeared. Among those two Buddhas, the Bodhisatta named Sumedha, who possessed great wisdom, fulfilled the perfections and was reborn in the Tusita heaven. Passing away from there, he was conceived in the womb of Queen Sudattā, the chief queen of King Sudatta in the city of Sudassana. When ten months were full, he was born from his mother's womb in the Sudassana garden like the rising sun. That Bodhisatta lived in the palace for nine thousand years. That prince had three palaces named Sucandana, Kañcana, and Sirivaḍḍhana. With Queen Sumana as the chief, there were forty-eight thousand...
234:
## 13. Sumedhabuddhavaṃsavaṇṇanā

After the Blessed One Padumuttara attained Parinibbāna and his Dispensation disappeared, for seventy thousand aeons (kappas), no Buddhas appeared; they were aeons void of Buddhas. Counting from this present aeon, thirty thousand aeons ago, in a single aeon, two Fully Enlightened Ones named Sumedha and Sujāta appeared. Among those two Buddhas, the Bodhisatta named Sumedha, who possessed attained wisdom, fulfilled the perfections and was reborn in the Tusita heaven. Passing away from there, he took rebirth in the womb of Queen Sudattā, the chief consort of King Sudatta, in the city of Sudassana. After ten months had passed, he was born in the Sudassana Park, like the young sun or like the moon emerging from the clouds. That Bodhisatta lived the household life for nine thousand years. He had three palaces named Sucandana, Kañcana, and SirivaḍḎhana. There were forty-eight thousand female attendants, headed by Chief Queen Sumana.

Having seen the four signs, and when a son named Punabbasu-mitta was born to Queen Sumana, he departed on the Great Renunciation (Mahābhinikkhamana) by an elephant-vehicle and became a monk. One hundred crore people also followed him and became monks. Surrounded by those monks, he practiced the ascetic life (padhāna-cariya) for half a month. On the full moon day of Visākha, he partook of the honey-milk rice offered by the daughter of the merchant Nakula in the village of Nakula. After spending the day-rest in a Sāla grove, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by the Ajivaka SirivaḍḎha. Having spread the grass mat, twenty cubits wide, at the foot of a Nīpa (Kadamba) Bodhi tree, he subdued the Mara and his army and attained Supreme Enlightenment. He uttered the solemn utterance: "Through many a birth in saṃsāra... I have reached the destruction of craving." He spent seven weeks near the Bodhi tree. In the eighth week, accepting the request of the Great Brahma to teach the Dhamma, he surveyed those capable of being tamed. He saw that his younger brother, Prince Saraṇa, Prince Sabba-kāmi, and the one hundred crore monks who had renounced with him were capable of penetrating the Four Noble Truths. Therefore, he traveled through the air and descended in the Sudassana Park near the city of Sudassana. He had the park keeper call his brothers and, in the midst of that assembly of monks, he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma. At that time, one hundred thousand crore beings attained the Dhamma (abhisamaya). This was the first realization. Therefore, the Blessed One said in the Pali text:

## 1. After Padumuttara, there appeared the Leader named Sumedha, the Conqueror, the supreme among gods and men. That Sage was difficult to approach, of fierce majesty, and supreme over the entire world.

## 2. He had clear eyes and a beautiful face; he had a large, straight, and radiant body. He sought the welfare of all beings and released many beings from their bonds.

## 3. When the Buddha reached the peerless and supreme Enlightenment, he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma in the city of Sudassana.
235:
After Padumuttara, there appeared the Leader named Sumedha, the supreme among gods and men. That Sage was difficult to approach, of fierce majesty, and supreme over the entire world.

He had clear eyes and a beautiful face; he had a large, straight, and radiant body. He sought the welfare of all beings and released many beings from their bonds.

When the Buddha reached the peerless and supreme Enlightenment, he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma in the city of Sudassana.

In the teaching of the Dhamma by that Blessed One, there were three realizations (abhisamaya) of the Truths by beings. The first realization was of one hundred thousand crore beings (thus it was said).

In those verses, 'uggatejo' means having majesty that has reached a supreme state. 'Pasannanetto' means having very clear eyes; his eyes were clear like polished and rubbed gem-spheres. Therefore, that Buddha Sumedha is called 'pasannanetto'. It means having clear eyes surrounded by soft, smooth, dark-blue, stainless, and delicate eyelashes. It is also appropriate to say 'one who has five types of very clear eyes'. 'Sumukho' means having a face like the full moon of the autumn season (the month of Tazaungmon). 'Brahā' means having a body eighty-eight cubits in height, thus being great; it means having a body size uncommon to others. 'Ujū' means having a straight body like the Great Brahma, a body that rises straight upwards; it means having a noble body like a golden archway erected in the city of the gods. 'Patāpavā' means having a radiant and glowing body. 'Hitesī' means one who seeks welfare. 'Abhisamaya tīṇi' means three realizations of the Truths; here, the neuter gender is used in place of the masculine.

Furthermore, the Blessed One Sumedha saw an ogre (yakkha) named Kumbhakaṇṇa, who had power like Kumbhakaṇṇa, who was a man-eater, who showed a terrifying body at the entrance of a great forest, and who wandered in the Vattani forest. At dawn, the Blessed One entered the attainment of Great Compassion, and upon emerging, he surveyed the world and saw that ogre. Alone and without a companion, he went to the ogre's abode, entered inside, and sat on the prepared glorious seat. Then, that ogre, unable to bear his resentment, became extremely angry like a fierce poisonous cobra that has been struck with a stick. Wishing to frighten the Ten-Powered One, he made his own form even more terrifying, making his head like a mountain, creating eyes like the sun's orb, and making very long, broad, and sharp fangs like the head of a plow. He appeared with a sagging, dark, broad, and uneven belly, arms like palm trees, a flat and ugly crooked nose, and a broad, red face like a mountain cave. With thick, tawny, fierce, and coarse hair, and a very terrifying appearance, he came and stood before the Blessed One Sumedha, emitting smoke and flames, and burning. Although he caused the nine kinds of rain to fall—namely, rocks, flames, water, mud, ashes, weapons, live coals, and sand—he was unable to move even a single hair of the Blessed One. Thinking, 'I will kill the Buddha by asking questions,' he asked questions like the ogre Āḷavaka. Then, the Blessed One tamed the ogre Kumbhakaṇṇa by answering the questions. Subsequently, on the second day, the people living in the country brought a prince along with rice carried by carts and gave them to the ogre Kumbhakaṇṇa. Then, the ogre offered the prince to the Blessed One Sumedha. The people standing at the gate of the forest...
236:
(That demon Kumbhakaṇṇa) created eyes resembling the sun's orb and tusks that were extremely long, broad, and sharp like the head of a plow. He had a pendulous, dark, broad, and uneven belly, arms like palm trunks, and a flat, ugly, and crooked nose. With a broad, red face like a mountain cave and thick, tawny, stiff, and rough hair, he appeared in an extremely terrifying form and stood before the Blessed One Sumedha. Emitting smoke and blazing with flames, he caused nine kinds of rain to fall—stones, fire-flames, water, mud, ashes, weapons, live coals, and sand—yet he was unable to move even a single hair of the Blessed One. Thinking, "I will kill the Blessed One by asking him a question," he asked a question just like the demon Āḷavaka. The Blessed One subdued that demon by answering the question. Then, on the second day, the citizens brought a prince along with a cartload of rice and gave them to the demon. The demon then offered the prince to the Buddha. The people standing at the forest gate approached the Blessed One. At that assembly, while the Ten-Powered One was preaching the Dhamma suitable to the demon's mind, he caused the Eye of Dhamma to arise in ninety thousand crores of beings. This was the second realization of the Truths (Dhammābhisamaya). Therefore, it was said:

"Furthermore, that Conqueror subdued the demon named Kumbhakaṇṇa; at that time, the second realization of the Truths occurred for ninety thousand crores of beings."

Again, when he revealed the Four Noble Truths in the Sirinanda Park in the city of Upakāri, the third realization of the Truths occurred for eighty thousand crores of beings. Therefore, it was said:

"Furthermore, the One of immeasurable fame revealed the Four Noble Truths; at that time, the third realization of the Truths occurred for eighty thousand crores of beings."

For the Blessed One Sumedha, there were also three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly at the city of Sudassana, there were one hundred crores of Arahants. Again, at Devakūṭa mountain during the spreading of the Kathina robe, there were ninety crores in the second assembly. Again, in the third assembly while the Blessed One was wandering on a journey, there were eighty crores. Therefore, it was said:

"There were three assemblies of the Great Sage Sumedha, consisting of Arahants who were stainless, of peaceful mind, and possessed of the quality of Tādi.

When the Conqueror approached the city named Sudassana, one hundred crores of Arahant monks first assembled."
237:
When the Conqueror reached the city named Sudassana, one hundred crores of Arahant monks assembled.

Furthermore, when the monks spread the Kathina robe at Devakūṭa mountain, the second assembly of ninety crores of monks took place.

Furthermore, when the Ten-Powered One was wandering on a journey, the third assembly of eighty crores of monks took place.

At that time, our Bodhisatta was a young man named Uttara, who was superior to all people. He gave up eighty crores of hoarded wealth and offered a great gift to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. Having heard the Dhamma of the Ten-Powered One at that time, he established himself in the refuges, went forth from the world, and became a monk. That Teacher, while performing the appreciation (anumodanā) for the meal, gave the prediction: "In the future, he will become a Buddha named Gotama." Regarding this, it was said:

At that time, I was a young man named Uttara; I had eighty crores of wealth accumulated in my house.

Having given all that wealth entirely to the Lord of the World together with the Saṅgha, I approached him for refuge and greatly delighted in the state of monkhood.

That Buddha also, while performing the appreciation, predicted of me: "In thirty thousand aeons from now, this person will become a Buddha."

Exerting effort in meditation... may we be in the presence of this Buddha.

The verses of the prediction should be expanded.

Having heard the words of that Blessed One, I gladdened my heart even further and undertook a superior practice to fulfill the ten perfections.

Having mastered the Suttanta, the Vinaya, and the entire nine-fold Dispensation of the Teacher, I graced the Dispensation of the Conqueror.

Living there heedfully in sitting, standing, and walking, and having reached the perfection of higher knowledge (abhiññā), I went to the Brahma realm.
238:
Among those words, 'sannicitaṃ' means that which is stored or accumulated by way of a hoard. 'Kevalaṃ' has the meaning of the whole. 'Sabbaṃ' means giving without remainder. 'Sasaṅghe' means together with the Saṅgha. 'Tassūpagacchiṃ' means I approached that Blessed One; here the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative. 'Abhirocayiṃ' means I went forth (ordained). 'Tiṃsakappasahassāmhi' means when thirty thousand aeons had passed.

The city of that Blessed One Sumedha was named Sudassana. His father was King Sudatta, and his mother was named Sudattā. Saraṇa and Sabbakāma were the two chief disciples (aggasāvaka). He had an attendant named Sāgara. Rāmā and Surāmā were the two chief female disciples (aggasāvikā). The Bodhi tree was a Great Neep tree (Mahānīpa). His height was eighty-eight cubits. His lifespan was ninety thousand years. He lived in the household for nine thousand years. His chief consort was named Sumanā, and his son was named Punabbasumitta. He renounced the world by an elephant vehicle. The remaining details can be found in the verses. Thus it was said:

"The city named Sudassana, the king named Sudatta,
The mother of the Great Sage Sumedha was named Sudattā.

Saraṇa and Sabbakāma were the chief disciples,
The attendant of the Great Sage Sumedha was named Sāgara.

Rāmā and Surāmā were the chief female disciples,
The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called the Mahānīpa.

Eighty-eight cubits tall was the Great Sage,
He illuminated all directions like the moon in the midst of the stars.

Just as the gem of a wheel-turning monarch shines for a league,
In the same way, the radiance of that Blessed One spreads for a league all around.

At that time, the lifespan was ninety thousand years,
Remaining for that long, he saved many beings.

With those who possessed the three knowledges and the six supernormal powers, who had attained psychic power,
With such noble Arahants, this Dispensation was well-intermingled.

All those of immeasurable fame, liberated and free from acquisitions,
Having shown the light of knowledge, those of great fame have attained Parinibbāna."
239:
In those verses, "Cando tāragane yathā" means just as the full moon in the sky illuminates and makes clear the host of stars, so too he illuminates all directions. Some teachers recite "Cando pannaraso yathā" (like the moon on the fifteenth day); that version also has a clear meaning.

"Cakkavattimaṇī nāma" means, for example, the gem-treasure of a wheel-turning monarch is four cubits long, has a circumference like the hub of a chariot wheel, and is surrounded by eighty-four thousand gems. It has the beauty of the accumulated glory of the full moon in the autumn season surrounded by the host of stars. When that gem-treasure, which is of most delightful appearance from Mount Vepulla, arrives as if invited, its radiance spreads over an area of one league all around. Similarly, the gem-like radiance from the body of the Blessed One Sumedha also spreads for one league all around.

"Tevijjachaḷabhiññehi" means with the three knowledges and the six supernormal powers. "Balappattehi" means with those who have attained psychic power. "Tādīhi" means with those who are endowed with the quality of being 'such' (equanimity). "Samākulaṃ" means crowded and shining everywhere with the color of saffron robes. "Idaṃ" refers to either this Dispensation (Sāsana) or the surface of the earth. "Amitayasā" means those who have immeasurable retinues or those who have incomparable fame. "Nirūpadhī" means those who are free from the four acquisitions (upadhi). The remaining terms in these verses are entirely clear.

## The Commentary on the Chronicle of Sumedha Buddha is finished.

## The Eleventh Chronicle of the Buddha is finished.

## 14. The Chronicle of Sujāta Buddha

Thereafter, in the period following that Blessed One Sumedha, in that same Maṇḍa-kappa, as the lifespan of beings gradually decreased from an immeasurable age and reached ninety thousand years, the Teacher named Sujāta, who possessed a beautiful physical body and a pure birth, appeared in the world. He also fulfilled the perfections, was reborn in the Tusita heaven, and after passing away from there, took conception in the womb of Queen Pabhāvatī, the chief consort of King Uggata in the city of Sumangala. After ten months had passed, he was born from his mother's womb. On the day of his naming, the name of that prince...
240:
Because he was born bringing happiness to all beings throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, they named the prince 'Sujāta'. Prince Sujāta lived in the household for nine thousand years. He had three palaces: Sirī, Upasirī, and Sirinanda. There were twenty-three thousand female attendants, headed by Queen Sirinandā.

Having seen the four great omens, and when his son named Upasena was born to Queen Sirinandā, the Bodhisatta departed on the noble horse named Haṃsavaha for the Great Renunciation and became an ascetic. One crore of people followed him and also became ascetics. Then, surrounded by those one crore monks, the Bodhisatta practiced asceticism for nine months. On the full moon day of Visākha, he partook of the most delicious milk-rice offered by the daughter of the merchant Sirinandana in the city of Sirinandana. He spent the day in a Sal grove. In the evening, accepting eight handfuls of grass offered by the Ajivaka named Sunanda, he approached the Bamboo Bodhi tree and spread a mat of grass thirty-three cubits wide. Even before the sun set, he defeated Māra and his army, attained Supreme Enlightenment, and uttered the solemn utterance common to all Buddhas. He spent seven weeks (forty-nine days) near the Bodhi tree. Being requested by the Great Brahmā to teach the Dhamma, he saw that his younger brother, Prince Sudassana, and the chaplain's son, Prince Deva, were capable of realizing the Four Noble Truths. He traveled through the air and descended at Sumangala Park near the city of Sumangala. Sending the park keeper to summon Prince Sudassana and Prince Deva, he sat in the midst of them and their retinue and set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma. In that preaching of the Dhammacakka, eighty crores of beings attained the realization of the Dhamma. This was the first realization (pathama-abhisamaya).

Furthermore, when the Blessed One performed the Twin Miracle (yamaka-pāṭihāriya) at the foot of a great Sal tree at the gate of Sudassana Park and entered the rains-retreat among the gods in Tāvatiṃsa, three million seven hundred thousand devas and brahmas attained the realization of the Dhamma. This was the second realization. When the Buddha Sujāta went to his father the King, six million beings attained the realization of the Dhamma. This was the third realization. Regarding this, it is said in the Pali:

'In that same Maṇḍa-kappa, there was a leader named Sujāta, with jaws like a lion and shoulders like a bull, immeasurable and unassailable.'
241:
Like the stainless moon, and like the radiant sun, the Buddha always shines beautifully with his glory.

Having reached the entirety of the supreme Enlightenment, the Buddha set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma in the city of Sumangala.

While Sujāta, the Leader of the World, was preaching the noble Dhamma, eighty crores of beings realized the Four Noble Truths at the first preaching of the Dhamma.

When Sujāta of immeasurable fame entered the rains-retreat among the gods, there was the second realization for three million seven hundred thousand.

When the peerless Sujāta approached his father, there was the third realization for six million.

In those verses, 'tattheva maṇḍakappamhi' means that the Buddha Sujāta was born in the same Maṇḍa-kappa in which the Buddha Sumedha was born. 'Sīhahanu' means having a jaw like a lion's. While only the lower jaw of a lion is full and not the upper, both the lower and upper jaws of this Great Man are full like the moon on the twelfth day of the waxing fortnight. Therefore, he is called 'Sīhahanu'. 'Usabhakkhandho' means shoulders as evenly rounded as those of a noble bull, shoulders like a well-rounded golden drum. 'Sataramsīva' means like the sun. 'Siriyā' means with the glory of a Buddha. 'Bodhimuttamam' refers to the supreme Enlightenment.

Having preached the Dhamma to the people who came to Sudhamma Park in the city of Sudhammavatī, and having ordained six million monks through the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' formula, he recited the Pātimokkha in their midst; this was the first assembly. After that, upon the Blessed One's descent from the celestial realm (Tidiva), there was the second assembly of five million monks. Again, hearing that 'Prince Sudassana has renounced the world in the presence of the Blessed One and attained Arahantship,' four hundred thousand men came saying, 'We too shall renounce.' Elder Sudassana took them and approached Sujāta, the Bull among Men. The Blessed One preached the Dhamma to them, ordained them as 'Ehi Bhikkhus', and recited the Pātimokkha in that assembly endowed with the four factors; this was the third assembly. Therefore, it is said:

7. For the Buddha Sujāta, there were three assemblies of Arahants who were free from the taints of defilements, possessed peaceful minds, and were endowed with the quality of 'tādi' (equanimity).

8. Six million Arahants, who had attained the power of higher knowledge (abhiññā) and would not be reborn in a new existence, assembled for the first time.

9. Then, at the assembly when the Buddha descended from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, there was the second assembly of five million Arahants.
242:
There were three assemblies of the Arahants of the Great Sage Sujāta, who were free from the defilements of impurities, possessed peaceful minds, and were endowed with the quality of equanimity (tādi).

Six million Arahants, who had attained the power of supernormal knowledge and would not be reborn again in the various states of existence, gathered in the first assembly.

Thereafter, in the assembly when the Blessed One descended from the celestial realm, there was a second gathering of five million Arahants.

The Elder Sudassana, the Chief Disciple, approached the Buddha, the Supreme Man, together with four hundred thousand Arahants.

In those verses, 'appattānaṃ' means those who have not reached the various states of existence (those who will not undergo further rebirth). There is also a reading 'appavattā bhavābhave', which has the same meaning. 'Tidivorohaṇe' should be understood as the agent (kattu-kāraka) meaning 'at the time of descending from the celestial realm'. It is stated with a change of grammatical case (kāraka-vipallāsa). Alternatively, 'tidivorohaṇe' means the descent from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. 'Jine' should be understood as 'Jinassa' (of the Conqueror Buddha), where the locative case is used in the sense of the genitive.

At that time, our Bodhisatta was a Cakkavatti King. Hearing that 'A Buddha has arisen in the world,' he approached the Blessed One, listened to the Dhamma, and offered the sovereignty of the four continents along with the seven treasures to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, and then ordained in the presence of the Teacher. The inhabitants of all the islands took the revenue and profits obtained from the country, performed the duties of monastery attendants (kappiya), and constantly gave great offerings to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. That Blessed One Sujāta also prophesied: 'In the future, he will become a Buddha named Gotama.' Therefore, it was said:

'At that time, I was the ruler of the four continents, a powerful Cakkavatti who could travel through the air.

Having offered the great sovereignty over the four continents and the seven excellent treasures to the Buddha, I ordained in his presence.

The monastery attendants collected the revenue from throughout the countryside and brought the four requisites and lodgings to the monastery for the Bhikkhu Saṅgha.'
243:
That Blessed One Sujāta, the Lord of the ten thousand world systems, also prophesied to me: 'This Cakkavatti, thirty thousand aeons from now, will become a Buddha who realizes the Four Noble Truths.'

Having exerted effort in the practice of meditation... they made the aspiration: 'May we be in the presence of this Blessed One Gotama.'

Hearing the prophecy of that Buddha, I felt extreme joy. I undertook the noble practice to fulfill the ten perfections (pāramīs).

I learned the Suttanta, the Vinaya, and the entire nine-fold Dispensation of the Teacher, and adorned the Dispensation of the Conqueror.

Living diligently in that Dispensation, developing the meditation of the Divine Abodes (Brahmavihāra), and reaching the perfection of supernormal powers (abhiññā), I went to the Brahma realm.

In those verses, 'catudīpamhi' means in the four great islands, each having five hundred satellite islands. 'Antalikkhacaro' means being able to travel through the sky preceded by the Wheel Treasure. 'Ratane sattā' refers to the seven treasures such as the Elephant Treasure. 'Uttame' means in the excellent treasures. Alternatively, it should be noted as 'to the Excellent Buddha'. 'Niyyātayitvāna' means having offered. 'Uṭṭhānaṃ' refers to the taxes and profits obtained from the country. 'Paṭipiṇḍiya' means having collected or gathered into a heap. 'Paccayaṃ' refers to the various four requisites such as robes. 'Dasasahassimhi issaro' means being the lord of the ten thousand world systems, and it should be understood that this refers to the field of birth (jātikhetta). The Blessed One is the lord of infinite world systems. 'Tiṃsakappasahassamhi' means at the end of thirty thousand aeons starting from this Maṇḍa kappa.

The royal city of that Blessed One Sujāta was named Sumangala. His father was King Uggata, and his mother was Pabhāvatī. Sudassana and Sudeva were the two Chief Disciples. Nārada was the attendant. Nāgā and Nāgasamālā were the two Chief Female Disciples. The Bodhi tree was a Great Bamboo (Mahāveဠu). That tree had small openings, a solid trunk, and was extremely delightful. It had wide branches covered with pure leaves the color of beryl (veဠuriya) gems, shining like a peacock's tail. The body of that Blessed One was fifty cubits high. His lifespan was ninety thousand years. His Chief Consort was named Sirīnandā, and his son was named Upasena. He renounced the world in an excellent horse-drawn carriage. He attained Parinibbāna at the Silārāma monastery in the city of Candavatī. Therefore, it was said in the Pali text: 'Sumangalaṃ nāma... sabbasaṅkhārā', and so on.

The royal city of the Blessed One Sujāta was named Sumangala. His father was King Uggata, and his mother was Pabhāvatī.

That Bodhisatta lived in the human realm for nine thousand years. There were three excellent palaces called Siri, Upasiri, and Nandā.

There were twenty-three thousand well-adorned female attendants. His consort was named Sirinandā, and his son was named Upasena.
244:
There is a city named Sumaṅgala; the king named Uggata was the father. The mother of the Exalted Sujāta was named Pabhāvatī.

Sudassana and Sudeva were the chief disciples (aggasāvaka). The attendant of the Exalted Sujāta was named Nārada.

Nāga and Nāgasamālā were the chief female disciples (aggasāvikā). The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called Mahāveḷu (the Great Bamboo).

That Bodhi tree has a solid trunk, small openings, and is covered with leaves. It has straight joints, is expansive, beautiful to behold, and delightful to the mind.

Having grown from a single trunk, five main branches spread out from there. Like a well-bound bundle of peacock feathers, that tree is beautiful.

There are no thorns on that Bodhi tree, nor were there any large hollows. It has wide-spreading branches, dense leaves, cool shade, and is delightful to the mind.

That Victorious One was fifty cubits in height. He was endowed with all excellent attributes and possessed all virtues.

The radiance of that Buddha was incomparable and radiated all around. It was immeasurable, peerless, and beyond comparison by any metaphors.

At that time, the lifespan was ninety thousand years. Remaining for that long, that Buddha saved many beings.

Just as waves in the ocean, or stars in the sky, so too was the Dispensation at that time adorned with Arahants.

That Buddha, who was peerless, and those incomparable virtues, have all disappeared. Are not all conditioned things indeed empty?

In that Pali, "acchiddo" means having small openings. It should be understood as in terms like "anudara kanyā (a maiden with a small waist)". Some teachers recite it as "chiddam hoti parittakam (there is a small opening)". "Pattiko" means having many leaves.
245:
'Kācamaṇivaṇṇehi pattehi sañchanno' means well-covered with leaves having the color of emeralds. 'Ujū' means not crooked or bent. 'Vaṃsa' means the bamboo tree. 'Brahā' means large all around. 'Ekakkhandho' means a single tree growing from the earth, without a second. 'PavaḍḎitvā' means having grown. 'Tato sākhā pabhijjati' means from the top of that bamboo tree, five branches emerged and spread out. There is also a reading 'Tato sākhā pabhijjhathā'. 'Subaddho' means well-bound in the manner of five bindings. 'Morahattho' means a bundle of peacock feathers made and tied to ward off the heat of the sun.

'Na tassa kaṇṭakā honti' means although it is a type of tree that usually has thorns, there were no thorns on that bamboo tree. 'Aviralo' means covered with branches that are not sparse. 'Sandacchāyo' means having dense shade; because the branches are not sparse, it is called 'sandacchāyo' (cool shade). 'Paññāsaratano āsi' means he was fifty cubits tall. 'Sabbākāravarūpeto' means he is called so because he was endowed with excellent qualities in every aspect. 'Sabbaguṇamupāgato' is merely a synonym of the preceding term.

'Appamāṇo' means having no measurable limit, or called so because one is unable to take a measurement. 'Atuliyo' means peerless, not like anyone else. 'Opammehi' means by comparable metaphors. 'Anūpamo' means having no comparison; it means incomparable because one cannot say 'he is like this person or that person'. 'Guṇāni ca tāni' refers to those virtues such as omniscience; it is stated with a change in gender. In all other places, the meaning is quite clear.

## The Explanation of the Chronicle of Sujāta Buddha is finished.
## The Twelfth Chronicle of the Buddhas is finished.
## 15. The Explanation of the Chronicle of Piyadassī Buddha

After the time of Sujāta Buddha, in an aeon one thousand eight hundred aeons ago from this Bhadda-kappa, three Buddhas named Piyadassī, Atthadassī, and Dhammadassī were born. Among those three Buddhas, the Blessed One named Piyadassī, having fulfilled the perfections, was reborn in the Tusita heaven, and passing away from there, [was reborn] in the city of Sudhaññavatī as the son of King Sudatta...
246: I shall now relate the chronicle of the Buddha Piyadassī, following the chronicle of the Buddha Sujāta. One thousand one hundred and eight aeons ago (one hundred and eighteen aeons ago according to the Atthasālinī), in a Vara-kappa (Excellent Aeon), three Buddhas appeared: Piyadassī, Atthadassī, and Dhammadassī. Among these three, the Buddha named Piyadassī, having fulfilled all the perfections, was reborn in the Tusita heaven. After passing away from there, he took conception in the womb of Queen Candādevī, who had a face like the moon and was the chief consort of King Sudatta in the city of Sudhaññavatī. After ten months, he was born in the Varuṇa Grove. On the day of his naming, because he displayed extraordinary and pleasing miracles to the people, they named him 'Piyadassī' (One of Pleasant Aspect). Prince Piyadassī lived in the palace for nine thousand years. He had three palaces named Sunimmala, Vimala, and Giribrā. Thirty-three thousand ladies-in-waiting, led by Queen Vimalā, attended upon him. After seeing the four omens and when his son named Kañcanaveḷa was born to Queen Vimalā, the Bodhisatta departed on the Great Renunciation in a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses and became an ascetic. One crore men followed him and also became ascetics. Surrounded by those monks, the Bodhisatta Piyadassī practiced the ascetic life (dukkara-cariyā) for six months. On the full moon day of Vesākha, he accepted and consumed the thick milk-rice offered by the daughter of the Brahmin Vasabha in the village of Varuṇa. After spending the day in a Sāla grove, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by an Ājīvaka named Sujāta and approached the Kakudha Bodhi tree (a Shishar/Wood-apple tree according to the Atthasālinī). Having spread the grass over an area of fifty-three cubits and sitting cross-legged, he realized Omniscient Wisdom (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). He then uttered the solemn utterance beginning with 'Aneka-jāti-saṃsāraṃ'. He remained there for seven weeks (forty-nine days). Knowing that the monks who had renounced with him were capable of realizing the Noble Dhamma, he traveled through the air and descended in the Usabhavatī Park near the city of Usabhavatī. Surrounded by one crore monks, he set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion. At that time, one thousand crore devas and humans attained the Dhamma (Dhamma-abhisamaya). This was the first Awakening. Furthermore, on Mount Sudassana near the city of Usabhavatī, there lived a king of devas named Sudassana. He held wrong views. Every year, the people of the entire Jambudīpa offered him sacrifices worth one hundred thousand. That deva-king Sudassana used to sit on the same seat as the human king to receive the offerings. Then, the Buddha Piyadassī, thinking, 'I shall dispel the wrong views of that deva-king Sudassana,' entered his palace while the deva-king was away at a meeting of Yakkhas. He ascended the glorious throne and, emitting the six-colored rays, sat there like the sun atop Mount Yugandhara during the autumn season. The goddesses who were his attendants worshipped the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala) with flowers and perfumes and stood surrounding him. When the deva-king Sudassana returned from the meeting of Yakkhas, he saw the six-colored rays emanating from his palace and thought, 'On other days, my palace has never shone with such a vast network of rays...'
247: When the deva-king Sudassana returned from the meeting of Yakkhas and saw the six-colored rays emanating from his palace, he thought: 'On other days, I have never seen such a magnificent display of light from many networks of rays in my palace. Who has entered here—a deva or a human?' While investigating, he saw the Blessed One sitting, blazing with a network of six-colored rays like the sun on an autumn day atop the peak of the Dawn Mountain (Udaya). He thought, 'This shaven-headed ascetic is sitting on my noble throne, surrounded by my own attendants and followers.' Overcome by anger, he thought, 'Now I shall show this ascetic my power,' and he turned that entire mountain into a single mass of flames. Thinking, 'By this mass of fire, that shaven-headed ascetic will be reduced to ashes,' he looked, but he saw the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala) still blazing, his noble body suffused with many networks of rays, his face serene and beautiful, and his complexion exceptionally clear. He thought, 'This ascetic can withstand fire. Now I shall kill this ascetic by drowning him in a flood of water.' He then directed a very deep flood of water toward the palace. However, although the palace was filled with the flood, not even a thread of the Blessed One's robes nor a single hair on his body became wet as he sat there. Then the deva-king Sudassana, thinking, 'By this water, the ascetic will be unable to breathe and will die,' withdrew the water and looked. He saw the Blessed One sitting, surrounded by his own followers, shining with various networks of rays like the autumn moon emerging from dark rain clouds. Unable to restrain his resentment, he thought, 'Now I shall kill him,' and caused a rain of nine kinds of weapons to fall. Then, by the power of the Blessed One, all those weapons became various beautiful and fragrant flower garlands and fell at the feet of the Ten-Powered One. Then, seeing that miracle, the deva-king Sudassana, with a heart full of extreme anger, seized the Blessed One by the feet with both hands. Wanting to expel him from his palace, he lifted him up, crossed the Great Ocean, and went to the Cakkavāḷa Mountains. Looking to see, 'Is the ascetic still alive or is he dead?' he saw the Buddha sitting on that very same seat [back in the palace]. He thought, 'Aho! This ascetic possesses great power. I am not able to expel this ascetic from this place.'
248:
That King of Devas, Sudassana, thought: “This monk possesses great psychic power; I am unable to drive him away from this place. If anyone should come to know of this, I shall suffer a great loss of reputation and followers. I will let this Buddha go and depart before anyone sees him.”

Then, the Blessed One Piyadassī, the Possessor of Ten Powers, knowing the thoughts of the King of Devas, made a resolution that all devas and humans should see him. On that day, one hundred and one kings from the entire continent of Jambudīpa had gathered to pay homage to King Sudassana. When those human kings saw King Sudassana, their King of Devas, sitting and holding the feet of the Buddha, the King of Sages, they thought: “Our King of Devas is performing service at the feet of the Teacher Piyadassī, the King of Sages. Oh, how wonderful are the Buddhas! Oh, how distinguished are the qualities of the Buddha!” With hearts full of devotion toward the Blessed One, all the kings stood with their hands clasped in reverence above their heads, bowing to the Buddha. Among that assembly of kings, the Blessed One Piyadassī preached the Dhamma, placing King Sudassana at the head of the assembly. At that time, nine hundred billion devas and humans attained Arahatship. This was the second occasion of the realization of the Truth (abhisamaya).

In the city of Kumuda, which was nine yojanas in extent, a thera named Soṇa—who was like Devadatta, an enemy of the Buddha—conspired with Prince Mahāpaduma. After they had killed the prince's father, Soṇa made various efforts to kill the Buddha Piyadassī but was unsuccessful. He then summoned an elephant trainer named Doṇamukha and, after enticing him, said: “When this monk Piyadassī enters this city for alms, release the noble elephant named Doṇamukha and kill the monk Piyadassī.”

Then that elephant trainer, who was a favorite of the king but lacked the ability to discern right from wrong, thought: “This monk might even cause me to be removed from my position.” Agreeing with the plan, he noted the time the Buddha would enter the city on the following day. He approached the elephant Doṇamukha—who possessed a forehead like a well-formed rice-pot, a trunk long like a bow, broad and soft ears, eyes yellow like honey, a fine back, rounded flanks, well-knit and hidden joints, beautiful tusks like plowshares, a fine tail, a decorated tail-tip, and was endowed with all auspicious marks, beautiful to behold like a dark rain cloud, walking with the majestic gait of a lion, like a moving mountain, standing firm on seven points, with sevenfold secretions of ichor dripping from all parts, appearing like the personification of Death (Antaka). The trainer made the elephant even more intoxicated and reckless with special offerings of food-balls, eye-salve, incense, and ointments. He then sent forth this elephant, who was like Erāvaṇa in blocking enemies, to kill the Great Elephant among Sages, the Buddha Piyadassī.

Then that noble elephant, as soon as he was released, killed elephants, buffaloes, horses, and people. With his tusks, trunk, and body smeared all over with the blood of those he had killed, his eyes bloodshot as if covered by a net of intestines, he destroyed carts, doors, houses, and gate-posts. Followed by crows, hawks, and vultures...
249:
Then that noble elephant, as soon as he was released from his bonds, killed elephants, buffaloes, horses, men, and women. With his tusks, trunk, and body smeared all over with the blood of those he had slain, his eyes bloodshot as if covered by a net of intestines, he broke and destroyed carts, door-leaves, gabled houses, and gate-arches. Constantly surrounded by crows, hawks, vultures, and the like, he bit and devoured the limbs of the slain buffaloes, humans, horses, and elephants, eating like a man-eating ogre (yakkha). Seeing from afar the Blessed One, the Possessor of Ten Powers, approaching surrounded by a host of disciples, he rushed toward the Blessed One with a speed like that of the wind or a Garuda.

At that time, the city-dwellers, their minds filled with fear and trembling, climbed onto palaces, walls, mounds, and trees. Seeing the elephant rushing toward the Tathāgata, they raised a great cry of alarm. Some lay devotees (upāsakas) attempted to stop the elephant by various means. Then the Buddha, the Great Elephant among Men, looked upon the approaching elephant and, with a heart cooled by the pervasion of compassion, suffused the elephant with loving-kindness (metta). Thereupon, that elephant, his heart softened by the pervasion of loving-kindness, recognized his own fault and offense. Overcome with shame, he did not dare to stand before the Blessed One and, as if sinking into the earth, he prostrated himself with his head at the Blessed One's feet. Lying there, that elephant of dark hue appeared as beautiful as a dark rain cloud resting near the peak of a noble golden mountain illuminated by the glow of twilight.

Seeing the king of elephants prostrating with his head at the feet of the King of Sages, the city-dwellers were filled with supreme joy and uttered cries of 'Sādhu', lion-like roars, and shouts of applause. They honored the Blessed One in various ways with fragrant garlands, sandalwood, scented powders, and ornaments. Everywhere, people danced and waved their garments. In the sky, celestial drums resounded. Then the Blessed One, looking at the noble elephant lying at his feet like a dark mountain peak, stroked the elephant's head with his palm—which was adorned with the marks of the goad, banner, net, conch, and wheel—and admonished him with a Dhamma teaching suited to the elephant's disposition:

“O noble elephant, listen to the words I speak; follow these words of mine which are fraught with benefit. O fair-tusked one, remove your corrupt nature that delights in killing, and attain peace.”

“O king of elephants, whoever harms or kills living beings through greed, hatred, or delusion, such a person who is habitually murderous experiences terrifying suffering in hell for a very long time.”

“Elephant, do not perform such unwholesome kamma again through heedlessness or intoxication. One who kills living beings suffers in the Avīci hell for an entire aeon (kappa).”
250:
Whether through greed, hatred, or delusion, whoever harms living beings, O King of Elephants, that killer of beings experiences terrifying suffering in hell for a very long time.

O Doṇamukha elephant, do not perform such acts of harming and killing again, whether through negligence or intoxication. One who takes the lives of beings reaches unbearable suffering in Avīci for an aeon.

After experiencing terrifying suffering in hell, if one returns to the human world, because of having been a harmer, one experiences special suffering, having a short life and a deformed appearance.

O gentle Doṇamukha elephant, just as living beings are very dear and precious to you among the multitude, knowing that life is likewise dear to others, one should abstain from taking life.

Knowing the fault of delighting in killing and harming, and the virtue of abstaining from taking life, if you desire happiness in the heavenly realm in the hereafter, abstain from taking life.

In this world, one who is well-restrained and abstains from taking life becomes beloved, pleasing, and uplifting to the heart. The Buddhas declare that after the breaking up of the body, such a person dwells in heaven.

No one in the world desires to reach suffering; every born being seeks only happiness. Therefore, O Great Elephant, abandoning harm, develop loving-kindness and compassion at all times.
251:
Then, while being thus admonished by the Buddha, the Possessor of Ten Powers, the noble elephant regained his mindfulness and became extremely disciplined, like a pupil endowed with the practice of discipline (Vinaya).

In this way, the Blessed One Piyadassī, just like our Teacher (Gotama Buddha) tamed the elephant Dhanapāla, tamed the noble elephant named Doṇamukha and preached the Dhamma to the great assembly of people. At that time, there was the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) by eighty thousand crores of beings. This was the third realization. Therefore, it was said in the Buddhavaṃsa:

After the Buddha Sujāta, there was the Self-Awakened Leader of the World,
Difficult to approach, peerless, the famous Piyadassī.

That Buddha of immeasurable fame also shone like the sun;
Having dispelled all darkness, he set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion.

For that Buddha of incomparable majesty, there were also three realizations;
The first realization was of a hundred thousand crores.

The king of gods named Sudassana delighted in wrong view;
Dispelling that king's wrong view, the Teacher preached the Dhamma.

There was an incomparable gathering of people and gods then;
The second realization was of ninety thousand crores.

When the Trainer of Men tamed the elephant Doṇamukha,
The third realization was of eighty thousand crores.

In the city of Sumangala, there were two friends: a prince named Pālita and the chaplain's son named Sabbadassī. While the Fully Enlightened Buddha Piyadassī was wandering on tour, they heard, "He has arrived at our city." They went out to welcome him with an entourage of a hundred thousand crores, listened to his Dhamma, and gave a great alms-offering for seven days. On the seventh day, at the conclusion of the Blessed One's appreciation (anumodanā) of the meal, they ordained along with a hundred thousand crores of people and attained Arahantship.

In the midst of those monks, the Blessed One recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha; that was the first assembly of disciples. At another time, in the assembly of the king of gods Sudassana, ninety thousand crores attained Arahantship. Surrounded by those monks, the Teacher recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha; this was...
252:
...the second assembly of disciples. Again, at the taming of the elephant Doṇamukha, eighty crores of people ordained and attained Arahantship. In the midst of those monks, the Blessed One recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha; this was the third assembly of disciples. Therefore, it was said:

“There were three assemblies for that Buddha Piyadassī;
The first gathering was of a hundred thousand crores of Arahants.

After that, ninety crores of sages gathered together;
In the third assembly, there were eighty crores of monks.”

At that time, our Bodhisatta was a Brahmin youth named Kassapa, who had reached the further shore of the three Vedas, with Itihāsa as the fifth. Having heard the Teacher's Dhamma desanā, he spent a hundred thousand crores to build and donate a supreme monastery (Saṅghārāma) and established himself in the three refuges and the five precepts. Then the Teacher prophesied to him: “One thousand eight hundred aeons from now, a Buddha named Gotama will arise in the world.” Therefore, it was said:

“At that time, I was a Brahmin named Kassapa,
A reciter, a master of mantras, who had reached the further shore of the three Vedas.

Having heard his Dhamma, I felt great devotion;
I built a Saṅghārāma with a hundred thousand crores of coins.

Having donated the monastery to that Buddha, with a joyful and stirred mind,
I firmly took and observed the refuges and the five precepts.

That Buddha also, sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha, prophesied of me:
‘One thousand eight hundred aeons hence, this person will become a Buddha.’

(Then the people,) exerting effort in meditation, prayed:
‘May we be those who realize Nibbāna in the presence of this Buddha Gotama.’

Having heard the words of that Buddha, I further gladdened my heart;
I undertook a superior practice to fulfill the ten perfections (pāramīs).”
253:
In those verses, 'Saraṇe pañcasīle ca' means the three refuges and the five precepts. 'Aṭṭhārase kappasate' means at the end of one thousand eight hundred aeons from this present aeon.

The royal city of that Blessed One was named Sudhañña. His father was the king named Sudatta, and his mother was the queen named Sucandā. Pālita and Sabbadassī were the pair of chief disciples (aggasāvaka). He had an attendant named Sobhita. Sujātā and Dhammadinnā were the pair of chief female disciples (aggasāvikā). The Bodhi tree was the Kakudha tree. His body was eighty cubits in height. His lifespan was ninety thousand years. He had a chief queen named Vimalā and a son named Kañcanāveḷa. That Bodhisatta departed for his renunciation in a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses. Therefore, it was said:

'The city was named Sudhañña, and the khattiya was named Sudatta.
The mother of the Teacher Piyadassī was named Candā.'

'Pālita and Sabbadassī were the chief disciples.
The attendant of the Teacher Piyadassī was named Sobhita.'

'Sujātā and Dhammadinnā were the chief female disciples.
The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called the Kakudha.'

'That Buddha of immeasurable glory, endowed with the thirty-two excellent marks, eighty cubits in height, appeared like a king of Sal trees.'

'There is no radiance in fire, the moon, or the sun comparable to the radiance of that peerless Great Sage.'

'The lifespan of that God of gods was also of that duration.
The One with Vision (Cakkhumā) remained in the world for ninety thousand years.'

'That peerless Buddha and those incomparable pairs [of disciples] have all disappeared. Are not all conditioned things (saṅkhāra) indeed empty?'

In those verses, 'sālarājā vā' means he appeared like a king of Sal trees in full bloom, most beautiful to behold, with a perfectly symmetrical trunk. 'Yugānipi tānī' refers to the pairs such as the chief disciples. In the remaining verses, the meaning is entirely clear.

## The Commentary on the Chronicle of Piyadassī Buddha is finished.
## The thirteenth Chronicle of the Buddha is finished.
254:
## 16. Commentary on the Chronicle of Atthadassī Buddha

After the Fully Enlightened Buddha Piyadassī attained Parinibbāna and his dispensation (sāsana) had vanished, the human lifespan fluctuated, gradually decreasing from an immeasurable age until it reached one hundred thousand years. At that time, the Buddha named Atthadassī appeared in the world.

That Bodhisatta Atthadassī, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramī), was reborn in the Tusita heaven. Passing away from there, he took conception in the womb of Queen Sudassanā, the chief queen of King Sāgara, in the most beautiful city named Sobhana. After remaining in the womb for ten months, he was born in the Sucindhana Grove. As soon as the Great Man (Mahāpurisa) was born from his mother's womb, great treasures that had been buried for a long time and passed down through generations were recovered by their owners. Therefore, on the day of his naming, they named him 'Atthadassī'.

That prince lived in the household life for ten thousand years. He had three palaces named Amaragiri, Suragiri, and Girivāhana, which were exceedingly fragrant. There were thirty-three thousand female attendants, headed by Queen Visākhā.

Having seen the four omens, and when a son named Prince Sela was born to Queen Visākhā, he departed on the Great Renunciation riding the horse king named Sudassana and became an ascetic. Nine crores of people followed him and became ascetics. Surrounded by those monks, that Great Man practiced austerities (dukkharacariyā) for eight months. On the full moon day of Kasone (Vesākha), he accepted and partook of the milk-rice with honey (madhupāyāsa) brought as an offering by the Nāga maiden Sucindharā, while the entire body of the Nāga maiden was visible to the multitude, and it was offered together with a golden bowl.

After spending the day's rest in a young Sal grove adorned with a hundred small trees, in the evening, he took eight handfuls of kusa grass offered by the Nāga king named Mahāruci, who delighted in the Dhamma, and approached the Campaka Bodhi tree. Having spread the grass mat fifty-three cubits in length and width, he sat in a cross-legged posture and attained Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi). He uttered the solemn utterance (udāna) that all Buddhas are accustomed to utter: 'Through many a birth in saṃsāra... I have attained the destruction of cravings.' He then spent seven weeks (sattasattāha) in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree.

Accepting the request of the Great Brahmā to teach the Dhamma, and seeing that the nine crores of monks who had renounced with him were capable of penetrating the Noble Dhamma, he traveled through the air and descended in the Anoma Grove near the city of Anoma. Surrounded by those monks, he preached the Dhammacakka sermon. At that time, the first realization of the Four Noble Truths (abhisamaya) occurred for one hundred billion beings.

Again, when the Blessed One traveled through the celestial realms and preached the Dhamma, the second realization occurred for one hundred billion devas and brahmās. Furthermore, just as our Buddha Gotama entered the city of Kapilavatthu and preached the Dhamma, the Buddha Atthadassī entered the city of Sobhana and preached the Dhamma, at which time the third realization occurred for one hundred billion beings. Therefore, it is stated in the Pali text: 'There were three realizations.'
255:
Surrounded by those monks, He turned the Wheel of Dhamma in that Anoma Garden. At that time, the first realization of the Truths (Dhamma-abhisamaya) occurred for one hundred thousand crores of humans, devas, and brahmas.

Again, when the Blessed One, the Leader of the World, wandered through the celestial realms and preached the Dhamma there, the second realization occurred for one hundred thousand crores of devas and brahmas. When the Blessed One Atthadassī entered the city of Sobhana and preached the Dhamma, just as our Blessed One Gotama entered the city of Kapilavatthu and preached the Dhamma, the third realization of the Truths occurred for one hundred thousand crores of humans, devas, and brahmas. Therefore, it was said:

"In that very Maṇḍa-kappa, the highly renowned Atthadassī, having dispelled the great darkness of ignorance, attained supreme Enlightenment.

Being requested by the Brahma, He turned the Wheel of Dhamma; He satisfied the world, including the devas of the ten thousand world systems, with the Deathless Nibbāna.

For that Lord of the World, there were also three realizations; the first realization was for one hundred thousand crores.

When the Buddha Atthadassī wandered through the celestial realms, the second realization was for one hundred thousand crores.
