Furthermore, when the Buddha preached in the presence of His father, the third realization was for one hundred thousand crores."

In those verses, "tattheva" means in that very kappa. Here, the Vara-kappa is intended by the term "Maṇḍa-kappa." It was stated below in the commentary on the Padumuttara Buddhavamsa: "The kappa in which three Buddhas arise is called a Vara-kappa (or Maṇḍa-kappa)." Therefore, in this context, the Vara-kappa is referred to as "Maṇḍa-kappa." "Nihantvāna" means having dispelled; or this itself is the original reading. "Santo" means being or having been. "Amatena" means by the drink of the Deathless, which is the attainment of the Path and Fruit. "Tappayī" means He satisfied or satiated. "Dasa-sahassī" refers to the ten thousand world systems. "Devacārikaṃ" means wandering in the deva world for the purpose of disciplining the devas.

It is heard that in the city of Sucandaka, a prince named Santa and a chaplain's son named Upasanta, seeing no essence in the three Vedas or in any other doctrines, stationed four wise and confident men at the four gates of the city, saying: "If you see or hear of any wise ascetic or brahmin, come and inform us."
256:
They stationed four wise and bold men at the four gates (of Sucandaka city), saying, "If you see or hear of any wise ascetic or brahmin, come and inform us of them." At that time, the Lord of the World, Atthadassī, arrived at the city of Sucandaka. Then, those men who were assigned to inform went and reported to them the arrival of the Possessor of Ten Powers (Dasabala) at that place. Then, Santa and Upasanta, hearing of the arrival of the Tathāgata, became very joyful in heart. Accompanied by a thousand followers, they went out to meet the peerless Blessed One, paid homage, and invited Him. For seven days, they gave an incomparable great alms-giving (Asadisa Mahādāna) to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. On the seventh day, together with the people living in the entire city, they listened to the Dhamma discourse. On that day, ninety-eight thousand people were ordained through the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination and attained Arahantship. In the midst of that assembly of monks, the Blessed One recited the Ovāda-pātimokkha; that was the first assembly.

When the Blessed One preached the Dhamma to His son, Sela Thera, He inspired eighty-eight thousand people with faith, ordained them as 'Ehi Bhikkhus,' and after they attained Arahantship, He recited the Pātimokkha; that was the second assembly. Again, at the gathering for the Mahāmaṅgala Sutta on the full moon day of Māgha, while preaching the Dhamma to devas and humans, He led seventy-eight thousand people to the attainment of Arahantship and recited the Pātimokkha; that was the third assembly. Therefore, it was said (in the Pali):

"There were three assemblies for that Great Sage (Mahesi) as well, consisting of Arahants who were free from taints, pure, peaceful in mind, and endowed with the quality of Tādi.

The first gathering was of ninety-eight thousand Arahants. The second gathering was of eighty-eight thousand Arahants.

The third gathering of the Great Sage (Mahesi) was of seventy-eight thousand Arahants, who were liberated without clinging and were free from taints."

At that time, our Bodhisatta was a wealthy Brahmin householder (Brāhmaṇa-mahāsāla) named Susīma in the city of Campaka, who was highly esteemed in the world. That Susīma Brahmin gave away all his wealth to the poor, the helpless, the destitute, and travelers, and went near the Himalayas to become an ascetic. Having become an ascetic, he attained the eight attainments and the five superknowledges...
257: (The brahmin Susīma, having become an ascetic,) having developed the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and meditative attainments (samāpatti), and being possessed of great psychic power and majesty, he remained waiting for the arising of a Buddha, while demonstrating to the great multitude of people the blameless and blameworthy nature of wholesome and unwholesome states. At another time, the Leader of the World named Atthadassī arose in the world. While He was raining down the rain of the Deathless Dhamma in the midst of the eight assemblies in the great city of Sudassana, Susīma heard the Dhamma of that Blessed One. He then went to the celestial realm and brought back divine flowers such as Mandārava, Paduma, and Pāricchattaka from the deva world. Displaying his own power and manifesting his physical form, he caused a rain of flowers to fall in the four directions like a great cloud covering the four continents. He created a flower pavilion, flower-wrought archways, and golden nets made of flowers all around, and worshipped the Dasabala (the Ten-Powered One) with a Mandārava flower-parasol. That Blessed One also prophesied to him: "In the future, there will be a Buddha named Gotama." Therefore, it was said: 9. "At that time, I was a matted-hair ascetic (jaṭila) of fierce austerity named Susīma, who was regarded as supreme on the earth." "Having brought divine Mandārava flowers, Paduma lotuses, and Pāricchattaka flowers from the deva world, I specially worshipped the Sambuddha." "That Buddha, the Great Sage Atthadassī, also prophesied to me: 'One thousand eight hundred aeons from now, this person will become a Buddha.'" "Having exerted effort in the practice of meditation... may we be in the presence of this Buddha." "Having heard the words of that Buddha, with a joyful and awestruck mind, I undertook further practices for the fulfillment of the ten perfections (pāramī)." In those verses, 'jaṭila' means one who has matted hair, hence an ascetic. 'Mahiyā seṭṭhasammato' means one who is regarded and honored by the entire world as the most noble, the most excellent, and the most distinguished. The capital city of that Blessed One was named Sobhana. King Sāgara was his father, and Sudassanā was his mother. The two chief disciples were the Elders Santa and Upasanta. Abhaya was the attendant. The two chief female disciples were the Elder Nun Dhammā and the Elder Nun Sudhammā. The Campaka tree was his Bodhi tree. His body was eighty cubits in height. 14. "The city was named Sobhana; the royal father was named Sāgara; the mother of the Buddha Atthadassī was named Sudassanā." "He lived in the household life for ten thousand years. There were three noble palaces named Amaragiri, Sugiri, and Vāhana."
258:
His bodily radiance always spread and remained for one yojana all around. His lifespan was one hundred thousand years. He had a chief queen named Visākhā and a son named Sela. He renounced the world on a horse-drawn carriage. Regarding this, it was said:

14. The city of the Buddha Atthadassī was named Sobhana. His father was King Sāgara, and His mother was Queen Sudassanā.

18-19. The Elder Santa and the Elder Upasanta were the chief disciples. The attendant of the Buddha Atthadassī was named Abhaya.

20. The Elder Nun Dhammā and the Elder Nun Sudhammā were the chief female disciples. The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called the Campaka.

22. That peerless Buddha was also eighty cubits tall. He was as beautiful as a king of Sāla trees, or like the full moon.

23. The natural rays of that Buddha were many hundreds of kotis. They always spread for one yojana upwards, downwards, and in the ten directions.

24. That Buddha, the bull among men, the supreme of all beings, the one endowed with the five kinds of vision, remained in the world for one hundred thousand years.

25. Having shown incomparable light and having illuminated the world together with the devas, that Buddha also reached impermanence, like a fire when its fuel is exhausted.

In those verses, "uḷurājāva pūrito" means like the full moon, the king of stars, which is full and free from the five kinds of taints in the autumn season. "Pākati kā" refers to the rays that arise naturally, not by the power of resolve (adhiṭṭhāna). When the Blessed One wished, He could spread His radiance even over many hundreds of thousands of kotis of world-systems. "Raṃsī" means rays. "Upādānasaṅkhayā" means due to the exhaustion of the fuel of grasping, like a fire being extinguished when its fuel is gone. That Blessed One also, through the exhaustion of the four kinds of grasping, attained Parinibbāna in the Anomārāma monastery in the city of Anupama, through the Nibbāna element without remainder. His relics, however, were dispersed and scattered by His resolve. The remaining words in these verses are clear.

## The Commentary on the Chronicle of Atthadassī Buddha is finished.
## The Fourteenth Chronicle of Buddha is finished.
259:
## 17. Commentary on the Chronicle of the Buddha Dhammadassī

After the Buddha Atthadassī attained Parinibbāna and the interval aeon (antarakappa) had passed, when the lifespan of beings, which had been immeasurable, gradually decreased to one hundred thousand years, the Teacher named Dhammadassī, who illuminates the world with radiance, who removes the world's stains such as greed, and who is the sole leader of the world, appeared in the world. That Blessed One, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), was reborn in the Tusita heaven. Passing away from there, He took conception in the womb of Queen Sunandā, the chief consort of King Saraṇa, who was the refuge of the entire world, in the city of Saraṇa. After ten months, the Bodhisatta was born from His mother's womb in the Saraṇa Grove, emerging like the full moon appearing from between the clouds during the rainy season.

At the very moment the Great Being was born from His mother's womb, unjust decisions in the legal treatises and law books vanished of their own accord, and only righteous decisions remained. Therefore, on the day of His naming ceremony, they gave Him the name "Dhammadassī" (Seer of Justice). The Prince lived in the household life for eight thousand years. He had three palaces named Araja, Viraja, and Sudassana. There were one hundred and twenty thousand female attendants, headed by Queen Vicikoḷī.

Having seen the four omens, and when a son named Puññavaḍḍhana was born to Queen Vicikoḷī, the Bodhisatta—who was extremely delicate like a divine prince and was enjoying splendor like that of the gods—arose from His bed in the middle watch of the night. While sitting there, He saw the unseemly state of the sleeping attendants and, being moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), He resolved to renounce the world. Immediately upon this thought, the Sudassana palace rose into the sky and, surrounded by the fourfold army, traveled like a second sun or a divine mansion, descending and stopping near a Red Kuravaka (Bimbijāla) Bodhi tree. It is said that the Great Being, having accepted the saffron robes offered by a Brahma, ordained as a monk and descended from the palace to stand nearby. The palace then traveled through the air again, enclosed the Bodhi tree within it, and settled on the ground. The women also descended from the palace with their attendants and stood about half a gāvuta away. Excluding the women and their maidservants, all the men in that assembly followed the Bodhisatta and ordained; there were one hundred thousand koṭis of monks.

Then, the Bodhisatta Dhammadassī, having practiced austere strivings (dukkaracariya) for seven days, partook of the honey-milk rice offered by Queen Vicikoḷī and spent the day-rest in a jujube grove (Badaravana)...
260:
In the evening, He accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by a barley-field watchman named Sirivaḍḍhana and approached the Bimbijāla (Red Kuravaka) Bodhi tree. He spread a grass mat fifty-three cubits wide and, sitting upon it, He realized Omniscient Wisdom. Uttering the solemn inspired utterance (udāna): "Through many births in saṃsāra... I have reached the destruction of craving," He spent seven weeks (sattasattāha) near the Bodhi tree. Having been requested by a Brahma, and knowing that the one hundred thousand koṭis of monks who had ordained with Him were capable of penetrating the True Dhamma, He traveled the eighteen-league journey in a single day to Isipatana. Surrounded by those monks, He set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion (Dhammacakkappavattana). At that time, the first realization of the Truth (abhisamaya) occurred for one hundred thousand koṭis of beings. Thus, the Blessed One said:

"In that same Maṇḍa aeon, the highly renowned Dhammadassī, having dispelled the darkness of ignorance, shone brilliantly in the world of gods and men.

At the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma by that One of incomparable majesty, the first realization of the Truth occurred for one hundred thousand koṭis of beings."

In those verses, "tamandhakāraṃ" means the darkness of delusion (moha) known as darkness (tamas).

At another time, in the city of Tagara, a king named Sañjaya, seeing the danger in sensual pleasures and the safety in renunciation, took up the life of a hermit. Ninety koṭis of people followed him into renunciation. All of them became attainers of the five superknowledges and the eight meditative attainments. Then, the Teacher Dhammadassī, seeing the maturity of the supporting conditions (upanissaya) of those hermits headed by Sañjaya, traveled through the air to the hermitage of the ascetic Sañjaya. Standing in the air, He preached the Dhamma according to the inclinations of those hermits and caused the Dhamma-eye (dhammacakkhu) to arise. That was the second realization. Thus, the Blessed One said:

"When the Buddha Dhammadassī disciplined the hermit Sañjaya, the second realization of the Truth occurred for ninety koṭis of beings."

At another time, Sakka, the king of the gods, desiring to hear the Dhamma of the One of Ten Powers, approached Him. At that time, the third realization occurred for eighty koṭis of beings. Thus, the Blessed One said:

"When Sakka, with his retinue, approached the Leader, the third realization of the Truth occurred for eighty koṭis of beings."
261:
When He caused His younger half-brothers, Prince Paduma and Prince Phussadeva, to be ordained along with their retinues in the city of Saraṇa, He performed the Visuddhipavāraṇā (Purification Invitation) in the midst of one hundred thousand crores of monks who had been ordained during that Rains Retreat. That was the first assembly. Again, when the Blessed One descended from the celestial realm, there was a second assembly of one hundred crores of monks. When He explained the virtues and benefits of the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) at the Sudassana Monastery and appointed the great disciple named Harita to the foremost rank (Etadagga), the Blessed One recited the Ovāda-pātimokkha in the midst of eighty crores of monks. That was the third assembly. Therefore, it was said:

'For that God of gods as well, there were three assemblies of the taintless Arahants, who possessed peaceful minds and the quality of steadfastness (tādi).

When the Buddha Dhammadassī entered the Rains Retreat in the city of Saraṇa, there was the first gathering of one hundred thousand crores.

Furthermore, when the Buddha came from the celestial realm to the human world, there was the second gathering of one hundred crores.

Furthermore, when the Buddha explained the virtues of the ascetic practices, there was the third gathering of eighty crores.'

At that time, our Bodhisatta was Sakka, the King of Devas. Coming from the two celestial realms surrounded by devas, he worshipped the Tathāgata with divine perfumes, flowers, and divine musical instruments. That Teacher also prophesied to him: 'In the future, he will become a Buddha named Gotama.' Therefore, it was said:

'At that time, I was Sakka, the giver of gifts (Purindada). I worshipped Him with divine perfumes, garlands, and music.

He also prophesied to me while sitting in the midst of the devas: "In one thousand eight hundred aeons from now, this person will become a Buddha."

Having exerted effort in meditation... may we be in the presence of this Buddha,' they prayed.
262:
Having heard the words of that Blessed One, I gladdened my mind even further and undertook a superior practice to fulfill the ten perfections (pāramīs).

The royal city of that Blessed One Dhammadassī was named Saraṇa. His father was the King named Saraṇa, and His mother was named Sunandā. Paduma and Phussadeva were the pair of chief disciples. The attendant was named Sunetta. Khemā and Sabbanāmā were the pair of chief female disciples. The Bodhi tree was the Bimbijāla (Red Kuravaka). His body was eighty cubits in height, and His lifespan was one hundred thousand years. His chief queen was named Vicikoḷidevī, and His son was named Puññavaḍḍhana. He renounced the world by means of a palace. Therefore, it was said:

'The city was named Saraṇa, and the khattiya (king) was named Saraṇa. Sunandā was the mother of the Teacher Dhammadassī.

Paduma and Phussadeva were the chief disciples, and Sunetta was the attendant of the Teacher Dhammadassī.

Khemā and Sabbanāmā were the chief female disciples. The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called Bimbijāla.

That Buddha, peerless and unequalled, rose to eighty cubits in height. He shone intensely with His majesty throughout the ten thousand world systems.

Like a kingly Sāla tree in full bloom, like a streak of lightning in the sky, or like the sun at midday—thus did He shine.

The lifespan of that One of incomparable majesty was equal (to the people of that time). The One with the Fivefold Vision remained in the world for one hundred thousand years.

Having shown the light and made the Dispensation (Sāsana) stainless, He passed away like the moon in the sky. He attained Parinibbāna along with His disciples.'

In those verses, 'Bimbijāla' refers to the Red Kuravaka tree. 'In the ten thousand world systems' means within the ten thousand world elements. 'Vijjūva' means like a streak of lightning. 'Shone' means that just as lightning in the sky and the sun at midday shine, so did the Blessed One shine. 'Equal' means that His lifespan was exactly equal to that of all human beings. 'Cavi' means passed away (deceased).
263:
It means he passed away like the moon from the sky. The Blessed One Dhammadassī attained Parinibbāna at the Kesārāma monastery in the city of Sālavatī. The remaining words in these verses are clear.

## The Commentary on the Chronicle of the Blessed One Dhammadassī is finished.

## The Fifteenth Chronicle of the Buddhas is finished.

## 18. Commentary on the Chronicle of Siddhattha Buddha

After the Blessed One Dhammadassī attained Parinibbāna and his Dispensation had disappeared, when that aeon had passed, and after one thousand, seven hundred, and six aeons had elapsed, ninety-four aeons ago from this Bhadda-kappa, in a single Sāra-kappa, the Teacher named Siddhattha, who practiced for the benefit of the world and realized the supreme truth, appeared in the world. Regarding this, it was said:

"After Dhammadassī, the leader of the world was Siddhattha; having destroyed all the darkness of delusion, he appeared like the rising sun."

The Bodhisatta Siddhattha, having fulfilled the perfections, was reborn in the Tusita heaven. Passing away from there, he took conception in the womb of Queen Suphassā, the chief consort of King Udena in the city of Vebhāra. After ten months, he was born in the Vīriya Garden. When the Great Being was born, the undertakings and desired goals of all people were accomplished. Therefore, his relatives named him "Siddhattha". Prince Siddhattha lived in the palace for ten thousand years. He had three palaces named Kokā, Suppala, and Paduma. Forty-eight thousand attendants, headed by Queen Somanassā, served him.

Having seen the four signs, and when his son Prince Anupama was born to Queen Somanassā, he renounced the world on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, departing on a golden palanquin to the Vīriya Garden to become a monk. One hundred thousand crores of people followed him and became monks. The Great Being practiced asceticism (dukkara-cariyā) with those monks for ten months. On the full moon day of Vesākha, in the Brahmin village of Asadisa, he accepted and consumed the honey-thickened milk rice offered by a Brahmin maiden named Sunettā. Having spent the day in a grove of jujube trees, in the evening, he accepted the eight handfuls of grass offered by a barley-field watchman named Varuṇa...
264:
Having taken conception, when ten months had passed, he was born from his mother's womb in the Vīriya Garden. When the Great Being was born, the undertakings of all people and their desired goals were accomplished. Therefore, his relatives named the prince "Siddhattha". Prince Siddhattha lived in the palace for ten thousand years. He had three palaces named Kokā, Suppala, and Paduma. Forty-eight thousand attendants, headed by Queen Somanassā, served him.

Having seen the four signs, and when his son Prince Anupama was born to Queen Somanassā, he renounced the world on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, departing on a golden palanquin to the Vīriya Garden to become a monk. One hundred thousand crores of people followed the Bodhisatta and became monks. The Great Being practiced asceticism (dukkara-cariyā) with those monks for ten months. On the full moon day of Vesākha, in the Brahmin village of Asadisa, he accepted and consumed the sweet honey-thickened milk rice offered by a Brahmin maiden named Sunettā. Having spent the day in a grove of jujube trees, in the evening, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by a barley-field watchman named Varuṇa and approached the Kaṇikāra Bodhi tree. He spread the grass mat, forty cubits wide, sat in the cross-legged posture, and attained Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). He uttered the solemn exclamation: "Through many births in saṃsāra... I have reached the end of craving." After spending seven weeks (forty-nine days), he saw that the one hundred thousand crores of monks who had renounced with him were capable of penetrating the Four Noble Truths. He traveled through the air, descended at the Gaya-migadāya, and turned the Wheel of Dhamma for them. At that time, the first awakening (abhisamaya) of one hundred thousand crores of devas and humans occurred. Regarding this, the Blessed One said in the Pali text:

## Even he, having attained Enlightenment and delivering the world including the devas,
## Rained down the cloud of Dhamma, bringing peace to the world including the devas.

## For him of incomparable power, there were three awakenings;
## The first awakening was for one hundred thousand crores.

In those verses, "sadēvakaṃ" means the world together with the devas. "Dhammameghena" means by raining down the great rain of Dhamma discourse. Again, in the city of Bhīmaratha, being invited by King Bhīmaratha, he sat in the assembly hall built in the center of the city. With a Brahma-voice that was as melodious as the song of the Karavīka bird, pleasant to hear, extremely sweet, reaching the hearts of wise men, like the sprinkling of the deathless nectar, he filled the ten directions and struck the great drum of the deathless Dhamma. At that time, the second awakening of ninety crores of devas and humans occurred. Regarding this, it was said in the Pali text:

## Furthermore, in Bhīmaratha, when he struck the drum,
## At that time, the second awakening was for ninety crores.

When he was teaching the Buddhavaṃsa (Chronicle of the Buddhas) at the gathering of relatives in the city of Vebhāra, he caused the Eye of Dhamma (Sotāpatti-magga-ñāṇa) to arise for ninety crores of devas and humans. That was the third awakening. Regarding this, it was said in the Pali text:

## When the Buddha taught the Dhamma in Vebhāra, that supreme city,
## At that time, the third awakening was for ninety crores.

In the city of Amara, which was as beautiful and delightful as a city of devas, two brothers named Sambhala and Sumitta reigned. Then, the Teacher Siddhattha, seeing the strong supporting condition (upanissaya) for these two royal brothers to attain the Paths and Fruits, traveled through the air and descended in the center of the city of Amara. He displayed his footprints (padacetī) as if treading on the ground with feet adorned with the wheel-marks. He went to the Amara Garden and sat on a stone slab that was very delightful and cooled by his own compassion. Then, the two royal brothers went to the presence of the Blessed One Siddhattha...
265:
Seeing the perfection of the strong supporting condition (upanissaya-sampatti) for the attainment of the Paths and Fruits of the royal brothers, the Buddha Siddhattha traveled through the air and descended in the middle of the city of Amara. Displaying his footprints (pada-cetiya) as if treading upon the ground with feet adorned with the wheel-marks (cakka-lakkhaṇa), he went to the Amaruyyāna garden and sat upon a stone slab that was exceedingly delightful and made cool by his own compassion. Then, the two royal brothers, seeing the footprints of the Possessor of Ten Powers (Dasabala), followed the tracks and approached the Teacher Siddhattha—the leader of the whole world who had attained the supreme benefit—along with their retinue. Having paid homage, they sat down surrounding the Blessed One. The Blessed One preached the Dhamma to them according to their dispositions (ajjhāsaya). Having heard the Dhamma discourse, faith arose in them; they all went forth as monks and attained Arahantship. In the midst of those one hundred crores of Arahants, the Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha; that was the first assembly (sannipāta). In the city of Vebhāra, in the midst of ninety crores of monks who had gone forth during the gathering of his relatives, he recited the Pātimokkha; that was the second assembly. In the Sudassana monastery, in the midst of eighty crores of monks who had gathered, he recited the Pātimokkha; that was the third assembly. Regarding this, it was said:

“There were three assemblies even in the time of that Supreme among Men,
Of the stainless Arahants, who were of peaceful mind and such (tādi).

One hundred crores, ninety crores, and also eighty crores,
These were the three occasions in the gathering of the stainless ones.”

In those verses, ‘navutīnaṃ, asītiyāpi ca koṭinaṃ’ means that there were assemblies of ninety crores and eighty crores of Arahants. ‘Ete āsuṃ tayo ṭhānā’ means that these three places (or occasions) of assembly occurred. There is also a variant reading: ‘ṭhānānetāni tīṇi ahesuṃ’.

At that time, our Bodhisatta was a Brahmin named Maṅgala in the city of Surasena. Having mastered the Vedas and the auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas), and having renounced a store of wealth amounting to many crores to the poor, the helpless, and others, he delighted in solitude and went forth as an ascetic. While living there, having developed the meditative absorptions (jhānas) and higher knowledges (abhiññās), he heard that “The Buddha named Siddhattha has appeared in the world.” He approached and paid homage to the Buddha, and after listening to the Dhamma discourse, he traveled by psychic power to the Jambu tree—by which this continent is known as Jambudīpa—and brought fruit from that tree. He then invited the Teacher Siddhattha, who was surrounded by ninety crores of monks, to stay at the Surasena monastery and served them with the Jambu fruits.
266:
He distributed and offered the fruits. Then the Teacher, having partaken of that fruit, gave the prophecy: “Ninety-four aeons (kappas) from now, he will become a Buddha named Gotama.”

Regarding this, it was said:
“At that time, I was an ascetic named Maṅgala,
Of fierce heat, difficult to overcome, and endowed with the power of higher knowledge.

Having brought fruit from the Jambu tree, I gave it to Siddhattha.
The Fully Enlightened One, having accepted it, spoke these words:

‘Behold this ascetic, a matted-hair one (jaṭila) of fierce austerity;
Ninety-four aeons from now, he will become a Buddha.’

‘Having exerted effort in meditation... may we be in the presence of this Buddha.’ (Thus the people prayed).

Hearing his words, I gladdened my heart even more,
And I undertook a superior practice for the fulfillment of the ten perfections (pāramīs).”

In that verse, “duppasaho” means difficult to approach. Or, the text remains as it is. The city of that Blessed One was named Vebhāra. His father was King Udena, also known by the name Jayasena. His mother was Suphassā. Sambhala and Sumitta were the two chief disciples. There was an attendant named Revata. Sīvalā and Surāmā were the two chief female disciples. The Kaṇikāra tree was his Bodhi tree. His body was sixty cubits in height. His lifespan was one hundred thousand years. Somanassā was the chief queen. Anupama was his son. He renounced the world by a golden palanquin (suvaṇṇasivikā).

Regarding this, it was said:
“The city was named Vebhāra, the king was named Udena,
The mother of the Great Sage Siddhattha was named Suphassā.

Sambhala and Sumitta were the chief disciples,
The attendant of the Great Sage Siddhattha was named Revata.

Sīvalā and Surāmā were the chief female disciples,
The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called Kaṇikāra.”
267:
That Blessed Siddhattha was sixty cubits tall and ascended into the sky. Resembling a golden sacrificial post, he shone brilliantly throughout the ten thousand world systems. That Buddha Siddhattha, who was equal only to the peerless Buddhas, without a rival or counterpart, and endowed with the five types of vision, remained in the world for a hundred thousand years. Having displayed a vast radiance, having caused his disciples to blossom (with the flowers of the paths, fruits, and attainments), and having sported with the noble attainments and supernormal powers, he attained Parinibbāna together with his disciples.

In those verses, 'saṭṭhiratanaṃ' means he ascended sixty cubits high into the sky. 'Kañcanagghiyasaṅkāso' means having an appearance like a golden sacrificial post (toraṇa) adorned with various jewels. 'Dasasahassī virocati' means shining brilliantly in the ten thousand world systems. 'Vipulaṃ' refers to the sublime radiance. 'Pupphāpetvāna' means causing them to blossom with the flowers of jhāna, supernormal powers, paths, fruits, and attainments, thereby bringing them to the pinnacle of supreme beauty. 'Vilāsetvā' means having sported or dwelled gracefully. 'Samāpatyā' means through the mundane and supramundane attainments and supernormal powers. 'Nibbuto' means he attained Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna).

It is said that the Teacher Siddhattha attained Parinibbāna in the Anoma Garden in the city of Kañcanaveḷu. Right there, a cetiya four leagues high, made of the seven kinds of jewels, was built for that Buddha. The meaning of the remaining verses is clear in every respect.

## The Commentary on the Chronicle of Buddha Siddhattha is finished.
## The Sixteenth Chronicle of the Buddhas is finished.
## 19. The Commentary on the Chronicle of Buddha Tissa

After the time of the Blessed Siddhattha, there was one aeon empty of Buddhas. Ninety-two aeons ago from this present aeon, two Buddhas, Tissa and Phussa, appeared in a single aeon (Maṇḍa-kappa). Among them, the Great Being named Tissa, having fulfilled the perfections, was reborn in the Tusita heaven. Passing away from there, he took conception in the womb of Queen Padumā, whose eyes were like lotus petals and who was the chief consort of King Janasandha in the city of Khemaka...
268:
After ten months had passed, he was born from his mother's womb in the Anoma Garden. He lived in the household life in the palace for seven thousand years. For that Bodhisatta, there were three palaces named Guhāsela, Nārisaya, and Nisabha. There were thirty-three thousand attendant women, headed by Queen Subhaddā.

Having seen the four omens, and when Prince Ānanda was born to Queen Subhaddā, the Bodhisatta departed on the Great Renunciation, riding the peerless noble horse named Sonuttara, and became a monk. Ten million people followed him and became monks. Surrounded by those monks, he practiced asceticism for eight months. On the full moon day of Visākha, having partaken of the honey-milk rice offered by the daughter of the merchant Vīra in the market town of Vīra, he spent the day's rest in the Salala forest. In the evening, accepting eight handfuls of grass offered by the barley-field guard named Vijitasaṅgāmaka, he approached the Asana Bodhi tree. Having spread the grass mat forty cubits wide and sitting cross-legged upon it, he defeated Mara and his army and attained Omniscience. He uttered the solemn utterance: 'Through many a birth in saṃsāra... I have attained the destruction of cravings.' He spent the seven weeks (satta-sattāha) near the Bodhi tree.

Seeing that the two princes, Brahmadatta and Udaya, in the city of Yasavatī, along with their retinues, possessed the supporting conditions (upanissaya) for attaining the paths and fruits, he traveled through the air and descended at the Yasavatī Migadāya. He sent the garden keeper to call the princes. Then, making the ten thousand world systems understand with his Brahma-like voice—which was distinct, pervasive, and sweet—he turned the Wheel of Dhamma for the princes and their retinues. At that time, the first realization of the Dhamma occurred for one billion beings. Referring to this, it was said:

'After Siddhattha, the peerless and unrivaled Tissa, the Leader of the World, of infinite power and immeasurable fame, appeared.

Dispelling the darkness and illuminating the world including the devas, the compassionate Great Hero, endowed with the five eyes, arose in the world.

For that Buddha, too, there was incomparable psychic power, and incomparable virtue and concentration. Having reached the pinnacle of all perfections, he turned the Wheel of Dhamma.'
269:
“That Buddha Tissa made known the pure word of Dhamma in the ten thousand world systems. In the first teaching of the Dhamma, a hundred crores of beings realized the Four Noble Truths.”

In that verse, ‘Sabbattha’ means having reached the further shore in all dhammas. ‘Dasasahassī’ means in the ten thousand world systems. Then, at another time, ten million monks who had ordained with the Teacher Tissa, having left the company of the Great Being at the time he approached the root of the Bodhi tree, went elsewhere. Hearing that “Tissa the Perfectly Enlightened One has set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma,” they came to the Yasavatī Deer Park, paid homage to the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala), and sat surrounding him. The Blessed One taught the Dhamma to them; at that time, there was the second realization of ninety crores of beings. Again, at the conclusion of the gathering for the Mahāmangala Sutta, there was the third realization of sixty crores of beings. Therefore, it was said:

“At that time, there was the second realization of ninety crores of beings, and the third realization of sixty crores of beings. The Buddha released humans, devas, and brahmas from their bonds.”

In that verse, ‘dutiyo navutikoṭīnaṃ’ means the second realization was for ninety crores of living beings. ‘Bandhanāto’ means from the bonds, meaning he released them from the ten fetters (saṃyojana). Now, wishing to show the beings who were released by their specific nature, he said ‘naramarū’. ‘Naramarū’ means humans and devas.

It is said that in the city of Yasavatī, surrounded by a hundred thousand Arahants who had ordained during the rainy season, he performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony; that was the first assembly of disciples. When the Lord of the World, the Buddha Tissa, arrived at the city of Nārivāhana, Prince Nārivāhana, the son of King Sujāta (who was well-born on both sides), went out with his retinue to meet him. He invited the One of Ten Powers together with the Saṅgha of monks, gave incomparable alms (asadisa-dāna) for seven days, handed over his kingdom to his son, and ordained as an ‘Ehi Bhikkhu’ in the presence of the Perfectly Enlightened One Tissa, the Sovereign of the whole world. That ordination of his was famous in all directions. Therefore, people from various places came and followed Prince Nārivāhana into ordination. At that time, the Tathāgata recited the Pātimokkha in the midst of nine million monks; that was the second assembly of disciples.

Again, at the gathering of relatives in the city of Khemavatī, having heard the Dhamma discourse on the Buddhavaṃsa, eight million people ordained in the presence of Buddha Tissa and reached the fruit of Arahantship. Surrounded by those monks, the Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha; that was the third assembly of disciples. Therefore, it was said:

“In the time of Buddha Tissa, the Supreme Leader of the World, there were three assemblies of Arahants who were free from the taints of defilements, possessed of peaceful minds, and endowed with the quality of Tādi.”
270:
At the gathering of relatives in the city of Khemavatī, having heard the Dhamma discourse on the Buddhavaṃsa, eight million people ordained in the presence of that Blessed One and attained the fruit of Arahantship. Surrounded by those monks, the Sugata recited the Pātimokkha; that was the third assembly. Referring to that, the Blessed One said:

“There were three assemblies in the time of Tissa, the Supreme Leader of the World, of Arahants who were stainless, of peaceful mind, and possessed of the quality of Tādi.”

“The first gathering was of a hundred thousand Arahants; the second gathering was of nine million.”

“The third gathering was of eight million Arahants, who were stainless and blossomed through liberation.”

At that time, our Bodhisatta was a king named Sujāta in the city of Yasavatī. Having abandoned the prosperous and flourishing kingdom, the accumulation of many crores of wealth, and his retinue of beloved people as if they were mere grass and reeds, his heart was struck with urgency (saṃvega) regarding birth and so on. He went forth and became an ascetic. Being possessed of great psychic power and majesty, when he heard “A Buddha has arisen in the world,” his whole body was suffused with fivefold joy. With a mind eager to listen, he approached and paid homage to the Blessed One Tissa and thought: “Now, I shall worship the Blessed One with divine flowers such as Mandārava and Pāricchattaka.”

Thereafter, that Bodhisatta ascetic, having thought thus, went to the heavenly realm by psychic power, entered the Cittalatā Grove, filled a jewel basket measuring a gāvuta with divine flowers such as Paduma, Pāricchattaka, and Mandārava, and returned through the sky. He worshipped the Blessed One with those divine fragrant flowers. Holding a lotus parasol—with a handle of gems, a canopy of gold, leaves of rubies, and fragrant filaments—over the head of the Blessed One, he stood in the midst of the fourfold assembly. Then the Blessed One prophesied to that ascetic: “Ninety-two aeons from now, there will be a Buddha named Gotama.” Referring to that, the Blessed One said:

“At that time, I was a kshatriya named Sujāta; having cast aside great wealth, I entered the life of a sage (isi).”
271:
When I had gone forth as an ascetic, the Leader of the World, the Blessed One Tissa, appeared. Hearing the word "Buddha", joy arose within me.

Taking divine Mandārava flowers, Paduma lotuses, and Pāricchattaka flowers in both hands, and shaking my bark garments, I approached the Blessed One Tissa.

Taking those flowers, I offered them by placing them over the head of the Conqueror, the Blessed One Tissa, the supreme Leader of the World, who was surrounded by the fourfold assembly.

That Buddha, seated in the midst of the people, also prophesied of me: "Ninety-two aeons from now, this ascetic will become a Buddha named Gotama."

They prayed: "Having exerted effort in the practice of meditation... may we realize Nibbāna in the presence of this Blessed One."

Hearing his words, I further gladdened my mind. To fulfill the Ten Perfections, I undertook a superior practice.

In those verses, "mayi pabbajite" means while I was in the state of an ascetic. Although it is written as "mama pabbajitaṃ santaṃ" in palm-leaf manuscripts, it should be understood as a scribal error due to negligence. "Upapajjatha" means it arose. "Ubho hatthehi" means with both hands. "Paggayha" means having taken and raised. "Dhunamāno" means shaking the bark garments. "Cātuvaṇṇaparivutaṃ" means one who is surrounded by the fourfold assembly (kings, brahmins, householders, and monks). Some read it as "catuvaṇṇehi parivutaṃ".

The city of that Blessed One was named Khemā. His father was a king named Janasandha, and his mother was Queen Padumā. Brahmadatta and Udaya were the two chief male disciples. His attendant was named Samaṅga. Phussā and Sudattā were the two chief female disciples. The Bodhi tree was the Asana tree. His body was sixty cubits in height, and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years. His chief queen was named Subhaddā, and his son was named Ānanda. He renounced the world on a horse-drawn carriage. Thus, the Blessed One said:

## Khemakaṃ nāma nagaraṃ, janasandho nāma khattiyo.
## Padumā nāma janikā, tissassa ca mahesino.
272:
The Elders Brahmadatta and Udaya were the chief disciples. The attendant named Samaṅga served the Great Sage, the Blessed One Tissa.

The nuns Phussā and Sudattā were the chief female disciples. The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called the Asana.

That Buddha, the Conqueror who overcame the five Maras, was sixty cubits in height. Peerless and incomparable, he appeared like the Himālaya mountains.

The lifespan of that Blessed One of incomparable majesty was also supreme. The Visionary (possessing the five eyes) remained in the world for one hundred thousand years.

Having enjoyed great fame—excellent, noble, and supreme—and having shone like a great mass of fire, he attained Parinibbāna together with his disciples.

Like a cloud dispersed by the wind, like a dewdrop evaporated by the sun, like darkness dispelled by a lamp, he attained Parinibbāna together with his disciples.

In those verses, 'uccattane' means in height. 'Himavā viya dissati' means he appears like the Himālaya mountains. Or it is just as the text says. Just as the Himālaya mountains, with five peaks and a height of one hundred yojanas, appear extremely delightful even to those standing far away due to their height and serene appearance, so too did the Blessed One appear. 'Anuttaro' means neither too tall nor too short. The lifespan was one hundred thousand years. 'Uttamaṃ pavaraṃ seṭṭhaṃ' are synonyms for each other. 'Ussavo' means a dewdrop. Just as clouds, dewdrops, and darkness are overcome by wind, sunlight, and lamps, so the Blessed One, together with his disciples, attained Parinibbāna, being overcome by the wind, sun, and lamp of impermanence.

The Blessed One Tissa attained Parinibbāna at the Sunandārāma monastery in the city of Sunandavatī. The meaning of the remaining verses is clear.

## The Commentary on the Chronicle of Tissa Buddha is finished.
## The seventeenth Chronicle of Buddhas is finished.
273:
## 20. Phussabuddhavaṃsavaṇṇanā

After the time of the Blessed One Tissa, as the lifespan gradually decreased and then increased to an immeasurable length, and then decreased again to ninety thousand years, the Teacher named Phussa appeared in the world in that same Maṇḍa kappa. That Blessed One also fulfilled the perfections, was reborn in the Tusita heaven, and passing away from there, took rebirth in the womb of Queen Sirimā, the chief consort of King Jayasena in the city of Kāsika. After ten months had passed, he was born from his mother's womb in the Sirimā Park. That Bodhisatta lived in the household life for nine thousand years. He had three palaces: Garuḷapakkha, Haṃsa, and Suvaṇṇabhāra. There were thirty thousand female attendants led by Kisāgotamī.

Having seen the four signs, and when a son named Anupama was born to Kisāgotamī, he departed on the back of a noble decorated elephant for the Great Renunciation and became a monk. One crore of people followed him and became monks. Surrounded by those monks, he practiced asceticism for six months. Then, leaving the group, he practiced alone for seven days. On the full moon day of Visākha, he partook of the honey-milk rice offered by a merchant's daughter named Sirivaḍḑhā in a certain city. After spending the day in a Siṃsapā grove, in the evening, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by a lay devotee named Sirivaḍḑha. Approaching the Āmalaka Bodhi tree, he defeated Māra and his army and attained Omniscience. He uttered the joyful exclamation (udāna): "Through many a birth in saṃsāra... I have reached the destruction of cravings." He spent seven weeks near the Bodhi tree. Seeing that the one crore of monks who had renounced with him were capable of realizing the Four Noble Truths, he traveled through the air and descended at the Isipatana Deer Park near the city of Saṅkassa. In the midst of those monks, he turned the Wheel of Dhamma. At that time, the first realization occurred for one hundred thousand crores of beings. Regarding this, the Blessed One said:

"In that same Maṇḍa kappa, there was the unsurpassed Teacher, incomparable and equal only to the unequaled, Phussa, the supreme leader of the world."

"He too, having destroyed all darkness and untangled the great tangle, satisfying the world including the devas, rained down the water of the Deathless."
274:
"When Phussa turned the Wheel of Dhamma under the auspicious constellation, the first realization occurred for one hundred thousand crores."

In those verses, "tattheva maṇḍakappamhi" means in the aeon where two Buddhas appear; that aeon was previously called "Maṇḍa kappa". "Vijaṭetvā" means having relinquished (untangled). In the word "mahājaṭaṃ", "jaṭā" is a synonym for craving (taṇhā). Indeed, that craving is called "jaṭā" (tangle) because it arises repeatedly in objects such as forms, etc., in an upward and downward manner, and because it binds things together, resembling a tangle of thread, a thicket, a net, or a cake. He untangled that great tangle. "Sadevakaṃ" means the world including the devas. "Abhivassi" means he rained down. "Amatambunā" means satisfying them with the water of Dhamma-talk known as the Deathless (Amata), he rained down.

Furthermore, at one time in the city of Bārāṇasī, a king named Sirivaḍḑha renounced his great mass of wealth and became an ascetic. The ascetics who renounced with that king numbered nine million. When the Blessed One preached the Dhamma to them, the second realization occurred for nine million (beings). Again, when he preached the Dhamma to his son, Prince Anupama, the third realization occurred for eight million (beings). Therefore, it was said:

"The second realization was for nine million, the third realization was for eight million."

Thereafter, at another time in the city of Kaṇṇakujja, Prince Surakkhita and the chaplain's son, Prince Dhammasena, when the Fully Enlightened One Phussa arrived at their city, went out to meet him with six million men, paid homage, and invited him. After giving a great alms-giving for seven days and hearing the Dhamma-talk of the One of Ten Powers, they gained faith in the Blessed One and renounced along with their followers, reaching Arahantship. In the midst of those six million monks, the Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha; that was the first assembly (sannipāta). Again, in the city of Kāsika, in the gathering of sixty relatives of King Jayasena, he preached the Buddhavaṃsa. Hearing that Dhamma, five million people renounced by the "Ehi Bhikkhu" ordination and reached Arahantship. In the midst of those Arahants, the Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha; that was the second assembly. Again, in the gathering for the Mahāmaṅgala Sutta, having heard the talk on blessings (maṅgala), four million men renounced and reached Arahantship. Having arrived in the midst of those Arahants...
275:
The Sugata recited the Pātimokkha; that was the third assembly. Regarding this, it was said:

“There were three assemblies of the Arahants for Phussa, the Great Sage—those whose taints were exhausted, who were stainless, of calm minds, and steadfast.

“The first gathering was of six million Arahants; the second gathering was of five million Arahants.

“The third gathering was of four million Arahants, who were liberated without clinging and for whom rebirth was cut off.”

At that time, our Bodhisatta was a King named Vijitāvī in the city of Arindama. Having heard the Dhamma of the Buddha Phussa, he gained faith in the Blessed One and gave a great offering. Renouncing his great kingdom, he became a monk in the presence of the Blessed One. Having mastered the Three Pitakas, he became a Bearer of the Three Pitakas (Tipiṭakadhara) and preached the Dhamma to the multitudes, and he fulfilled the Perfection of Virtue (Sīla-pāramī). The Buddha Phussa also prophesied of him, “This person will become a Buddha.” Regarding this, it was said:

“At that time, I was a King named Vijitāvī. Having renounced my great kingdom, I became a monk in his presence.

“That Buddha Phussa, the Chief Leader of the World, also prophesied of me: ‘In the ninety-second kappa from now, this person will become a Buddha.’

“Striving in exertion... for the fulfillment of the ten perfections.

“Having mastered all the Suttanta, the Vinaya, and the ninefold Dispensation of the Teacher, I adorned the Dispensation of the Conqueror.

“Dwelling there heedfully, having developed the meditation of the Divine Abodes (Brahmavihāra) and reached the peak of supernormal knowledges (abhiññā), I went to the Brahma world.”

The city of that Blessed One was named Kāsika. King Jayasena was his father, and Sirimā was his mother. Surakkhita and Dhammasena were the two chief disciples. Sabhiya was the attendant. Cālā and Upacālā were the two chief female disciples. The Bodhi tree was the Wood-apple (Āmalaka). His body was fifty-eight cubits in height.
276:
The lifespan of the Buddha Phussa was ninety thousand years. His chief queen was named Kisāgotamī, and his son was named Anupama. He renounced the world by means of an elephant carriage. Regarding this, it was said:

14. The city was named Kāsika; the King was named Jayasena. The mother of the Buddha Phussa was named Sirimā.

15. He lived for ninety thousand years ruling the palace. That Bodhisatta had three noble palaces: Garuḷapakkhā, Haṃsā, and Suvaṇṇabhāra.

16. There were thirty thousand well-adorned court ladies. The queen was named Kisāgotamī, and the son was named Anupama.

17. Having seen the four omens, he renounced the world by an elephant carriage. He practiced the ascetic life for six months.

18. Being requested by the Brahma, the Buddha Phussa, the foremost leader of the world, of great exertion, the supreme among men, preached the Wheel of Dhamma in the Migadāya (Deer Park).

19. The Elder Surakkhita and the Elder Dhammasena were the chief disciples of the Buddha Phussa. The attendant was named Sabhiya.

20. The Theri Cālā and the Theri Upacālā were the chief female disciples. The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called Āmaṇḍa (Wood-apple).

21. The lay disciples Dhanañjaya and Visākha were the chief male attendants. The lay disciples Padumā and Nāgā were the chief female attendants.

22. That Buddha was fifty-eight cubits in height, and he was as radiant as the sun and as the full moon.

23. At that time, the lifespan was ninety thousand years. Remaining for that long, he saved many beings.

24. Having exhorted many beings and saved many people, that Teacher of incomparable fame attained Parinibbāna together with his disciples.

In those verses, "Āmaṇḍa" refers to the Wood-apple tree. "Ovāditvā" means having given advice or instruction. "So pi satthā atulayaso" means that Teacher also had immeasurable retinue or glory. There is also a reading "So jahitvā amitayaso," which means that the Buddha, having left behind all the extraordinary qualities mentioned, [attained Parinibbāna].

It is said that Phussa the Perfectly Enlightened One attained Parinibbāna at the Senārāma monastery in the city of Kusinārā. His relics were widely distributed. The meaning of the remaining verses is clear in all respects.

## The Chronicle of Phussa Buddha is finished.
## The Eighteenth Chronicle of Buddhas is finished.
277:
## 21. Commentary on the Chronicle of the Buddha Vipassī

After the time of the Buddha Phussa, when that aeon and others had passed, ninety-one aeons ago from this present Bhadda-kappa, the Teacher named Vipassī arose in the world. He was one who had conquered all life-spans, whose intentions were devoted to the welfare of others, and who saw clearly in all things. Having fulfilled the perfections, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven, which shines with the brilliance of many jewels and gems. Passing away from there, he took conception in the womb of Queen Bandhumatī, the chief consort of King Bandhumat, who had many kinsmen, in the city of Bandhumatī.

After ten months had passed, he was born from his mother’s womb in the Khema Migadāya (Deer Park), like the full moon emerging from a dark rain cloud. On the day of his naming, the readers of marks and his relatives named him 'Vipassī' because they could see clearly and purely even during the intervals of blinking, which normally cause darkness, or because he looked with open eyes. Some also say he was called 'Vipassī' because he saw after investigating and discerning. He lived in the household life for eight thousand years. He had three palaces named Nanda, Sunanda, and Sirimā.

There were one hundred and twenty thousand female attendants, headed by Queen Sudassanā. Queen Sudassanā was also known as Sutanū. After eight thousand years had passed, having seen the four signs, and when a son named Samavaṭṭakkhandha was born to Queen Sutanū, he departed on the Great Renunciation by a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses and became an ascetic. Eighty-four thousand men followed him into the ascetic life. That Great Being, surrounded by those monks, practiced austerities for eight months. On the full moon day of Visākha, having partaken of the honey-milk rice offered by the daughter of the wealthy merchant Sudassana, he spent the day in a Sāla grove adorned with flowers. Accepting eight handfuls of grass offered by a barley-field guard named Sujata, and seeing the adorned Pāṭali Bodhi tree, he approached it from the southern direction.

The trunk of that Pāṭali tree rose up fifty cubits on that day, and its branches were fifty cubits long, reaching a total height of one hundred cubits. On that very day, that Pāṭali tree was entirely covered from its roots with extremely fragrant flowers, as if they had been arranged in clusters. Divine scents wafted around. At that time, not only did this single Pāṭali tree bloom, but in the ten thousand universes...
278:
...all Pāṭali trees bloomed. Not only the Pāṭali trees, but all trees, shrubs, and creepers in the ten thousand universes also bloomed. The great ocean was covered with five-colored lotuses—the Paduma, Kuvalaya, Uppala, and Kumuda—and its waters became cool and sweet. The entire interior of the ten thousand universes was filled with banners and garlands. In various places, the ground was decorated with various fragrant flowers mixed with flower garlands, and it became dark with the smoke of incense and aromatic powders.

Approaching that spot, he spread a mat of grass fifty-three cubits wide. Resolving with effort endowed with four factors, he sat down, making the vow: 'As long as I have not become a Buddha, I shall not rise from this seat.' Having sat thus, he defeated the Lord of Māra together with the host of Māra. Then, through the sequence of the Paths, he attained the four Path Knowledges, and immediately following the Paths, the four Fruit Knowledges, the fourfold Analytical Insights, the knowledge of discerning the four modes of birth, the knowledge of discerning the five destinations, the four Intrepidities, the six Uncommon Knowledges, and all the qualities of a Buddha. With his aspirations fulfilled, while still seated on the throne of enlightenment, he uttered this inspired verse:

'Through many a birth in saṃsāra have I wandered, seeking but not finding the builder of this house. Sorrowful is repeated birth. O house-builder, you are seen! You shall not build the house again. All your rafters are broken, the ridge-pole is shattered. My mind has reached the unconditioned; I have attained the destruction of craving.'

'Just as the destination of a bright fire, struck by a blacksmith’s iron hammer, is not known as it gradually goes out; even so, there is no way to describe the destination of those who are well-liberated, who have crossed the flood of the bonds of sensual desire, and who have attained the unshakable bliss of Nibbāna.'

Having uttered these inspired verses, he spent seven weeks near the Bodhi tree. Accepting the request of the Brahma, he looked for the spiritual potential (upanissaya) of his half-brother Prince Khaṇḍa and the chaplain’s son Tissa. He traveled through the air and descended at the Khema Migadāya. He had the park keeper summon those two, and in the midst of their followers, he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma. At that time, there was the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) by countless devas. Referring to this, it was said:

'After the Buddha Phussa, the Buddha named Vipassī, the best of bipeds, the one endowed with vision, arose in the world.'
279:
“Having destroyed all ignorance and attained the supreme enlightenment, He set out for the city of Bandhumatī to turn the Wheel of Dhamma.

“The Teacher turned the Wheel of Dhamma and caused both Khaṇḍa and Tissa to realize the Four Noble Truths. The first realization of the devas and humans was so vast that it could not be expressed in numbers.”

In those verses, 'padāletvā' means having broken or destroyed; it means having destroyed the darkness of ignorance. There is also a variant reading “vattevta cakkamārāme”; in that reading, 'ārāme' means in the Migadāya (Deer Park) named Khema. 'Ubho bodhesi' means He caused those two—His younger brother Prince Khaṇḍa and the chaplain’s son Tissa—to realize the Truths. 'Gaṇanāya na vattabbo' means that by way of the realization of the devas and Brahmas, there is no limit to the count.

Then, on another occasion, He caused the eighty-four thousand monks, who had followed Prince Khaṇḍa and the chaplain’s son Tissa into monkhood, to drink the nectar of Dhamma. That was the second realization. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Furthermore, the Buddha of immeasurable fame and glory revealed the Truths there in that city of Bandhumatī. At that time, the realization of the Truths by eighty-four thousand [beings] was the second realization.”

In that verse, 'tattha' means in the Migadāya named Khema. In the passage “caturāsītisahassāni, sambuddhamanupabbajuṃ,” those men called the eighty-four thousand were only the attendants of Prince Vipassī. Those men came early in the morning to serve Prince Vipassī, but not seeing the prince, they went to have breakfast. After eating breakfast, they asked, “Where is the prince?” and hearing that “He has gone to the garden,” they set out thinking, “We shall see him right there in that garden.” Seeing the charioteer returning, they heard that “The prince has renounced.” Right at the place where they heard this, they cast off all their ornaments, had saffron-colored robes brought from the market, shaved their hair and beards, and became monks. After becoming monks, they went and surrounded the Great Man.

Then the Bodhisatta Vipassī thought, “While I am practicing the life of striving, I am living crowded with people; this is not suitable. Just as these people used to surround and follow me when I was a layman, they are doing the same now. What is the use of this group?” Thus, becoming weary of the crowd, he thought, “I will go this very day,” but then thought again, “Today is not the right time; if...”
280:
“...if I go today, all these monks will know; I will go only tomorrow.” On that day, in a village similar to Uruvelā, the villagers invited the Great Man along with his followers for the next day. They prepared only thick milk-rice (pāyāsa) for those eighty-four thousand monks and the Great Man. Then, on the following day, the Full Moon of Vesākha, the Great Man Vipassī finished his meal with those monks in that village and returned to his usual dwelling. There, those monks performed the major and minor duties for the Great Man and entered their respective night and day quarters.

The Bodhisatta also entered his leaf-hut, sat down, and thought, “Now is the time to leave.” He left the hut, closed the door, and set out towards the Bodhi-maṇḍa (Seat of Enlightenment). In the evening, those monks went to serve the Bodhisatta and sat surrounding the hut. Saying, “It is very late, let us investigate,” they opened the door of the hut. Although they did not see the Bodhisatta, they did not follow and search for him, asking “Where has the Great Man gone?” They thought, “The Great Man, seemingly weary of living in a group and wishing to live alone, we shall see that Lord only when he has become a Buddha.” Then they set out on a journey towards the interior of Jambudīpa.

Later, those monks heard that “Vipassī Buddha has attained Buddhahood and preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta.” Consequently, they gathered at the Migadāya named Khema in the royal capital of Bandhumatī. Then the Blessed One preached the Dhamma to those monks, and at that time, eighty-four thousand monks attained the realization of the Dhamma. That was the third realization of the Truths. Therefore, it was said:

“Eighty-four thousand people followed the Buddha into monkhood;
To them who had reached the monastery, the One with Vision preached the Dhamma.
Hearing the words of the Buddha who spoke in every way, while sitting nearby,
They too realized the Noble Dhamma, and that was the third realization.”

In that verse, in the phrase “caturāsītisahassāni, sambuddhaṃ anupabbajuṃ,” it should be understood that the word “sambuddhaṃ” is used in the accusative case because of its association with the prefix “anu.” It means they became monks following after the Buddha. The grammatical characteristics should be taken from the grammar texts. There is also a variant reading “tattha ārāmapattānaṃ.” 'Bhāsato' means of the one who is preaching (the Buddha). 'Upanisādino' means of the one who, having gone and relied upon, gives the gift of Dhamma. 'Te pi' means those...”
281:
Eighty-four thousand monks were the attendants of Vipassī Buddha. Having gone there and understood His Dhamma, the third 'Abhisamaya' (realization of the Four Noble Truths) occurred for them. While sitting in the midst of six million eight hundred thousand monks who had followed Him into the monkhood at the Khema Deer Park, the Vipassī Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, recited this Ovāda Pātimokkha:

"Enduring patience is the highest austerity; the Buddhas say Nibbāna is supreme. One who injures others is not a renunciant (pabbajita); one who harms others is not an ascetic (samaṇa).

Not doing any evil, the undertaking of what is wholesome, the purification of one's own mind—this is the teaching of the Buddhas.

Not reviling, not harming, restraint in the Pātimokkha, moderation in eating, dwelling in a secluded place, and devotion to the higher mind (samāpatti)—this is the teaching of the Buddhas."

It should be understood that these verses are the Pātimokkha exhortations of all Buddhas. That was the first assembly. Again, after seeing the Twin Miracle, a second assembly of one hundred thousand monks who had entered the monkhood took place. When the three half-brothers of Vipassī Buddha had pacified the border regions and received the boon of serving the Blessed One, they invited Him to their city and, after hearing the Dhamma while serving Him, they entered the monkhood. Sitting in the midst of those eight million monks, the Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha at the Khema Deer Park; that was the third assembly. Regarding this, it was said:

"There were three assemblies of the great sage Vipassī, consisting of Arahants who were free from taints, stainless, peaceful in mind, and possessed of the quality of 'Tādi' (equanimity).

The first gathering consisted of six million eight hundred thousand Arahants. The second gathering consisted of one hundred thousand monks.

The third gathering consisted of eighty thousand monks. In the midst of that group of monks, the Perfectly Enlightened One shone brilliantly."

In those verses, 'aṭṭhasaṭṭhisatasahassānaṃ' refers to six million eight hundred thousand monks. 'Tattha' means in that Khema Deer Park. 'Bhikkhugaṇamajjhe' means in the midst of the assembly of monks.

At that time, our Bodhisatta was a Naga King named Atula, possessed of great psychic power and majesty. Surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of crores of nagas, with a heart cooled by compassion and incomparable power...
282:
In those verses, 'aṭṭhasaṭṭhisatasahassānaṃ' means six million eight hundred thousand (or one hundred sixty-eight thousand) Arahants. 'Tattha' means in that Khema Deer Park. 'Bhikkhugaṇamajjhe' means in the midst of the assembly of monks. There is also a variant reading 'tassa bhikkhugaṇamajjhe', which also means in the midst of that assembly of monks.

At that time, our Bodhisatta was a Naga King named Atula, possessed of great psychic power and majesty. Surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of crores of nagas, he desired to pay homage to the Blessed One who possessed the Ten Powers, incomparable strength and virtue, and a heart cooled by compassion. He had a pavilion (maṇḍapa) constructed, adorned with the seven gems, resembling the lunar disc, and possessing a delightful essence. Having invited the Buddha to stay there, he offered a great gift suitable for divine wealth for seven days. He then offered the Blessed One a golden throne (pīṭha) of great value, encrusted with the seven gems and brilliant with the radiance of various jewels. At the conclusion of the appreciation (anumodanā) for the gift of the throne, the Buddha prophesied: 'This Naga King, in the ninety-first aeon from now, will become a Buddha.' Therefore, in the Buddhavamsa, the Blessed One said:

"At that time, I was a Naga King of great psychic power, named Atula, meritorious and possessing radiance.

Surrounded then by many crores of nagas, and making offerings with divine musical instruments, I approached the Buddha, the Foremost of the World.

Having approached the Perfectly Enlightened One, Vipassī, the Leader of the World, and having invited the King of Dhamma, I offered a golden throne encrusted with jewels and pearls and adorned with all kinds of ornaments.

That Buddha also, sitting in the midst of the Sangha, prophesied of me: 'In the ninety-first aeon from this one, he will become a Buddha.'

Leaving the delightful city named Kapila, the Tathāgata, having exerted the Great Effort and performed the difficult austerities (dukkarakārikā), [will become a Buddha].

Sitting at the foot of the Ajapāla Banyan tree, the Tathāgata, having accepted milk-rice (pāyāsa) there, will approach the Nerañjarā River.

Having consumed the milk-rice on the banks of the Nerañjarā River, that Conqueror (Jina) will approach the foot of the Bodhi tree by the excellent path prepared by the devas."
283:
Then, having circumambulated the Bodhimaṇḍa, the peerless one of great fame will realize the Supreme Enlightenment at the foot of the Assattha tree.

The biological mother of this Blessed One will be the queen named Māyā, and the father will be the king named Suddhodana. This [Blessed One] will be Gotama.

Kolita and Upatissa, who are free from taints, free from lust, of peaceful mind and concentrated, will be the chief disciples. The monk named Ānanda will be the attendant and will serve this Victorious One (Jina).

Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā, who are free from taints, free from lust, of peaceful mind and concentrated, will be the chief female disciples. The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called the Assattha... etc...

Having heard the words of that Blessed One, I felt even greater devotion in my heart. I undertook the superior practice to fulfill the ten perfections (pāramīs).

In those verses, 'puññavanto' means one who has merit, one who has a well-accumulated store of merit. 'Jutiandharo' means one endowed with radiance. 'Nekānaṃ nāgakoṭīnaṃ' means by many crores of Nagas; here the genitive case should be understood in the sense of the instrumental. 'Parivāretvāna' means surrounding the Blessed One. 'Ahaṃ' refers to oneself. 'Vajjanto' means playing, beating, or striking [musical instruments]. 'Maṇimuttaratanakhacitaṃ' means adorned with various jewels such as rubies and pearls. 'Sabbābharaṇabhūsitaṃ' means decorated with all kinds of ornaments made of jewels, such as animal figures. 'Suvaṇṇapīṭhaṃ' means a golden bench or chair. 'Adāsahaṃ' means I gave.

The city of that Blessed One Vipassī was named Bandhumatī. The father was the king named Bandhumā, and the mother was named Bandhumatī. The two chief disciples were Khaṇḍa Thera and Tissa Thera. The attendant was named Asoka. The two chief female disciples were Candā Therī and Candamittā Therī. The Bodhi tree was the Pāṭali tree. His body was eighty cubits in height. The radiance of his body always spread and remained for seven leagues. His lifespan was eighty thousand years. The chief queen was named Sutanu. His son was named Samavaṭṭakkhandha. He renounced the world in a noble chariot. Therefore, the Blessed One said in the Pali:

The city of the Blessed One named Vipassī was Bandhumatī. The king who was the father was named Bandhumā. The mother was the queen named Bandhumatī.

That Bodhisatta reigned over the kingdom for eight thousand years. That Bodhisatta had three noble palaces: Nanda, Sunanda, and Sirimā.

There were forty-three thousand well-adorned court ladies. The queen was named Sudassanā. The son was named Samavaṭṭakkhandha.

Having seen the four omens, he renounced the world by chariot. The Victorious Blessed One practiced the meditation for eight full months.
284:
The city was named Bandhumatī; the king was a Khattiya named Bandhumā. The mother of the Blessed One Vipassī was named Bandhumatī.

Khaṇḍa Thera and the one named Tissa were the chief disciples (aggasāvaka) of the Blessed One Vipassī. The Thera named Asoka was the attendant of the Blessed One Vipassī.

Candā Therī and Candamittā Therī were the chief female disciples (aggasāvikā). The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called the Pāṭali tree.

Vipassī, the Leader of the World, was eighty cubits high. The radiance of that Buddha spread and shimmered for seven leagues all around.

At that time, the lifespan of the Buddha was eighty thousand years. Remaining for that long a period, he saved a great multitude of beings.

He liberated many devas and humans from bonds (such as sensual lust). He also taught the remaining worldlings (puthujjana) what is the path and what is not the path.

Having shown the light and preached the Deathless state (Nibbāna), that Blessed One, together with his disciples, attained Parinibbāna like a great mass of fire being extinguished.

The noble psychic power, the noble merit, and all the blossomed marks have disappeared. Are not all conditioned things (saṅkhāra) indeed empty?

In those verses, 'bandhanā' means liberating devas and humans from bonds such as the fetter of sensual lust; it means causing them to blossom. 'Maggāmaggañca ācikkhi' means he preached to the remaining worldlings: 'This Middle Way, free from the views of annihilationism and eternalism, is the only true path for the attainment of the Deathless; this practice such as self-mortification is not the path.' 'Ālokaṃ dassayitvāna' means showing the light of Path-knowledge and the light of Insight-knowledge. 'Lakkhaṇañca kusumitaṃ' refers to the body of the Blessed One, which was blossomed and adorned with the marks of a great man. The meaning of the remaining verses is clear.

## The Commentary on the Chronicle of Buddha Vipassī is finished.
## The nineteenth Chronicle of Buddhas is finished.
285:
## 22. Sikhībuddhavaṃsavaṇṇanā

In the period after the Buddha Vipassī, when that aeon had disappeared, for fifty-nine aeons thereafter, no Buddhas appeared in the world. The world remained devoid of the light of Buddhas. The sole sovereignty of the Māra of defilements (Kilesa-māra) and the Māra of the celestial son (Devaputta-māra) prevailed, free from any obstacles.

Thirty-one aeons prior to this Bhadda Kappa, two Fully Enlightened Ones, the Buddha Sikhī and the Buddha Vessabhū, appeared in the world. Like a smokeless flame (sikhī) fueled by smooth, dry heartwood and poured with abundant ghee, the Buddha Sikhī appeared. Among those two Buddhas, the Buddha Sikhī, having fulfilled the Perfections (pāramīs), was reborn in the Tusita heaven. Passing away from there, he took conception in the womb of Queen Pabhāvatī, the chief consort of King Aruṇavā (also known as Aruṇa), who was endowed with supreme virtues, in the city of Aruṇavatī, also called Kusalakaraṇavatī. The Queen possessed a delightful radiance like a statue made of red gold. After ten months had passed, he was born from his mother's womb in the Nisabha Grove. When the fortune-telling brahmins were bestowing a name upon the prince, they named him "Sikhī" because his cranial protuberance (uṇhīsa) rose up like a flame (sikhā).

That Bodhisatta Sikhī lived in the household life for seven thousand years. There were three palaces named Sucandaka, Sirigiriyasa, and Narivasabha. Twenty-four thousand female attendants, headed by Queen Sabbakāmā, waited upon him.

After seeing the four omens, and when a son named Atula, who was a peerless collection of virtues, was born to Queen Sabbakāmā, the Bodhisatta Sikhī departed for the Great Renunciation (Mahābhinikkhamana) on an elephant, mounted upon the noble elephant's shoulder, and became an ascetic. Seven million men followed him into the ascetic life. Surrounded by those monks, he practiced the ascetic struggle (dukkaracariyā) for eight months. On the full moon day of Visākha, leaving his followers, he partook of the thick milk-rice offered by the daughter of the merchant Piyadassī in the village of Sudassana. After spending the day's rest in a young Khadira grove, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by the ascetic named Anomadassī and approached the Puṇḍarīka (White Mango) Bodhi tree. The size of that Puṇḍarīka Bodhi tree was equal to that of a Pāṭali tree. On that very day, the trunk of that White Mango tree rose up to fifty cubits, and its branches also extended to fifty cubits. It was covered with divine scents and divine flowers. Not only was it covered with flowers, but it was also covered with fruits. On one side of the White Mango tree, tender fruits hung; on another side, medium-sized fruits; on another, fruits that were not overripe; and on another, fruits that were delicious as if infused with divine essence, endowed with perfect color, fragrance, and taste, hanging from various parts. Just as it was with that White Mango tree, so too in the ten thousand world systems, the flowering trees were adorned with flowers and the fruit-bearing trees were adorned with fruits.

The Bodhisatta Sikhī spread a carpet of grass twenty-four cubits wide at the foot of that White Mango Bodhi tree, sat in a cross-legged posture, and resolved with fourfold effort. While sitting thus, he conquered the army of Māra together with Māra himself, which extended thirty-six leagues, and attained Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi). He then uttered the solemn utterance (udāna): "Through many a birth in saṃsāra... [etc.] ...I have attained the destruction of craving."
286:
Just as it was at the foot of that White Mango Bodhi tree of the Bodhisatta Sikhī, so too in the ten thousand world systems, the flowering trees were adorned with flowers and the fruit-bearing trees were adorned with fruits. That Bodhisatta Sikhī spread a carpet of grass twenty-four cubits wide at the foot of that White Mango Bodhi tree, sat in a cross-legged posture, and resolved with fourfold effort. While sitting thus, he blew away and destroyed the army of Māra together with Māra himself, which extended thirty-six leagues, and attained Supreme Enlightenment. Having uttered the solemn utterance: "Through many a birth in saṃsāra... [etc.] ...I have attained the destruction of craving," he spent seven weeks (forty-nine days) in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree. Accepting the request of the Great Brahma to teach the Dhamma, and seeing the spiritual potential (upanissaya-sampatti) of the seventy thousand monks who had gone forth with him, he traveled through the air and descended at the Migācī Grove near the royal capital of Aruṇavatī, also known as Vividhāvaraṇavatī. Surrounded by that assembly of sages, he set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion (Dhammacakkappavattana) in their midst. At that time, the first realization of the Four Noble Truths (abhisamaya) occurred for one hundred billion beings. Therefore, it was said in the Buddhavaṃsa:

"After the time of Vipassī, the Fully Enlightened One, the Supreme among bipeds,
The Conqueror named Sikhī arose, peerless and without equal.

Having crushed the army of Māra, he attained the supreme Enlightenment,
And set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion out of compassion for living beings.

While the Conqueror, the Bull among Men, Sikhī, was setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion,
The first realization occurred for one hundred billion beings."

Again, near the royal capital of Aruṇavatī itself, he taught the Dhamma to the two princes, Prince Abhibhū and Prince Sambhava, along with their retinues, and let ninety billion beings drink the nectar of Dhamma. That realization was the second abhisamaya. Therefore, it was said:

"Furthermore, while the Supreme among Men, the Best of the Group, was teaching the Dhamma,
The second realization occurred for ninety billion beings."

At the time when the Blessed One was performing the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya) at the foot of a Campaka tree at the gate of Suriyavatī city, for the purpose of crushing the pride and arrogance of the heretics and for the purpose of liberating all people from their bonds, he taught the Dhamma. At that time, the third realization occurred for eighty billion beings. Therefore, it was said:

"When the Buddha performed the Twin Miracle of water and fire in the world including the devas,
The third realization occurred for eighty billion beings."

While residing in the midst of one hundred thousand Arahants who had gone forth together with Prince Abhibhū and Prince Sambhava, he recited the Pātimokkha. That event was the first assembly (sannipāta). While residing in the midst of eighty thousand monks who had gone forth during the assembly of his relatives in the city of Aruṇavatī, he recited the Pātimokkha. That event was the second assembly. At the time of disciplining the Naga king Dhanapāla in the city of Dhanañjaya, those who had gone forth...
287:
When the Blessed One preached the Dhamma, there occurred the third realization (abhisamaya) of eighty billion human and celestial beings. Therefore, it is said in the Pali:

''When He displayed the Twin Miracle to the world including the devas, there occurred the third realization of eighty billion beings.''

Sitting in the midst of one hundred thousand Arahants who had gone forth together with the princes Abhibhū and Sambhava, He recited the Pātimokkha; that was the first assembly. Sitting in the midst of eighty thousand monks who had gone forth at the gathering of relatives in the city of Aruṇavatī, He recited the Pātimokkha; that was the second assembly.
