Thus they requested. ## Then the Great Being (Mahāsatta), being thus requested by the deities, did not yet give his consent to them, but instead made the Five Great Observations (Mahāvilokana) regarding the time, the continent, the region, the family, and the lifespan of the mother. Among those five observations, he first observed the time: "Is it now the right time for a Buddha to appear, or is it not yet the time?" Therein, a period when the lifespan is longer than one hundred thousand years is not the right time. Why? Because at that time, birth, aging, and death are not apparent to beings, and the Dhamma teaching of the Buddhas is never free from the Three Characteristics (Tilakkhana). When they speak of "impermanence, suffering, and non-self" (anicca, dukkha, anattā), those beings do not think it is something to be listened to or believed, asking "What are they talking about?" Therefore, the realization of the Four Noble Truths (abhisamaya) does not occur. Without that realization, the Dispensation (Sāsana) does not lead to liberation from suffering. Therefore, that is not the right time. A period when the lifespan is less than one hundred years is also not the right time. Why? Because at that time, beings have excessive defilements (kilesa), and advice given to those with excessive defilements does not remain in the place of advice; it disappears quickly like a line drawn on water with a stick. Therefore, that too is not the right time. The period when the lifespan is below one hundred thousand years and above one hundred years is indeed the right time. At that time, the human lifespan was one hundred years. Then the Great Being saw the time, thinking, "It is the time to be born." ## Then, observing the continent, he looked at the four great continents along with their surrounding islands and saw: "Buddhas are not born in the other three continents; they are born only in Jambudīpa." ## Then, thinking, "Jambudīpa is large, measuring ten thousand yojanas. In which region do Buddhas appear?", he observed the location and saw the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa). He came to the conclusion: "There is a city named Kapilavatthu; I should be born there."
319: Then, observing the family: "Buddhas are not born in a merchant family or a low-caste family. They are born in either the warrior-noble (Khattiya) family or the priestly (Brāhmaṇa) family, which are esteemed by the world. At present, the Khattiya family is esteemed by the world. I shall be born in that family; King Suddhodana will be my father." Thus he saw the family. ## Then, observing the mother: "The mother of a Buddha is not flighty or a drunkard. Having fulfilled the perfections for a hundred thousand aeons, she is one who has kept the five precepts unbroken since birth. This Queen Mahāmāyā is such a person. She shall be my mother. How long is her lifespan?" He observed and saw: "It is only ten months and seven days." ## Having thus made these Five Great Observations, he gave his consent to the deities, saying, "Friends, it is time for me to become a Buddha," and dismissed them, saying, "You may go." Surrounded by the Tusita deities, he entered the Nandana Grove in the Tusita heaven. Indeed, there is a Nandana Grove in all the deva realms. There, the deities wandered about, reminding him of his past meritorious deeds, saying, "When you pass away from here, go to a happy destination (sugati)." While the Bodhisatta was wandering in that grove, surrounded by the deities reminding him of his merit, he passed away and took conception in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā under the Uttarāsāḷha nakshatra. At the moment the Great Being (Mahāpurisa) took conception, the entire ten-thousandfold world system shook all at once. Thirty-two omens appeared clearly. ## To prevent harm to the Bodhisatta who had thus taken conception and to the Bodhisatta’s mother, four young deities holding swords took up guard. No lustful thoughts toward men arose in the Bodhisatta’s mother. She reached the pinnacle of great gain and fame, and remained happy, without physical or mental fatigue. She saw the Bodhisatta within her womb like a pure white thread passed through a clear ruby. Because the womb where a Bodhisatta has resided is like the inner chamber of a cetiya (shrine), no other being can reside in or use it. Therefore, seven days after giving birth to the Bodhisatta, the mother passed away and was reborn in the Tusita heaven. While other women may give birth before or after ten months, and while sitting or lying down, it is not so for the Bodhisatta’s mother. The Bodhisatta’s mother, having carried the Bodhisatta in her womb for exactly ten months, gives birth while standing. This is the natural law (dhammatā) for the mothers of Bodhisattas.
320:
Queen Mahāmāyā, having carried the Bodhisatta in her womb for ten months and her pregnancy being fully mature, desired to go to her relatives' home and informed King Suddhodana, saying, "Great King, I wish to go to the city of Devadaha." The King, consenting with "Very well," had the road from the city of Kapilavatthu to the city of Devadaha leveled and decorated with plantain trees, full water pots, banners, and flags. He then had her seated in a new golden palanquin and sent her forth with great ceremony and a large retinue. Between the two cities, there was a festive Sal grove named Lumbinī Grove, which was shared by the inhabitants of both cities. At that time, the entire grove was in full bloom from the base to the tips of the branches. Seeing the beauty of that grove—which resembled the Nandana Grove of the gods, with the branches and flowers filled with the sweet and delightful songs of intoxicated bees and cuckoos that seemed to enjoy the five kinds of musical instruments—the Queen felt a desire to play in the Sal grove.

"Adorned and agitating the foolish, with limbs decorated like a garlanded maiden,
Always attracting the swarms of bees that are the eyes of the people, the Lumbinī garden shines intensely as if plundering (the hearts of men)."

The ministers informed the King and, taking the Queen, entered that Lumbinī Grove. She went to the foot of a majestic Sal tree and desired to hold a branch of that Sal tree, which had a straight and round trunk and was adorned with flowers, fruits, and young shoots. That Sal branch, like a weak person or as if moved by the hearts of the people, bent down of its own accord and reached the palm of the Queen's hand. Then, with her right hand—which was most delightful, adorned with new golden bracelets, and had fingers as round as lotus petals and bright with reddish long nails—she reached out and held the Sal branch. Standing there holding the Sal branch, the Queen shone like a crescent moon emerging from dark clouds, like a flash of lightning that lasts but a moment, or like a goddess born in the Nandana Grove. At that very moment, the birth-pains (kammaja-vātā) began to move within her. Then, the multitude of people set up a curtain-wall around her and withdrew. While she was thus standing and holding the Sal branch, the birth of the child took place.
321:
At that very moment, four Great Brahmas of pure mind arrived, bringing a golden net. Receiving the Bodhisatta with that golden net and placing him before his mother, they said, "Be joyful, O Queen! A son of great power is born to you." Just as other beings, when emerging from their mother's womb, come out smeared with repulsive impurities, the Bodhisatta was not like that. The Bodhisatta, with both hands and both feet stretched out, emerged from his mother's womb standing, unsmeared by any impurity of the womb, pure and clean, shining like a precious gem placed on a cloth from Kāsī. Even though he was thus pure, for the sake of honoring the Bodhisatta and his mother, two streams of water descended from the sky and balanced the temperature in the bodies of the Bodhisatta and his mother.

Then, from the hands of the Brahmas who stood receiving him with the golden net, the four Great Kings received him with a ceremonial rug of antelope skin (ajinappaveṇī) which was considered auspicious and pleasant to the touch. From the hands of those Great Kings, humans received him with a cushion of fine dukūla cloth. Releasing himself from the hands of the humans and standing upon the earth, he looked towards the East, and ten thousand world-systems became a single open space. There, gods and humans honored him with scents, flowers, incense, and the like, saying, "O Great Being, there is no one like you here; how could there be anyone superior?" Having thus surveyed the ten directions and seeing no one equal to himself, he faced the North and took seven strides. As he walked, he moved only upon the earth, not through the air. He moved without clothing, not with clothing. He moved as an infant, not as a sixteen-year-old. However, to the multitude of people, it appeared as if he were traveling through the air, as if he were fully adorned, and as if he were sixteen years of age. Then, standing at the seventh step, he uttered the noble words beginning with "I am the foremost in the world" (Aggo'hamasmi lokassa) and made his Lion's Roar.

The Bodhisatta uttered words immediately upon emerging from his mother's womb in only three existences: in the existence as Mahosadha, in the existence as Vessantara, and in this existence. It is said that in the existence as Mahosadha, as soon as he emerged from his mother's womb, Sakka, the king of gods, came and placed a piece of sandalwood in his hand and left; he emerged holding that sandalwood in his fist. Then his mother asked, "Dear son, what..."
322:
"What have you come holding?" she asked. "Mother, I have come holding medicine," he replied. Because he came holding medicine in this way, they named the boy "Osadhakumāra."

In the existence as King Vessantara, however, as soon as he emerged from his mother's womb, he stretched out his right hand and said, "Mother, is there any wealth in the house? I wish to give alms," and thus he was born. Then his mother said, "Dear son, you are born into a wealthy family," and taking her son's hand, she placed it on her palm and gave him a bag of a thousand coins.

In this present existence as well, he uttered such a lion's roar (sīhanāda). Thus, in three existences, the Bodhisatta uttered words as soon as he emerged from his mother's womb. At the moment of his birth, the thirty-two omens also became manifest. At the very time our Bodhisatta was born in the Lumbinī grove, the Queen Mother of Rāhula, Ānanda, the minister Channa, the minister Kāḷudāyī, the royal horse Kaṇṭhaka, the Great Bodhi tree, and the four great treasure jars were also born (appeared). Among those four great treasure jars, one was a gāvuta in size, one was half a yojana, one was three gāvutas, and one was a yojana in size. These seven are known as the co-borns (sahajāta).

The kings residing in both cities (Devadaha and Kapilavatthu) took the Great Being and returned only to the city of Kapilavatthu. On that very day, the hosts of deities in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, being joyful and delighted, played and celebrated by tossing their robes and so on, saying, "In the city of Kapilavatthu, the son of King Suddhodana will sit at the foot of the Bodhi tree and become a Buddha."

At that time, a hermit named Kāḷadevala, who was an intimate of King Suddhodana's household and an attainer of the eight meditative attainments, having finished his meal, went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven for his daytime rest. While sitting there for his daytime rest, he saw those deities playing with joyful minds and asked, "For what reason are you playing with such joyful minds and delighted hearts? Tell me the reason."

Then the deities said, "Sir, a son has been born to King Suddhodana. That son will sit at the seat of enlightenment (Bodhimanda), become a Buddha, and set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka). We are joyful because we shall have the opportunity to behold the infinite beauty of the Buddha."

Then the hermit, having heard the words of those deities, descended from the celestial world, which was full of most beautiful jewels, and entered the King's palace...
323:
He sat on the prepared seat. Then, after exchanging friendly greetings (paṭisanthāra) with the King, he said, "Great King, I hear that a son has been born to you; let me see that son."

The King had the adorned son brought and presented him to pay respects to the hermit Devala. The feet of the Great Being (the Bodhisatta) turned up and, like a flash of lightning, rested upon the matted hair of the hermit, which resembled a dark rain cloud. Indeed, in that existence, there was no one else worthy of being saluted by the Bodhisatta. Then the hermit rose from his seat and raised his hands in salutation (añjali) to the Bodhisatta. The King, seeing that wonder, paid respects to his own son.

The hermit, seeing the perfection of the Bodhisatta's marks, reflected and investigated, "Will he become a Buddha, or will he not?" Knowing through the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa) that "He will undoubtedly become a Buddha," he smiled, thinking, "This is a wonderful man."

Then, investigating further, "Will I get to see him when he has become a Buddha, or not?" he saw, "I will not get to see him. I will pass away in the interval and be reborn in the Formless Realm (arūpabhava), where I would be unable to understand even if a hundred or a thousand Buddhas were to come and teach." Realizing this, he wept, saying, "I will not get to see such a wonderful man when he has become a Buddha. Great indeed will be my loss!"

When the people saw this, they asked, "Our master was just smiling and now he has started to weep again. Venerable sir, will there be any danger to our master's son?"

The hermit replied, "There is no danger for him; he will undoubtedly become a Buddha." "If so, why did you weep?" they asked. He replied, "I weep because I am grieving for myself, thinking that I will not get to see such a wonderful man when he has become a Buddha, and that great indeed will be my loss."

Then, on the fifth day, after having the Bodhisatta's head washed, the King, thinking, "We shall perform the naming ceremony," had the palace smeared with four kinds of perfumes, scattered flowers including parched rice as the fifth, and had thick milk-rice (pāyāsa) cooked. He invited one hundred and eight Brahmins who had reached the further shore of the three Vedas, seated them in the palace, fed them the honeyed milk-rice, and after making offerings to them, had them examine the marks, asking, "What will he become?"

Among those Brahmins, eight Brahmin scholars, including Rāma, were the examiners of the marks. Among those eight, seven Brahmins raised two fingers and made a dual prediction: "One endowed with these marks, if he lives the household life, will become a Wheel-Turning Monarch (Cakkavatti); if he goes forth, he will become a Buddha." However, the youngest among them...
324:
A Brahmin named Koṇḍañña by clan, seeing the perfection of the Bodhisatta’s excellent marks, raised only one finger and made a definitive prediction: "There is no reason for this Great Man to remain in the midst of a household; he will certainly become a Buddha who has opened the veil of defilements." Then, when they gave the prince a name, they named him "Siddhattha" because he would fulfill the welfare of the entire world.

Then those Brahmins returned to their homes, called their sons, and said: "We are old; we may or may not live to see the son of King Suddhodana attain Buddhahood. But you, when he renounces the world and attains omniscience, should ordain in the dispensation of that Buddha." Subsequently, seven of those men lived out their lives and passed away according to their kamma. The young Koṇḍañña, however, remained healthy and free from disease.

Then King Suddhodana, hearing the words of those Brahmins, asked: "Having seen what will my son renounce the world?" They replied: "The four great omens, O King." "Which ones?" he asked. "An old man, a sick man, a dead man, and an ascetic," they replied. The King said: "From this day forward, do not let such people come near my son," and to prevent the sight of old men and others from entering the prince's field of vision, he stationed guards in the four directions at intervals of one gāvuta.

On that day, eighty thousand families of relatives who had assembled for the auspicious ceremony each pledged one son, saying: "Whether this prince becomes a Buddha or a Universal Monarch, we will each give one son. If he becomes a Buddha, he will wander surrounded by warrior-monks. If he becomes a Universal Monarch, he will wander surrounded by warrior-princes." Then the King provided sixty-four nurses, who were of supreme beauty and free from all defects, for his son, the Great Man. The Bodhisatta grew up with infinite attendants and great accumulation of glory.

Then one day, the King’s Plowing Festival (Vappa-maṅgala) was to be held. On that day, the King, departing from the city with great pomp and a large retinue, took his son along. At the site of the plowing, there was a most delightful Jambu tree with thick, dense shade. Having prepared a bed for the prince beneath it, and having hung a red cloth canopy decorated with excellent golden stars above, he had it enclosed with curtains and stationed guards. The King, adorned with all ornaments and surrounded by a host of ministers, went to the place where the plowing was to be done. At that auspicious site, the most excellent...
325:
King Suddhodana took up a golden plow, while the ministers and others took up silver plows and so forth. On that day, a thousand plows were yoked together. The nurses who sat surrounding the Bodhisatta, saying, "We shall watch the King’s splendor," went outside from within the curtains.

Then the Bodhisatta, looking here and there and seeing no one, quickly arose, sat cross-legged, and practicing Ānāpānasati meditation, attained the first jhāna. The nurses, wandering among the various kinds of food and snacks, delayed for a short while. While the shadows of the other trees had shifted, the shadow of that Jambu tree remained circular and stayed in that very place. The nurses, thinking, "The prince is all alone," quickly lifted the curtain and searched; seeing the Bodhisatta sitting cross-legged on the auspicious bed and witnessing that miracle, they went and reported the matter to the King. The King came quickly, and seeing that miracle, he bowed to his son, saying, "Dear son, this is my second salutation to you."

Then the Great Man gradually reached the age of sixteen. The King had three palaces built for the Bodhisatta, suitable for the three seasons, named Ramma, Suramma, and Subha. One was nine stories high, one seven stories, and one five stories. All three palaces were equal in height, but there were differences in the number of stories.

Then the King thought: "My son has reached maturity; I shall see him enjoy the glory of kingship under the white umbrella." He sent messages to the Sakyans: "My son has reached maturity; I shall establish him in the kingship. If there are young maidens of age in your houses, send them to this palace." Hearing the King’s message, those kings said: "The prince is only possessed of beauty; he knows no arts or sciences. He will not be able to support a wife and children. We will not give our daughters." When the King heard this, he went to his son and told him the matter. The Bodhisatta asked: "What art must I demonstrate?" The King replied: "Dear son, it is proper to string a bow that requires the strength of a thousand men." "Then have that bow brought," he said. The King had the bow brought and given to him. It took a thousand men to lift and string that bow, and a thousand men to set it down. The Great Man had that bow brought, and while sitting cross-legged, he wound the bowstring around his big toe, and pulling it, he strung the bow with his big toe alone. Then, holding the staff with his left hand and pulling with his right, he fixed the string. The entire city resounded as if it were about to fly away.
326:
The entire city seemed as if it were about to take flight. When asked, "What is this sound?" they said, "It is the sound of thunder." Then others said, "Do you not know? It is not thunder; it is the sound of the bowstring being struck by Prince Aṅgīrasa, who has the strength of a thousand men, after he had strung the bow." Upon hearing this, the Sakyans were uplifted in spirit and became exceedingly joyful and glad.

Then the Great Being (Mahāpurisa) asked, "What else should be done?" They replied, "It is fitting to pierce an iron plate eight finger-breadths thick with an arrow." After piercing that, he asked again, "What else should be done?" They replied, "It is fitting to pierce a Padauk wood board four finger-breadths thick." After piercing that too, he asked again, "What else should be done?" They replied, "It is fitting to pierce a fig-wood (udumbara) board one span thick." Having pierced that as well, he asked, "What else should be done?" Then they said, "The sand-carts." The Great Being (Mahāsatta) pierced through both the sand-carts and the straw-carts, sending the arrow to a distance of one usabha in water and eight usabhas on land. Then they said to him, "It is fitting to hit a hair-tip designated as a brinjal." Saying, "In that case, have a brinjal tied at a distance of one yojana," he had the hair-tip tied at a distance of one yojana, designated as a brinjal, and shot the arrow in the darkness of night when the directions were covered by layers of clouds. That arrow went and split the hair-tip at a distance of one yojana and entered the earth. Not only this much, but on that day, the Great Being demonstrated all the arts existing in the world.

Then the Sakyans adorned their daughters and sent them to him. There were forty thousand dancing women. The mother of Rāhula, the queen, became the chief consort. The Great Being, like a celestial youth surrounded by goddesses, was surrounded by human maidens and attended by musical instruments played only by women. Enjoying great prosperity, he dwelt in those three palaces according to the seasons. Then one day, the Bodhisatta, wishing to go to the park, called the charioteer and said, "Prepare the chariot; I will go to see the park." The charioteer replied, "Very well," and prepared a noble chariot, worthy of the exalted, with a beautiful and firm yoke and leather straps, with very strong rims and hubs, with a pole-tip inlaid with gold, silver, and precious gems, with the sides of the rims inlaid with gold and silver stars, glorious with various fragrant flower garlands, and as beautiful to behold as the sun's chariot. He harnessed four auspicious Sindh horses, white in color like the moon and the white lotus, and as swift as the wind or a Garuḍa. Having adorned the noble chariot, he informed the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta mounted that noble chariot, which was like a celestial mansion, and set out towards the park.

Then the deities thought, "The time for Prince Siddhattha to become a Buddha is near; let us show him the omens." They created the form of an old man with broken teeth, grey hair, a bent body, leaning on a staff and trembling, and showed it to him. Both the Bodhisatta and the charioteer saw that old man. Then the Bodhisatta asked, "Charioteer, who is this man? His hair is not like that of others," following the method described in the Mahāpadāna Sutta. Upon hearing the charioteer's answer, he said, "Friends, since aging is clearly manifest for one who has taken rebirth, therefore, being reborn is..."
327:
The charioteer prepared the noble chariot, which was adorned with an array of gold and silver stars, graced with the beauty of various fragrant flower garlands, and as delightful to behold as the chariot of the Sun. He yoked four noble Sindh horses, white in hue like the moon or white lotuses and as swift as the wind of the King of Garudas, and informed the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta, mounting that noble chariot which resembled a celestial mansion, set out toward the park.

At that time, the deities thought, 'The time for Prince Siddhattha to penetrate the Four Noble Truths is drawing near; let us show him the portents.' They created the form of a deity as an old man—with broken teeth, grey hair, a bent body, leaning on a staff, and trembling with age—and showed him. Both the Bodhisatta and the charioteer saw the old man. Then the Bodhisatta, following the method described in the Mahāpadāna Sutta, asked, 'Charioteer, who is this man? Even his hair is not like that of others.' Upon hearing the charioteer’s reply, he felt a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), thinking, 'O friends, how loathsome is birth (jāti), since for one who is born, old age (jarā) must surely manifest.' He turned back from that very spot and ascended his palace.

The King asked, 'For what reason has my son returned?' They replied, 'Your Majesty, he returned after seeing an old man.' Then the King, his heart trembling, stationed guards within a radius of half a yojana. On another day, as the Bodhisatta was going to the park, he saw a sick man afflicted by disease, also created by those same deities. Having questioned as before and feeling spiritual urgency, he returned and ascended his palace. The King, after inquiring, sent female dancers, thinking, 'I will prevent his mind from turning toward renunciation.' He increased the security, stationing guards within a radius of three gāvutas.

Once more, as the Bodhisatta was going to the park, he saw a dead man created by the deities in the same manner. Having questioned as before and feeling spiritual urgency, he returned and ascended his palace. The King, after inquiring about the reason for his return, again increased the security, stationing guards within a radius of one yojana.

Once more, as the Bodhisatta was going to the park, he saw an ascetic, well-clad and well-robed, created by the deities in the same manner. He asked, 'Friend charioteer, who is this man?' Although the charioteer did not truly know of ascetics or the virtues of an ascetic because it was not an era when a Buddha had appeared, by the power of the deities, he replied, 'Prince, this is called an ascetic,' and he praised the virtues of renunciation.

Thereupon, the Bodhisatta, having conceived a desire for renunciation, proceeded to the park that day. Long-lived Bodhisattas see each portent after the passing of a hundred years. However, because our Bodhisatta appeared in a time of short lifespan, he saw each portent in succession every four months as he went to the park. The elders who were reciters of the Dīgha Nikāya, however, say, 'Having seen the four portents...'
328:
...on a single day, he went forth.' In that version, having played during the day and enjoyed the delights of the park, the Bodhisatta bathed in the royal lotus pond. At sunset, he sat upon the royal stone slab, desiring to adorn himself. Then, Sakka, the King of Devas, knowing his thought, commanded the young deity Vissakamma to go. Vissakamma arrived, took the form of a barber, and adorned him with celestial ornaments. While the Bodhisatta was thus fully adorned, and while musicians displayed their respective skills and Brahmins offered various auspicious words of praise such as 'May you be victorious and rejoice' during the auspicious ceremonies, he mounted the noble chariot. At that moment, hearing that 'The mother of Rahula has given birth to a son,' King Suddhodana sent a message, saying, 'Inform my son of this joy.' When the Bodhisatta heard this, he said, 'A Rāhu (an impediment) has been born; a bond has been born.' The King, having asked what his son had said and hearing those words, declared, 'From this day forth, let my grandson’s name be Prince Rāhula.'

The Bodhisatta, riding that noble chariot, entered the city with a great retinue and exceedingly delightful splendor. At that time, a kshatriya princess named Kisāgotamī, who was endowed with beauty and virtue, was on the upper terrace of her palace. Seeing the beauty of the Bodhisatta as he entered the city, she was filled with joy and delight and uttered this inspired verse (udāna):

'Cool (nibbutā) indeed is that mother,
Cool indeed is that father,
Cool indeed is that woman,
Who has such a husband as this!'

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta thought, 'This princess has made me hear a word well worth hearing. I am one who wanders seeking Nibbāna. This very day, I shall abandon the household life...'
329: "It is proper for me to go forth, become a monk, and seek Nibbāna," he thought. Thinking, "Let this pearl necklace be the teacher's fee for Kisāgotamī," he removed the pearl necklace worth a hundred thousand from his neck and sent it to Kisāgotamī. Kisāgotamī, for her part, was filled with joy, thinking, "Prince Siddhattha's heart is bound to me, and he has sent me a gift." The Bodhisatta, with great glory, ascended to his magnificent palace and lay down on his royal couch. At that moment, noble young women—with faces as beautiful as the full moon, lips like ripe bimba fruit, teeth white, clean, even, and closely set, eyes and hair as black as night, eyebrows well-formed, dark blue, and curved, breasts as even as those of a swan, wearing noble waistbands of gold and silver set with delightful jewels, with broad and firm hips, thighs like an elephant's trunk, skilled in dancing, singing, and music, and possessing beauty like that of celestial nymphs—surrounded the Great Being, holding sweet-sounding instruments, and performed dances, songs, and music to delight him. However, the Bodhisatta, whose mind was detached from defilements, took no delight in the dancing and singing, and fell asleep for a moment. Seeing him, those women thought, "The prince for whom we are performing has fallen asleep; why should we weary ourselves further?" They then lay down, leaning against their instruments. The scented oil lamps continued to burn. The Bodhisatta woke up and, sitting cross-legged on the couch, saw those women sleeping while leaning on their instruments—some with saliva trickling, their cheeks and bodies wet; some grinding their teeth; some snoring; some muttering in their sleep; some with mouths wide open; some with clothes and waistbands loosened, revealing repulsive parts; some with disheveled hair—looking like corpses in a cemetery. Seeing this transformation of the women, the Great Being became even more detached from sensual pleasures. To the Bodhisatta, even the magnificent palace floor, decorated like the abode of the King of Devas, appeared extremely loathsome, like a charnel ground filled with discarded, rotting corpses. The three worlds appeared like a house engulfed in flames. He uttered the words, "How oppressed it is! How afflicted it is!" His mind inclined strongly toward renunciation.
330: The Bodhisatta thought, "I should depart on the Great Renunciation this very day." Rising from his royal couch, he went to the door and asked, "Who is there?" Channa, who was lying with his head on the threshold, replied, "It is I, my lord, Channa." Then the Great Being said, "I wish to depart on the Great Renunciation today. Without letting anyone know, quickly prepare a swift Sindh horse." Channa replied, "Very well, my lord," and taking the horse's trappings, went to the stable. Seeing the noble horse Kanthaka standing in a delightful spot under a canopy of jasmine-patterned cloth, where scented oil lamps were burning, he thought, "Today, I should prepare this very auspicious horse for my lord's departure." He then saddled Kanthaka. While being saddled, Kanthaka realized, "This saddling is very firm; it is not like the saddling for trips to the pleasure garden on other days. Undoubtedly, my lord will depart on the Great Renunciation today." Filled with joy, he neighed loudly. That powerful neighing would have echoed throughout the entire city of Kapilavatthu, but the devas muffled the sound so that no one could hear it. The Bodhisatta thought, "I will first see my son." Rising from where he stood, he went to Yasodharā's quarters and opened the chamber door. At that moment, a scented oil lamp was burning inside the chamber. Rāhula's mother, Yasodharā, was sleeping on a noble bed strewn with an ambaṇa (a large measure) of jasmine and other flowers, with her hand resting on her son's head. The Bodhisatta stood with one foot on the threshold and looked in, thinking, "If I remove the queen's hand to take my son, the queen will wake up. If she wakes, it will be an obstacle to my Great Renunciation. Only after becoming a Buddha will I return to see my son." He then descended from the palace. Going near Kanthaka, he said, "Dear Kanthaka, help me cross over this one night. Depending on you, I shall become a Buddha who realizes the Four Noble Truths and save the world including the devas." Then, he leaped onto Kanthaka's back. Kanthaka was eighteen cubits long from the neck and was proportionately tall. He was endowed with great beauty and strength, entirely white like a washed conch shell. Then, the Bodhisatta, having mounted the noble horse, had Channa hold the horse's tail and reached the great city gate at midnight. At that time, King Suddhodana, in order to prevent the Bodhisatta's departure, had arranged for a thousand men to open each of the two gate leaves and had placed many men as guards at that gate. The Bodhisatta [saw] the multitude of men...
331:
At that time, the King, in order to prevent the Bodhisatta's departure, had each of the two gate-leaves opened by a thousand men and stationed many guards there. It is said that the Bodhisatta possessed the strength of a hundred thousand crores of men and a thousand crores of elephants. Therefore, the Bodhisatta thought: "If the gate is not opened, today, sitting on the back of the horse Kanthaka, I will have the minister Channa hold onto the tail, and together with Channa, I will squeeze Kanthaka with my thighs, leap over the eighteen-cubit wall, and cross over." Channa also thought: "If the gate is not opened, I will place my noble master on my shoulders, embrace Kanthaka with my right hand, holding him under my arm, and leap over the wall to cross over." Kanthaka also thought: "If the gate is not opened, I will leap over with my noble master sitting as he is and with Channa holding my tail, and land in front of the wall." Thus did these three think. The deities residing at the gate opened the great gate.

At that moment, Māra the Evil One, thinking "I will turn the Bodhisatta back," came and stood in the sky, saying:
"O Great Hero, do not go forth! On the seventh day from now, your divine Wheel-treasure will surely appear.
You shall rule over the four great islands surrounded by two thousand small islands. Turn back, sir!"
The Great Being asked, "Who are you?" "I am Vasavattī (Māra)," he replied.

"O King Māra, I know that my Wheel-treasure will appear. However, I have no desire for the sovereignty of a Universal Monarch. Go away, Māra! Do not stay here.
I shall indeed become a Buddha, the Leader and Guide of the world, making the entire ten-thousandfold world-system resound," he declared. That Māra then vanished on the spot.

The Bodhisatta, at the age of twenty-nine, renounced the sovereignty of a Universal Monarch that was within his reach, as if it were a glob of spit, without any lingering attachment. Leaving the royal palace, the abode of the glory of a Universal Monarch, he departed from the city on the full moon day of Āsāḷhī (Waso), while the constellation Uttarāsāḷha was in the ascendant at midnight.
332:
The Bodhisatta desired to look back at the city. Immediately upon his thought, that patch of earth rotated like a potter's wheel. While remaining in his position, the Great Being saw the city of Kapilavatthu. Having pointed out the site for the shrine named Kanthakanivattana on that spot, he proceeded, facing the direction of his journey, with the horse Kanthaka in the lead, accompanied by great honor and sublime glory. At that time, as the Great Being was traveling, deities held six million torches before him. Likewise, six million behind, six million on the right, and six million on the left. Other deities followed, surrounding him and honoring him with fragrant flowers, garlands, wreaths, sandalwood powder, yak-tail whisks, banners, and flags. Divine songs and many musical instruments resounded.

Traveling with such glory, the Bodhisatta crossed three kingdoms in a single night, covered a distance of thirty leagues, and reached the bank of the Anomā River. Then, standing on the riverbank, the Bodhisatta asked Channa: "What is the name of this river?" "My Lord, it is named Anomā," he replied. "Our renunciation, too, shall be 'Anomā' (illustrious)," he said, and signaling the horse Kanthaka with his heels, he gave the sign. The horse leaped and stood on the far bank of the Anomā River, which was eight usabhas wide. The Bodhisatta dismounted from the horse's back and, standing on the sandy beach which was like a heap of pearls, addressed Channa: "Friend Channa, take my ornaments and Kanthaka and go back. I shall go forth into homelessness." Channa said, "My Lord, I too will go forth." The Bodhisatta said, "It is not possible for you to go forth yet. You must go back," and having forbidden him three times, he handed over the ornaments and Kanthaka. He then thought: "These locks of hair of mine are not suitable for a recluse. I shall cut them with my sword." Holding the most sharp and noble sword in his right hand and the topknot together with the crest-lock in his left hand, he cut them. The hair remained two finger-breadths long and, curling to the right, adhered to his head. For the rest of his life, his hair remained that same length, and his beard was proportionate to it. Thereafter, he had no further need for the task of shaving his hair or beard. The Bodhisatta, holding the topknot together with the crest-lock, made a resolution: "If I am to become a Buddha, let this stay in the sky; if not, let it fall to the ground," and he tossed it into the air. That crest-jewel bundle traveled to a height of one league and remained suspended in the sky.
333:
Then, Sakka, the King of Devas, looking with his divine eye, received that sacred hair with a jeweled casket one league in size and established the Cūḷāmaṇi Cetiya, three leagues in height and made of the seven kinds of jewels, in the Tāvatiṃsa realm. Regarding this, it was said:

'Having cut the top-knot scented with excellent fragrance, the Supreme Person threw it into the sky; Vasava, the thousand-eyed one, received it on his head with a magnificent golden casket.'

Again, the Bodhisatta thought: "These Kāsika cloths are very costly; they are not suitable for a monk like me." Then, the Mahābrahmā Ghaṭīkāra, an old friend from the time of Kassapa Buddha, whose friendship had remained unbroken for an entire interval between Buddhas (buddhantara), thought: "Today my friend has gone forth in the Great Renunciation; I will go taking the monastic requisites for him."

'The three robes, the bowl, the razor, the needle, the girdle, and the water-filter—these eight are suitable for a monk devoted to practice.'

Bringing these eight monastic requisites, he offered them. The Great Being, having donned the robes which are the banner of Arahantship and assuming the noble appearance of a monk, threw the pair of cloths into the sky. Mahābrahmā received them and, having built a cetiya twelve leagues in size made of all kinds of jewels in the Brahma realm, enshrined them within it. Then the Great Being dismissed Channa, saying: "Channa, tell my mother and father in my name that I am well."

Then the minister Channa, having paid homage to the Great Being and circumambulated him clockwise, departed. As for Kanthaka, listening to the words of the Bodhisatta as he conversed with Channa, he stood there thinking, "Now I shall never see my master again." As the Bodhisatta passed out of his sight, unable to endure the grief of separation, his heart broke, and he died, being reborn as a deva named Kanthaka in the Tāvatiṃsa realm, which is difficult for the Asuras to overcome. The account of his rebirth should be understood from the Vimānavatthu Commentary (Vimalatthavilāsinī). At first, Channa had only a single grief.
334:
That minister Channa, oppressed by a second grief—the death of the horse Kanthaka—went back weeping and lamenting in great distress. The Bodhisatta, having gone forth, spent seven days in that very place in the mango grove named Anupiya, passing the time in the bliss of monkhood. Thereafter, like the full moon in the autumn season (the month of Tazaungmon) enveloped by clouds tinged with the glow of twilight, and though alone, appearing as if surrounded by a great multitude, being wrapped in the excellent saffron-dyed robes, he shone brilliantly. Acting as if providing the nectar of immortality for the eyes of the forest animals and birds, the Lion of Men, like a solitary lion, walking with the majestic grace of a rutting elephant, as if comforting the earth with the soles of his feet, traveled a distance of thirty leagues in a single day. Having crossed the River Ganges, which has high waves and is free from attachment, he entered the city named Rājagaha, which shines with a mass of jewel-like radiance and is possessed by noble kings. Having entered the city, he wandered for alms from house to house. At that time, the entire city was thrown into a stir upon seeing the physical form of the Bodhisatta, like the city when the elephant Dhanapālaka entered, or like the city of devas when Rāhu, the lord of Asuras, enters. While the Great Person was wandering for alms, the townspeople, seeing the form of the Great Being, were filled with joy and wonder, their hearts being drawn to the physical appearance of the Bodhisatta.

Among those people, one said: "Friends, is this the full moon that has descended to the human world, hiding its rays for fear of Rāhu?" Another, smiling, said: "Friend, what are you saying? When have you ever seen the full moon descend to the human world? In truth, this must be the flower-bannered Kāmadeva (God of Love) who, having taken another form, has come to play after seeing the supreme glory and splendor of our Great King and the citizens." Another, smiling, said: "Friend, are you mad? This is not the God of Love whose body was burnt by the fire of the Great Lord’s (Īsvara) anger. This is the thousand-eyed Lord of Devas (Sakka) who has come here, mistaking this for the city of the immortals!" Another, laughing slightly, said: "Friends, what are you saying? Your words are inconsistent. Where are his thousand eyes? Where is his thunderbolt? Where is the elephant Erāvaṇa? Surely, this is Mahābrahmā who, knowing the brahmins are negligent, has come to urge them in the Vedas and Vedāngas." Rejecting all of them, a wise person said: "This is neither the moon, nor Kāmadeva, nor Sakka, nor Mahābrahmā. This is a wonderful human being, a Teacher, the leader of the whole world."

While the citizens were talking thus, the king's men went and reported the matter to King Bimbisāra: "Great King, is it a deva, or a gandhabba, or a naga king, or a yakkha? Who is it? He is collecting alms in our city of Rājagaha..."
335:
“This person is not the full moon, nor the god of desire (Kāmadeva), nor the thousand-eyed Sakka, nor the Brahma king. He is the wonderful human Teacher, the leader of the whole world,” (the people said).

While the citizens were speaking thus, the king’s men went and reported the matter to King Bimbisāra, saying, “Great King, is it a god, or a gandhabba, or a nāga king, or a yakkha? Who is it that is wandering for alms in our city?” Hearing this, the King stood on the upper terrace of the palace, and upon seeing the Great Man, his mind was filled with wonder and amazement. He commanded his men, “Go, friends, and investigate him. If he is a non-human, he will leave the city and vanish. If he is a deity, he will travel through the air. If he is a nāga king, he will dive into the earth and depart. If he is a human, he will consume the alms food he has obtained.”

The Great Man, with calmed senses and a peaceful mind, as if drawing the eyes of the multitude by the beauty of his form, looking only a yoke’s length ahead, collected just enough mixed alms food for his sustenance. He departed from the city by the same gate he had entered and sat facing the east in the shade of Paṇḍava Hill. There, he reflected on the alms food and consumed it without any change in his composure. Then, the king’s men went and reported this to the King. Upon hearing the messengers' words, King Bimbisāra—the lord of Magadha, who is difficult for the foolish to follow, whose strength is firm like the essence of Mount Meru, and who is the essence among beings—felt a great desire to see him just by hearing of the Bodhisatta’s virtues. He quickly left the city, went towards Paṇḍava Hill, descended from his carriage, and approached the Bodhisatta. Having received permission from the Bodhisatta, he sat on a stone slab as cool as the love of kinsmen. Being inspired by the Bodhisatta’s deportment, he exchanged friendly greetings, inquired about his name and lineage, and offered him his entire kingdom. The Bodhisatta said, “Great King, I have no need for the objects of sensual pleasure (vatthu-kāma) or the defilements of passion (kilesa-kāma). Indeed, I have renounced the world seeking the supreme Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa).” Although the King pleaded in various ways, he could not win over the Bodhisatta’s mind. He then said, “You will certainly become a Buddha. When you have become a Buddha, please come first to my kingdom,” and then he returned to the city.

“Then, when the noble King of Men had gone to the noble city of Rājagaha,
The noble King of Sages, who is like the noble King of Mountains,
The Sugata, who moves like the noble King of Lions, also departed.”
336:
The Great Being, who is like the King of Mountains, who is the King of Sages, who moves like the King of Lions, and whose destination is excellent like that of previous Bodhisattas, also departed (towards Rājagaha).

Then the Bodhisatta, wandering by stages, approached the ascetic Āḷāra Kālāma and Uddaka Rāmaputta, the son of Rāma. Having attained the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti), he realized, “This is not the path to the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship or Omniscience.” Not delighting in the cultivation of those attainments and wishing to strive in the great exertion (mahāpadhāna), he went to Uruvelā. Thinking, “This piece of ground is truly delightful,” he took up residence there and practiced the great exertion. The five people—the four sons of the brahmins who recognized the marks and the brahmin Koṇḍañña—who had renounced the world earlier, were wandering for alms in villages, market towns, and royal capitals when they reached the Bodhisatta in that place. Then, for six years while he was practicing the great exertion, they attended to him with major and minor duties such as sweeping the grounds, thinking, “Now he will become a Buddha, now he will become a Buddha,” and remained in his presence. The Bodhisatta also thought, “I will perform the most extreme austerities (dukkaracariyā),” and spent his time consuming only a single sesame seed or a single grain of rice. He eventually cut off all food entirely. Deities also injected divine essence (ojā) through his pores.

Then, due to that lack of food, his body became extremely emaciated; his golden-hued body became dark in color, and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man became hidden. Then, having reached the limit of austerities, the Bodhisatta reflected, “This austerity is not the path to the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship.” To consume solid food, he wandered for alms in villages and market towns and took nourishment. Then, his thirty-two marks of a Great Man reappeared as before, and his body became golden-hued again. When the group of five monks (Pañcavaggiya) saw him, they thought, “This Great Being could not realize Omniscience even while practicing austerities for six years. Now that he wanders for alms in villages, market towns, and royal capitals and consumes solid food, how will he be able to realize Omniscience? He has become luxurious and has turned away from the struggle. What use is he to us?” Thinking thus, they abandoned the Great Man and went to Isipatana in Vārāṇasī.

At that time, on the full moon day of Visākha, there was a young woman named Sujātā, born in the house of the householder Sena in the market town of Senāni in Uruvelā. After consuming the sweet milk-rice (madhupāyāsa) into which deities had infused divine essence, offered by the exceptionally devoted Sujātā, the Bodhisatta took the golden bowl and floated it upstream in the Nerañjarā River, thereby waking the sleeping Kāla, the Nāga King. Then, the Bodhisatta spent the day-rest in the delightful Sāla grove, which was adorned with fragrant flowers and had a dark-blue radiance, on the bank of the Nerañjarā River...
337:
In the evening, the Bodhisatta set out towards the Bodhi tree along a path decorated by the deities. Devas, Nāgas, Yakkhas, Siddhas, and others honored him with celestial flowers, scents, and ointments. At that time, a grass-cutter named Sotthiya, coming from the opposite direction with grass, recognized the signs of a Great Man and offered eight handfuls of grass. The Bodhisatta took the eight handfuls of grass and approached the foot of the victorious Assattha Bodhi tree, the king of trees, which stood resplendent among the groves of trees—resembling Mount Asitañjana, appearing like a net of sunbeams, cool with compassion like his own heart, providing cool shade, free from the gathering of various birds, adorned with thick branches swaying in the gentle breeze, appearing as if dancing with joy or being enamored. He circumambulated the Assattha tree three times and, standing on the northeastern side, held the tips of the eight handfuls of grass and shook them. At that very moment, a throne fourteen cubits in size appeared. The blades of grass appeared like lines drawn by a master painter. On that fourteen-cubit carpet of grass, the Bodhisatta sat cross-legged in a triple-jointed posture, resolving with fourfold energy. He sat with his back against the fifty-cubit trunk of the Bodhi tree, like a silver mass placed on a golden pedestal, while the branches of the Bodhi tree overspread him like a jeweled parasol from above. The shoots of the Bodhi tree falling upon his golden-colored robes shone like corals placed on a golden plate.

While the Bodhisatta was thus seated on the throne, the Māra Deva of the Vasavatti realm thought, "Prince Siddhattha wishes to transcend my domain; I will not allow him to transcend it now." He informed his army and set out. That Māra army extended twelve leagues in front of Māra, twelve leagues to the right and left, and behind it reached the edge of the universe. Upwards, it was nine leagues high. The roar of that shouting army was heard from ninety thousand leagues away, like the sound of the earth splitting. At that time, Sakka, the king of devas, stood blowing the conch named Vijayuttara. That conch was one hundred and twenty cubits long. The deva Pañcasikha stood playing the Beluva-paṇḍu lute, three gāvutas in length, singing auspicious songs. King Suyāma stood gently fanning with a celestial yak-tail fan, three gāvutas long, having the splendor of the moon in the autumn season. Brahma Sahampati stood holding a white parasol three leagues wide, like a second full moon. The Naga king Mahākāla stood praising and bowing to the Bodhisatta, surrounded by eighty thousand Naga dancers. In the ten thousand world-systems, all the deities stood honoring him with various celestial flower garlands, incense, and powders, uttering cries of "Sādhu!"

Then Māra mounted the noble elephant named Girimekhala, which was one hundred and fifty leagues high, resembling a snow-capped mountain peak, extremely beautiful to behold, adorned with jewels, and capable of repelling all enemies...
338:
Brahma Sahampati also stood holding the white parasol, three leagues wide and like a second full moon, over the Blessed One. The Naga king Mahākāla also stood bowing to the Bodhisatta, surrounded by eighty thousand Naga dancers, singing songs of praise and adoration. The deities of the ten thousand world-systems also stood honoring him with various fragrant flower garlands and scented powders, giving shouts of "Sādhu!"

Then Māra, mounting the noble elephant Girimekhala—one hundred and fifty leagues high, like a snow-capped peak, magnificent to behold, jewel-encrusted, and the repeller of enemies—created a thousand arms and seized various weapons. Māra's army also came, wielding swords, axes, arrows, spears, and other weapons; raising bows, pestles, plowshares, spikes, long spears, forks, stones, clubs, rings, iron spikes, destructive weapons, discs, arm-guards, and blades. They had faces like deer, lions, rhinoceroses, sambar deer, wild boars, tigers, monkeys, snakes, cats, and owls; others had faces like buffaloes, spotted deer, horses, and elephants. With various terrifying, distorted, and loathsome bodies, resembling humans, Yakkhas, and Pisācas, they surrounded the Bodhisatta seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree, overwhelming him and awaiting Māra's command.

As the Māra army approached the Bodhimaṇḍa, not a single one of the deities, including Sakka, could remain; they fled in all directions. Sakka, the king of devas, fled with the Vijayuttara conch on his back and stood at the edge of the universe. Mahābrahmā left the white parasol at the edge of the universe and returned to the Brahma realm. The Naga king Kāla abandoned all his dancers, dived into the earth, and went to the Mañjerika Naga realm, five hundred leagues away, where he lay down covering his face with his hands. Not a single deity was able to remain at the Bodhimaṇḍa. The Bodhisatta, the Great Man, sat alone like Mahābrahmā in an empty mansion. "Now Māra will come," and many undesirable and evil omens appeared beforehand.

At the time of the battle with the Friend of Negligence,
And during the time of the Friend of the Three Worlds,
Terrifying torches fell from all around,
And the quarters were shrouded in smoke and darkness.

The inanimate earth, as if it possessed volition, like a woman separated from her beloved husband, shaken by fierce winds, the earth with its various names, along with the ocean, trembled.
339:
This great earth, though insentient, trembled violently as if it were sentient, like a woman separated from her husband, or like a creeper struck by a strong wind; the earth, bearing various jewels along with the oceans, shook greatly.

The oceans had turbulent waves. The rivers flowed backwards, upwards. The peaks of the mountains, along with various groups of trees, broke and fell to the ground.

Harsh winds blew from all directions. A terrifying, tumultuous sound arose. The sunlight vanished, and a thick, dreadful darkness ensued. In the sky, headless forms (kabandha spirits) wandered about.

Such inauspicious, undesirable, and terrifying omens of many kinds, occurring in the sky and on the ground, appeared everywhere upon the arrival of Māra.

Seeing Māra, who wished to destroy the Buddha, the God of gods, the hosts of devas, moved by compassion, cried out "Alas, alas!" together with the celestial nymphs.

Later, they saw the numerous army of Māra, looking as if they had been thoroughly subdued, fleeing in all directions. They dropped and abandoned the weapons and sword-hilts from their hands.

Like a Garuḍa in the midst of birds, like a noble lion in the midst of deer, the Buddha of great fame sat boldly and without fear in the midst of Māra's army.
340:
Then Māra, thinking, "I will frighten Prince Siddhattha and make him flee," attempted to drive the Bodhisatta away with nine kinds of Māra's supernatural powers: the rain of wind, the rain of weapons, the rain of stones, and again the rain of glowing coals, the rain of hot ashes, the rain of sand, the rain of mud, and the rain of darkness. Failing to do so, with an angry mind, he commanded his followers, "Friends, why do you stand still? Make this Prince Siddhattha one who fails to achieve his goal; seize him, kill him, cut him, bind him, do not let him go, make him flee!" He himself sat upon the shoulder of the elephant Girimekhala, brandishing an arrow with one hand, and approached the Bodhisatta, saying, "O Siddhattha, rise from this seat!" The followers of Māra also inflicted most terrifying harassment upon the Great Being.

Then the Great Man (Mahāpurisa) spoke words such as, "O wicked Māra, when did you ever fulfill the perfections (pāramīs) for the sake of this seat?" and reached down his right hand toward the earth. At that very moment, the wind and water supporting the earth—which is one million leagues thick plus an additional fourteen thousand—first trembled, and thereafter this great earth, two million leagues thick plus an additional forty thousand, shook in six ways. In the sky above, thousands of streaks of lightning and thunderbolts struck. Then the elephant Girimekhala fell to its knees. Māra also fell from the back of the elephant Girimekhala to the ground. The followers of Māra scattered in all directions like a handful of chaff.

Then the Great Man, having conquered and destroyed Māra and his army through the power of his perfections such as patience (khanti), loving-kindness (mettā), energy (viriya), and wisdom (paññā), attained the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsanussati-ñāṇa) in the first watch of the night. In the middle watch, he purified the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). At dawn, he directed his knowledge into the law of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), which is the practice of all Buddhas. Having attained the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna) and using that very jhāna as a basis, he developed insight (vipassanā). Through the fourth path (arahatta-magga) attained in the sequence of the paths, he exhausted all defilements. Having realized all the qualities of a Buddha, he uttered the solemn utterance (udāna) practiced by all Buddhas:

Through many a birth in saṃsāra have I wandered, seeking but not finding the builder of this house.
Painful is birth again and again.
O house-builder, you are seen!
You shall not build the house again.
All your rafters are broken; the ridge-pole is shattered.
My mind has reached the unconditioned; I have attained the destruction of craving.

Thus he uttered the solemn utterance.
341:
## The Account of the Proximate Cause

After uttering the inspired utterance, the following thought occurred to the Blessed One as he sat: "For the sake of this throne, I have wandered for four incalculable periods and a hundred thousand aeons. This throne of mine is the Throne of Victory, the Auspicious Throne. As long as my resolve is not yet fulfilled while sitting upon this throne, I shall not rise from it." Thus thinking, he remained sitting there for seven days, entering into many hundreds of billions of meditative attainments. With reference to this sitting in meditative attainment, it was said: "Then the Blessed One sat for seven days in a single cross-legged posture, experiencing the bliss of liberation."

Then, a doubt arose in the minds of some deities: "Does Prince Siddhattha still have some task to perform even today? For he does not yet relinquish his attachment to the throne." Then the Teacher, knowing the thought of the deities, rose into the air to calm their thoughts and displayed the Twin Miracle. Having thus calmed the thoughts of the deities with this miracle, he stood at a spot slightly to the north, leaning towards the east from the throne, and spent seven days gazing with unblinking eyes at both the throne—the place where he attained the fruit of the perfections fulfilled for four incalculable periods and a hundred thousand aeons—and the Bodhi tree, thinking, "Indeed, upon this throne, I have realized Omniscient Wisdom." That place became known as the Animisa Cetiya.

Then, having created a walkway between the throne and the place where he had stood, he spent seven days walking to and fro on the Jeweled Walkway, which was long from east to west. That place became known as the Ratana-caṅkama Cetiya.

In the fourth week, the deities created a Jeweled House in the northwest of the Bodhi tree. Sitting there in a cross-legged posture, he spent seven days contemplating the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. That place became known as the Ratana-ghara Cetiya.

In this way, the Blessed One spent four weeks in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree, and in the fifth week, he proceeded from the foot of the Bodhi tree to the Ajapāla Banyan tree. There also, he sat contemplating the Dhamma and experiencing the bliss of liberation.

The Teacher spent seven days there and then went to the foot of the Mucalinda tree. There, when a rainstorm lasted for seven days, the Naga King Mucalinda encircled him with seven coils to ward off the cold and other elements, and the Blessed One stayed as if he were dwelling in a spacious perfumed chamber...
342:
...experiencing the bliss of liberation. After spending seven days there, he proceeded to the foot of the Rājāyatana tree. There also, he sat for seven days experiencing the bliss of liberation. By this time, the seven weeks (forty-nine days) were complete. During these seven weeks, the Blessed One did not wash his face, attend to his body, or partake of food; he spent the time solely with the bliss of fruition. Then, at the end of the seven weeks, on the forty-ninth day, he washed his face with the Nāgalatā tooth-stick and water from Lake Anotatta, which were offered by Sakka, the King of Devas, and sat at the foot of that same Rājāyatana tree.

At that time, two merchant brothers named Tapussa and Bhallika, encouraged by a deity who was their relative, wished to offer food to the Blessed One. They brought parched corn and honey balls, approached the Teacher, and stood there, saying, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept this food out of compassion for us." Since the bowl offered by the deities had disappeared on the very day he accepted the milk-rice, the Blessed One thought, "Buddhas do not receive food in their hands. In what shall I receive this food?" Then, knowing the Blessed One's intention, the Four Great Kings from the four quarters offered four bowls made of sapphire. The Blessed One rejected them. Again, they offered four stone bowls the color of mung beans. Out of compassion for those four young deities, the Blessed One accepted them and resolved that the four bowls should become one. He then received the food in that newly formed stone bowl, partook of it, and gave a blessing of appreciation. Those two merchant brothers took refuge in the Buddha and the Dhamma, becoming lay followers of the two-fold word (dvevācika upāsaka).

Thereafter, the Teacher returned to the Ajapāla Banyan tree and sat at its foot. While sitting there, as he contemplated the profundity of the Dhamma he had realized, a thought arose in him, as is the custom of all Buddhas: "This Dhamma I have realized is indeed..." and so forth, leading to a state of reluctance to teach the Dhamma to others. Then, Brahma Sahampati, thinking, "Alas, the world is perishing! Alas, the world is utterly perishing!" brought Sakka, Suyama, Santusita, Nimmanarati, and Paranimmita-vasavatti devas, along with the Great Brahmas from ten thousand world systems, and approached the Teacher, entreating him to teach the Dhamma, saying, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One preach the Dhamma," and so forth.
343:
Then the Blessed One, having given his assent to Brahma Sahampati, thought, "To whom should I first preach the Dhamma?" Knowing that the ascetics Āḷāra and Uddaka had passed away, he reflected on the group of five monks, thinking, "The group of five monks were very helpful to me." While considering where they were currently staying, he knew, "They are staying at the Deer Park in Isipatana near Bārāṇasī." Thinking, "I will go there and set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion," he stayed for two or three days near the vicinity of the Bodhi tree wandering for alms, and then on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, thinking "I will go to Bārāṇasī," he took his bowl and robes and set out on the journey of eighteen yojanas. On the way, he saw an Ājīvaka named Upaka who was in a joyful state, and having informed him of his Buddhahood, he arrived at the Isipatana forest on the evening of that very day.

The group of five monks saw the Tathāgata coming from afar and made a pact: "Friends, this ascetic Gotama is coming; he has returned to a life of abundance, is full-bodied, with radiant faculties and a golden complexion. Let us not perform acts of respect such as bowing to him; let us merely prepare a seat for him." The Blessed One, knowing their thoughts, concentrated his mind of loving-kindness (mettā) which is capable of pervading all beings without limit, and then pervaded them with a specific mind of loving-kindness. Touched by the Blessed One's loving-kindness, those five monks were unable to stick to their pact when the Tathāgata approached, and they performed all duties such as bowing. The detailed account should be understood as stated in the Vinaya Mahāvagga and other texts.

Then the Blessed One, having informed them of his Buddhahood, sat on the noble Buddha-seat that had been prepared. While the moon was in conjunction with the constellation of Uttara-āsāḷha, surrounded by eighteen crores of Brahmas, he addressed the elders of the group of five and preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta. Among them, the Elder Aññāsi Koṇḍañña, directing his wisdom according to the teaching, was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) along with eighteen crores of Brahmas at the end of the discourse. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"I am now the Fully Enlightened One, Gotama, the nourisher of the Sakyans;
Having exerted effort in striving, I have attained the supreme Enlightenment.
Requested by the Brahma, I set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion;
There was the first realization of the Truths for eighteen crores [of devas and brahmas]."
344:
In these verses, 'ahaṃ' refers to himself. 'Etarahi' means at this time. 'Sakyavaḍḍhana' means one who increases the lineage of the Sakyans. There is also a reading 'Sakyapuṅgava'. 'Padhāna' refers to effort (vīriya). 'Padahitvāna' means having striven or having performed difficult practices. 'Aṭṭhārasannaṃ koṭīnaṃ' means that during the preaching of the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta at the Isipatana Deer Park in Bārāṇasī, there was the first realization of the Four Noble Truths by eighteen crores of Brahmas, led by the Elder Aññāsi Koṇḍañña.

Now, the Blessed One, after speaking of the past, wishing to speak of the realization that will occur in the future, said the following verse:

## “Tato parañca desente, naradevasamāgame,
## Gaṇanāya na vattabbo, dutiyābhisamayo ahū”ti.

In that verse, 'naradevasamāgame' means that on another occasion, at the assembly for the preaching of the Mahāmaṅgala Sutta, among the devas and humans from ten thousand universes, at the conclusion of the Maṅgala Sutta, there will be the second realization of the truths by an uncountable number of humans and devas. Although the future tense should be used, the past tense 'ahū' is used because it follows the sequence of events or due to a shift in tense. This method also applies to similar expressions hereafter. Furthermore, when the Rāhulovāda Sutta was preached, he made uncountable beings drink the nectar of the Dhamma. This is the third realization of the truths. Therefore, he said:

## “Idhevāhaṃ etarahi, ovadiṃ mama atrajaṃ,
## Gaṇanāya na vattabbo, tatiyābhisamayo ahū”ti.

For the Blessed One, there was only one assembly of disciples. There was an assembly of one thousand former matted-hair ascetics, such as Uruvela Kassapa and others, and two hundred and fifty disciples of the two chief disciples; thus, there was an assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty monks. Therefore, he said:

## “Ekosi sannipāto me, sāvakānaṃ mahesinaṃ,
## Aḍḍhateḷasasatānaṃ, bhikkhūnāsi samāgamo”ti.

In that verse, 'ekosi' means there was only one. 'Aḍḍhateḷasasatānaṃ' means there was an assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty of my disciple monks.
345:
(It) happened only once. Having reached the midst of those monks, the Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha in an assembly endowed with four factors.

Then, the Blessed One, wishing to show the account of his own life, said:
“Shining and stainless, in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, I give all that is desired, like a wish-fulfilling gem that grants all wants.”

In that verse, ‘Virocamāno’ means shining with the infinite glory of a Buddha. ‘Vimalo’ means being free from the stains of defilements such as lust. ‘Maṇīva sabbakāmado’ means that like the Cīntāmaṇi gem which can grant whatever is desired, I also give all the specific worldly and supramundane happiness that is wished for and yearned for.

Now, wishing to show the aspiration for what is desired, he said:
“To those desiring the fruit, seeking to abandon the desire for existence, I proclaim the Four Truths out of compassion for beings.”

In that verse, ‘Phalaṃ’ means the fourfold fruit, such as the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). ‘Bhavacchandajahasinaṃ’ means those who have abandoned the craving for existence, or those who wish to abandon the craving for existence. ‘Anukampāya’ means out of compassion.

Now, wishing to show the realization (abhisamaya) in the proclamation of the Four Truths, he said “Dasavīsatasahassānaṃ” and so on.

Therein, ‘Dasavīsatasahassānaṃ’ means the realization of the Dhamma by ten thousand and twenty thousand (totaling thirty thousand) beings. The ninth and tenth verses have clear meanings.

11-12. In the eleventh and twelfth verses, both terms ‘idāni’ and ‘etarahi’ have the same meaning; they are spoken like the terms for persons (purisapuggala) by way of those to be led (veneyya). 23-24. Those incomparable powers, these ten strengths, and this body, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and bearing noble qualities, and the six-colored rays that illuminate the ten directions like the sun—all these shall disappear and perish. Are not all conditioned things (saṅkhāra) indeed empty?

'Tāni ca atulatejāni' refers to those incomparable powers, such as those of the pair of chief disciples and others. 'Imāni ca dasabalāni' refers to these ten physical strengths of the body. 'Guṇadhāraṇo deho' refers to this body which bears qualities such as the six unique knowledges (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa). 'Tamantarahissanti' means all these aforementioned things will disappear and perish. In the phrase 'Nanu rittā sabbasaṅkhārā', the word 'nanu' is a particle (nipāta) used in the sense of agreement. 'Rittā' means empty, because they are devoid of any permanent or stable essence. All conditioned things (saṅkhata) are impermanent (anicca) because they have the nature of exhaustion, decay, fading away, and cessation, and thus lack existence. They are suffering (dukkha) because they are oppressed by arising and so on. They are non-self (anattā) because they are not subject to one's will. Therefore, having applied the three characteristics to conditioned things and developed insight (vipassanā), reach Nibbāna, which is deathless, unconditioned, and unchanging. This is our advice to you; this is our teaching. Fulfill it with diligence (appamāda). At the conclusion of the teaching, it is said that the minds of a hundred thousand crores of deities were liberated from the taints (āsava) without clinging and became Arahats. Those who were established in the remaining paths and fruits were beyond counting.

Thus, the Blessed One, while walking on the jeweled walkway in the sky, recounted the entire Chronicle of Buddhas (Buddhavamsa) defined by aeons, names, and lineages. Having caused his relatives to pay homage, he descended from the sky and sat on the noble Buddha-seat prepared for him. While the Blessed One, the Protector of the World, was thus seated, there was a gathering of relatives that reached its peak. All the relatives sat with one-pointed minds. Then, the great Pokkharavassa rain fell. At that moment, the waters flowed down with a roar. It moistened only those who wished to be moistened. Not a single drop of rain fell on the bodies of those who did not wish to be moistened. Seeing that wonder, all the relatives, with minds full of amazement and praise, exclaimed, "Oh, how wonderful! Oh, how extraordinary!" Hearing those words, the Blessed One said, "The Pokkharavassa rain does not fall on the gathering of my relatives only now; it has fallen in the past as well," and on account of this occurrence, he preached the Vessantara Jātaka. That Dhamma teaching was of great benefit to the multitude of people. Then, the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered the monastery.

Thus, in this order, the Commentary on the Buddhavamsa named Madhuratthavilāsinī is completed.
