## Vemattakathā
In this entire Buddhavamsa, the eight kinds of differences (vematta) among the twenty-five Buddhas mentioned should be understood. What are the eight? They are: difference in lifespan, difference in stature, difference in clan, difference in exertion, difference in radiance, difference in vehicle, difference in Bodhi tree, and difference in throne.

Among those eight, the difference in lifespan (āyuvematta) means that some Buddhas have long lives and some have short lives. This is true; to elaborate—these nine Buddhas: Dīpaṅkara, Koṇḍañña, Anomadassī, Paduma, Padumuttara, Atthadassī, Dhammadassī, Siddhattha, and Tissa, had a lifespan of one hundred thousand years. Maṅgala, Sumana, Sobhita...
349:
The eight Buddhas, namely Nārada, Sumedha, Sujāta, Piyadassī, and Phussa, had a lifespan of ninety thousand years. The two Buddhas, Revata and Vessabhū, had a lifespan of sixty thousand years. The Blessed One Vipassī had a lifespan of eighty thousand years. The four Buddhas, Sikhī, Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa, had lifespans of seventy thousand, forty thousand, thirty thousand, and twenty thousand years respectively. The lifespan of our Blessed One, however, was one hundred years. Even for the Buddhas who have accumulated the requisites of merit and are endowed with kamma conducive to longevity, their lifespan varies according to the era (yuga). This is known as the variation in lifespan (āyuvematta) among the twenty-five Buddhas.

Variation in stature (pamāṇavematta) means that some Buddhas are tall and some are short. To elaborate: the height of the Buddhas Dīpaṅkara, Revata, Piyadassī, Atthadassī, Dhammadassī, and Vipassī was eighty cubits. The height of the Buddhas Koṇḍañña, Maṅgala, Nārada, and Sumedha was eighty-eight cubits. The height of the Buddha Sumana was ninety cubits. The height of the Buddhas Sobhita, Anomadassī, Paduma, Padumuttara, and Phussa was fifty-eight cubits. The Buddha Sujāta had a height of fifty cubits. The Buddhas Siddhattha, Tissa, and Vessabhū were sixty cubits in height. The Blessed One Sikhī was seventy cubits in height. The Buddhas Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa were forty, thirty, and twenty cubits in height respectively. Our Blessed One was eighteen cubits in height. This is known as the variation in stature (pamāṇavematta) among the twenty-five Buddhas.

Variation in lineage (kulavematta) means that some Buddhas were born into the warrior-noble (Khattiya) caste, while others were born into the brahmin (Brāhmaṇa) caste. This is true: the Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa were born into the brahmin caste. The twenty-two Buddhas from Dīpaṅkara to Gotama were born only into the warrior-noble caste. This is known as the variation in lineage (kulavematta) among the twenty-five Buddhas.

Variation in exertion (padhānavematta), [referring to] the practice of austerities (dukkaracariyā), means that the Buddhas Dīpaṅkara, Koṇḍañña, Sumana, Anomadassī, Sujāta, Siddhattha, and Kakusandha practiced austerities for ten months. The Buddhas Maṅgala, Sumedha, Tissa, and Sikhī practiced for eight months. The Buddha Revata practiced for seven months. The Buddha Sobhita practiced for four months. The Buddhas Paduma, Atthadassī, and Vipassī practiced for half a month (fifteen days). The Buddhas Nārada, Padumuttara, Dhammadassī, and Kassapa practiced for seven days. The Buddhas Piyadassī, Phussa, Vessabhū, and Koṇāgamana practiced for six months. Our Buddha practiced austerities for six years. This is known as the variation in exertion (padhānavematta).

Variation in radiance (rasmivematta) means that the bodily radiance of the Blessed One named Maṅgala spread and remained throughout ten thousand world systems. The radiance of the Buddha Padumuttara extended for twelve yojanas. The radiance of the Blessed One Vipassī extended for seven yojanas. The radiance of the Buddha Sikhī was three yojanas in extent. The radiance of the Buddha Kakusandha was ten yojanas in extent. For our Blessed One, [the radiance] from all around...
350:
The difference in the extent of body radiance (rasmi-vematta): It is said that the body radiance of Maṅgala Buddha spread throughout and remained in ten thousand world systems. The body radiance of Padumuttara Buddha was 12 yojanas. The body radiance of Vipassī Buddha was 7 yojanas. The body radiance of Sikhī Buddha was 3 yojanas in extent. The body radiance of Kakusandha Buddha was 10 yojanas. The body radiance of our Buddha (Gotama) was about one fathom (byāma) all around. The radiance of the remaining Buddhas was not fixed. This difference in body radiance is connected to their personal inclination (ajjhāsaya). Whatever extent a Buddha desired, his body radiance would spread to that extent. However, regarding the qualities of the Buddha (guṇa) realized through penetration, there is no difference among them. This is called the difference in body radiance (rasmi-vematta).

The difference in vehicles (yāna-vematta): Some Bodhisattas depart on their renunciation by an elephant vehicle, some by a horse vehicle, and others by one of the vehicles such as a chariot, on foot, a palace, or a palanquin. To explain this: Dīpaṅkara, Sumana, Sumedha, Phussa, Sikhī, and Koṇāgamana Buddhas departed by elephant vehicle. Koṇḍañña, Revata, Paduma, Piyadassī, Vipassī, and Kakusandha Buddhas departed by chariot. Maṅgala, Sujāta, Atthadassī, Tissa, and Gotama Buddhas departed by horse vehicle. Anomadassī, Siddhattha, and Vessabhū Buddhas departed by palanquin (sivikā). Nārada Buddha departed on foot. Sobhita, Padumuttara, Dhammadassī, and Kassapa Buddhas departed by palace (pāsāda). This is called the difference in vehicles (yāna-vematta).

The difference in Bodhi trees (bodhi-vematta): The Bodhi tree of Dīpaṅkara Buddha was the Kapītana tree (or Sirīsa). The Bodhi tree of Koṇḍañña Buddha was the Sālakalyāṇi tree. The Bodhi tree of Maṅgala, Sumana, Revata, and Sobhita Buddhas was the Nāga (Ironwood) tree. The Bodhi tree of Anomadassī Buddha was the Ajjuna tree. The Bodhi tree of Paduma and Nārada Buddhas was the Mahāsoṇa tree. The Bodhi tree of Padumuttara Buddha was the Salala (Pine) tree. The Bodhi tree of Sumedha Buddha was the Nīpa (or Kadamba) tree. The Bodhi tree of Sujāta Buddha was the Veḷu (Bamboo) tree. The Bodhi tree of Piyadassī Buddha was the Kakudha tree. The Bodhi tree of Atthadassī Buddha was the Campaka tree. The Bodhi tree of Dhammadassī Buddha was the Rattakuravaka tree. The Bodhi tree of Siddhattha Buddha was the Kaṇikāra tree. The Bodhi tree of Tissa Buddha was the Asana tree. The Bodhi tree of Phussa Buddha was the Āmalaka (Myrobalan) tree. The Bodhi tree of Vipassī Buddha was the Pāṭali tree. The Bodhi tree of Sikhī Buddha was the Puṇḍarīka (White Mango) tree. The Bodhi tree of Vessabhū Buddha was the Sāla tree. The Bodhi tree of Kakusandha Buddha was the Sirīsa tree. The Bodhi tree of Koṇāgamana Buddha was the Udumbara (Cluster fig) tree. The Bodhi tree of Kassapa Buddha was the Nigrodha (Banyan) tree. The Bodhi tree of Gotama Buddha was the Assattha (Sacred fig) tree. This is called the difference in Bodhi trees (bodhi-vematta).

The difference in the size of the throne (pallaṅka-vematta): The thrones of Dīpaṅkara, Revata, Piyadassī, Atthadassī, Dhammadassī, and Vipassī Buddhas were 53 cubits. The thrones of Koṇḍañña, Maṅgala, Nārada, and Sumedha Buddhas were 57 cubits. The throne of Sumana Buddha was 60 cubits. The thrones of Sobhita, Anomadassī, Paduma, Padumuttara, and Phussa Buddhas were 38 cubits. The throne of Sujāta Buddha was 32 cubits. The thrones of Siddhattha, Tissa, and Vessabhū Buddhas were 40 cubits. The throne of Sikhī Buddha...
351:
(The throne of Sikhī Buddha) was 32 cubits, the throne of Kakusandha Buddha was 26 cubits, the throne of Koṇāgamana Buddha was 20 cubits, the throne of Kassapa Buddha was 15 cubits, and the throne of Gotama Buddha was 14 cubits. This is called the difference in thrones (pallaṅka-vematta). These eight kinds of differences are known as 'vematta'.

## Discussion on the Unchanging Places (Avijahitaṭṭhāna-kathā)
There are four unchanging places (avijahitaṭṭhāna) for all Buddhas. The Bodhi-throne (Bodhipallaṅka) of all Buddhas is in the exact same place. The place where the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka) is turned in the Isipatana Migadāya wood is also unchanging. The place where the feet first touch the ground at the gate of Saṅkassa city during the descent from the celestial realm (Devorohaṇa) is also unchanging. The places where the four legs of the bed are set in the Gandhakuti of Jetavana are also unchanging. The monastery itself may be small or large; while the monastery location is not forsaken, the city may be.

## Discussion on Co-natals and Constellations (Sahajāta-pariccheda-nakkhatta-pariccheda-kathā)
Furthermore, the divisions of co-natals (sahajāta) and constellations (nakkhatta) of our Buddha shall be shown. Along with our Omniscient Bodhisatta, these seven were born simultaneously: the mother of Rāhula, Ānanda Thera, Channa the Minister, Kaṇṭhaka the King of Horses, the four great treasure jars (nidhikumbha), the Great Bodhi tree, and Kāḷudāyī the Minister. This is the division of co-natals.

The Bodhisatta, as a Great Man (Mahāpurisa), entered his mother's womb, renounced the world, turned the Wheel of Dhamma, and performed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya) under the constellation of Uttarāsāḷha. He was born, attained supreme enlightenment, and entered Parinibbāna under the constellation of Visākha. The assembly of his disciples and the relinquishing of his life-principle (āyu-saṅkhāra-vossajjana) occurred under the constellation of Māgha. The descent from the celestial realm occurred under the constellation of Assayuza. This is the division of constellations.

## Discussion on Common Characteristics (Sadhammatā-kathā)
Now, we shall declare the common characteristics (sadhammatā) of all Buddhas. There are thirty kinds of common characteristics for all Buddhas. They are: In his final existence, the Bodhisatta enters his mother's womb with full awareness; he sits cross-legged in the mother's womb facing outward; the Bodhisatta's mother gives birth while standing; the birth occurs only in a forest; immediately after emerging from the mother's womb, he stands on golden plates, walks seven steps toward the north, surveys the four directions, and utters a bold speech (sīhanāda); the Bodhisattas renounce the world only after seeing the four omens and when a son is born; they practice asceticism (dukkharacariyā) for at least seven days after ordaining and donning the robes which are the banner of the Arahants; they partake of milk-rice on the day of attaining Buddhahood; they attain omniscience while sitting on a mat of grass; they practice the meditation on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati); they conquer the army of Māra; they realize the three knowledges (vijjā) and unique qualities such as the uncommon knowledges (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa) at the Bodhi-throne; they spend the seven weeks (sattasattāha) only in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree; and they are requested by Mahābrahmā to teach the Dhamma.
352:
Walking seven steps facing the north, looking in the four directions and uttering a lion's roar; the Great Beings (Mahāsattas) going forth into homelessness just after the birth of their sons upon seeing the four omens; taking the robe which is the banner of the Arahants and renouncing, then practicing asceticism (dukkharacariyā) for at least seven days; partaking of milk-rice on the day of attaining Enlightenment (Sambodhi); attaining omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) while sitting on a grass mat; practicing the meditation on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati); defeating the forces of Māra; attaining the three knowledges (vijjā) and extraordinary qualities such as the unique knowledges (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa) at the very seat of Enlightenment (Bodhi-pallaṅka); spending seven weeks (49 days) in the very vicinity of the Bodhi tree; being requested by the Great Brahmā to teach the Dhamma; turning the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta) in the Deer Park at Isipatana; reciting the Pātimokkha at the assembly endowed with four factors on the full moon day of Māgha; residing regularly at the Jetavana monastery; performing the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya) at the gate of the city of Sāvatthī; teaching the Abhidhamma in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven; descending from the deva world at the gate of the city of Saṅkassa; constantly entering the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti); surveying the world for beings to be guided twice a day; prescribing training rules (sikkhāpada) when an occasion arises; relating Jātaka stories when appropriate circumstances occur; teaching the Buddhavamsa at the assembly of kinsmen; exchanging friendly greetings with visiting monks; not departing without taking leave of the hosts who invited them for the rains retreat; performing the duties of the pre-meal, post-meal, first watch, middle watch, and last watch every day; partaking of the meat-flavored meal (maṃsarasa-bhojana) on the day of Parinibbāna; and attaining Parinibbāna after entering 2.4 trillion attainments (samāpatti)—these thirty points are the natural custom (dhammatā) of all Buddhas.

## Anantarāyika-dhamma-kathā
There are four things that cannot be obstructed for all Buddhas. What are the four? No one can obstruct the four requisites brought and offered specifically for the Buddhas. No one can obstruct the lifespan of the Buddhas. For it has been said: "It is impossible, monks, it cannot happen that one could deprive the Tathāgata of life by means of an attack" (Cūḷavagga). No one can obstruct the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisa-lakkhaṇa) and the eighty minor characteristics (anubyañjana) of the Buddhas. No one can obstruct the rays of the Buddhas. These four are called the Anantarāyika-dhamma (unobstructable things).

353:
## Nigamana-kathā
To this extent, the commentary on the Buddhavamsa-pāḷi, which is beautiful with various methods known through excellent syllables and words, and with a sequence of sounds and meanings, has reached completion.

I have composed this commentary on the Buddhavamsa by following the path of the ancient commentary that explains the meaning of the Buddhavamsa-pāḷi.

Because it thoroughly and well explains the sweet, excellent, and pleasant meanings, avoiding excessive elaborations, I have named and composed this commentary on the Buddhavamsa as 'Madhuratthappakāsinī'.

In the city of Kāvirapaṭṭana, a seaport city which is pleasant and bustling with various groups of people, where the ground is purified by the overflowing waters of the Kāverī river; in that monastery built by the virtuous donor named Kaṇhadāsa, who possesses gentle speech—a monastery endowed with various beautiful walls and gates, filled with shade and water, delightful to behold and pleasing to the heart, free from the disturbance of wicked people, and peaceful and auspicious with the three kinds of seclusion (viveka)—there, in the extremely cool upper floor of the Eastern Mansion (Pācīna-pāsāda), I, Buddhadatta, residing there, have composed this commentary explaining the meaning of the Buddhavamsa-pāḷi.

Just as this commentary explaining the Buddhavamsa-pāḷi has reached successful completion without any obstacles, likewise, may all the righteous thoughts of good people reach completion without any obstacles.

By the merit that has arisen from my composing this commentary on the Buddhavamsa, may the world always reach the ultimate peace, the absolute truth of Nibbāna, through the power of that merit and the devas.
354:
May all diseases among humans vanish; may the devas also rain at the proper time during the rainy season. May even the denizens of hell always possess excellent happiness; may the hungry ghosts (pisācas/petas) be free from thirst.

May the devas, together with the hosts of celestial nymphs and others, long enjoy celestial happiness in the deva world. May the Dhamma of the Lord of Munis (the Buddha) long endure in the world. May the world-protecting deities (Lokapālas) happily protect the earth.

The Elder renowned as Buddhadatta, by the name given by his venerable teachers, composed this commentary named Madhuratthavilāsinī.

Having left behind this commentary, which brings benefit to successive generations, he has, alas, passed into the power of Death due to the nature of not enduring for long.

Thus, by way of recitations (bhāṇavāra), there are twenty-six recitations; by way of text units (gantha), there are six thousand five hundred; and by way of syllables (akkhara), there are two hundred and three thousand.

Just as this commentary has reached completion without any obstacles, so may the noble intentions of beings associated with the Dhamma be fulfilled.

## Thus the Madhuratthavilāsinī,
## the Commentary on the Buddhavaṃsa, is finished.
